collections.label: Psychology of Command, Fear and Aftermath

entries.name: The Combat Novel
entries.description: Fiction whose central business is the phenomenology of fighting — what organised violence does to perception, time, the body and the possibility of meaning.
entries.principle: The combat novel's whole difficulty is the legibility trade. Fighting as experienced is fragmentary, sensorily overloaded, largely invisible to the people inside it and mostly boring; narrative is ordered, compressed and clear. Every sentence buys clarity with falsification or fidelity with incomprehension, and the clarifying sentence is also the exciting one.
entries.example: Stephen Crane's The Red Badge of Courage (1895) renders a battle no character can see whole; Gert Ledig's Die Stalinorgel (1955) refuses coherence so completely that the reader is denied a vantage; Karl Marlantes's Matterhorn (2010) sustains procedural clarity and then charges for it.
entries.application: Decide before drafting where on the legibility trade the book sits, and hold that position — the failure is not choosing clarity or chaos but drifting toward clarity scene by scene because it reads better.

entries.name: The Command Novel
entries.description: Fiction whose central subject is the decision that spends lives — its information, its time horizon, its irreversibility, and the person carrying it.
entries.principle: A commander is a character defined by what they cannot see, and the novelist knows everything. Every scene decides whether to grant the reader knowledge the commander lacks, and that choice is the book's verdict — dramatic irony indicts, restriction exonerates. Command is also the one war role whose interiority is structurally unspeakable to anyone present in the scene.
entries.example: C. S. Forester's The General (1936) holds its protagonist inside his own limitations without editorial rescue; Michael Shaara's The Killer Angels (1974) narrates a documented battle from both commands; Herman Wouk's The Caine Mutiny (1951) puts the reader in the position of judging a decision made without the information the reader has.
entries.application: Fix the commander's information horizon explicitly, scene by scene, and never let a sentence give him a fact he could not have had — the moment he knows what the reader knows, the book has stopped being about command.

entries.name: The Small-Unit Novel
entries.description: Fiction in which the squad, platoon, crew or company is the unit of character, and the group's cohesion and dissolution is the plot.
entries.principle: The form runs on an ensemble ledger — a dozen named people with equal claim on the reader and unequal narrative time — and its oldest cheat is the cross-section platoon, one of each background, which converts characters into a demographic argument. Its deepest trap is the unit-as-family whose losses purchase something, which is glorification with a human face.
entries.example: Norman Mailer's The Naked and the Dead (1948) and James Jones's The Thin Red Line (1962) distribute attention across a company without resolving it into a lesson; Gustav Hasford's The Short-Timers (1979) refuses the consolation of cohesion; Tim O'Brien's The Things They Carried (1990) makes the ledger itself the subject.
entries.application: Audit what each death is made to buy. If a loss purchases growth, unity or meaning for the survivors, the book has closed the gap — and the fix is usually to let the death be structurally wasted, as most were.

entries.name: The Sealed-Crew Novel
entries.description: Fiction in which a small crew inside a single machine — submarine, bomber, tank — is the entire narrative world, and the machine's integrity is the plot.
entries.principle: Enclosure supplies the form's method: no horizon, no visual field, sound as the only channel, the enemy present solely as an instrument reading. Its gift is that it cannot glorify by spectacle, because there is nothing to see. Its trap is claustrophobia rendered as thrill, and deaths handled as a machine failure rather than as deaths.
entries.example: Lothar-Günther Buchheim's Das Boot (1973) makes waiting and sound the substance; Len Deighton's Bomber (1970) puts the reader in the aircraft and under it in the same raid; Sven Hassel's Panzer sequence, from Legion of the Damned (1953), is the tradition's disputed-provenance case and its clearest instance of enclosure sold as sensation.
entries.application: Build the crew's sensory world from instruments and sound before writing a single external description, then keep the external view out entirely — the moment the narration leaves the hull, the form's only real advantage is gone.

entries.name: The Naval Novel and the Fighting Ship
entries.description: Fiction in which the ship is the world, the sea an adversary equal to the enemy, and the naval hierarchy the moral system.
entries.principle: The tradition's pleasure is competence rendered in technical language, and that is precisely the mechanism by which war becomes enjoyable — the reader is placed at the working end of a system that is functioning. Age-of-sail adds a distance problem: a war far enough away to be safely delightful.
entries.example: Patrick O'Brian's Master and Commander (1969) delivers seamanship so exact it functions as characterisation; Nicholas Monsarrat's The Cruel Sea (1951) keeps the technical pleasure and charges for it in attrition; C. S. Forester's The Happy Return (1937) establishes the command-and-competence template the tradition still runs on.
entries.application: Grant the reader the pleasure of competence, then make the book pay for it — the fighting ship that never produces a cost the technical prose cannot absorb has argued that war is a craft rather than a killing.

entries.name: The Air-War Novel
entries.description: Fiction of combat conducted at range, at speed, and against people the fighter cannot see.
entries.principle: Air war is the range problem in its extreme form, and the bomber crew is the genre's cleanest laboratory for moral distance: total lethality, no contact, and crew mortality high enough that the aircrew are simultaneously killers and among the war's most likely dead. A book that renders only one of those two facts has taken a side without arguing for it.
entries.example: Len Deighton's Bomber (1970) narrates a single raid from the aircraft and from the German village beneath it; Joseph Heller's Catch-22 (1961) makes the mission count the entire moral architecture; James Salter's The Hunters (1956) renders air combat as a competitive pleasure and lets the reader feel how easily it becomes one.
entries.application: If the book contains a bombing run, decide whether the ground under it will be interiorised at any point in the novel — and if not, know that the omission is the book's argument, not an absence of one.

entries.name: The Counterinsurgency and Small-Wars Novel
entries.description: Fiction of war without fronts, against an enemy indistinguishable from the population, where the mission's own logic is the antagonist.
entries.principle: The form's structural problem is that counterinsurgency has no battles, so shape must be found in patrols that produce nothing. Its ethical problem is the un-narratable enemy: an insurgent with no interiority makes the population scenery, and an insurgent with too much produces a false symmetry that flatters the reader rather than implicating him.
entries.example: Graham Greene's The Quiet American (1955) puts the mission's logic on trial through a narrator implicated in it; Jean Lartéguy's Les Centurions (1960) argues the practitioners' case and lets the reader see what accepting it costs; Kevin Powers's The Yellow Birds (2012) finds its shape in repetition and aftermath rather than engagement.
entries.application: Write the patrol that produces nothing and keep it — the temptation to insert a contact for structural relief is the point at which a counterinsurgency novel becomes a combat novel wearing the wrong clothes.

entries.name: The Civil-War Novel
entries.description: Fiction of war inside one society, where the enemy is a neighbour and no settlement returns anyone to before.
entries.principle: International war offers a nation to address; civil war offers only the other half of the readership. Every civil-war novel is read inside its own dispute, frequently by survivors of both sides, which makes it the sharpest available form of the question of what a book owes the people it happened to.
entries.example: Ernest Hemingway's For Whom the Bell Tolls (1940) stages atrocity committed by the side the book is sympathetic to; Elias Khoury's Bāb al-Shams (1998) builds its structure out of the impossibility of a single account; Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie's Half of a Yellow Sun (2006) carries the war through intimate lives without resolving the political dispute for the reader.
entries.application: Identify who is still alive to read the book on each side before drafting, and test every scene of atrocity for whether it would be recognised as fair by a survivor of the side that committed it.

entries.name: The Siege Novel
entries.description: Fiction of an enclosed population under sustained attack, in which combatant and civilian pressures become the same pressure.
entries.principle: The siege novel's unit of description is the diminishing resource, and its clock runs on shrinking world and expanding time. Its characteristic failure is the atrocity ledger — escalating deprivation for effect — and because each escalation is individually defensible as accuracy, this is where representation becomes consumption most easily and least visibly.
entries.example: Ismail Kadare's Kështjella (1970) narrates a siege from the besieging side's bureaucracy; Vasily Grossman's Жизнь и судьба, completed by 1959 and published in Switzerland in 1980, holds Stalingrad's military and civilian pressures in one structure; Priscilla Morris's Black Butterflies (2022) keeps a besieged city at the scale of one life.
entries.application: Set the floor of deprivation early and refuse to lower it for effect later — if the book's second half is more harrowing than its first only because the writer needed the escalation, the escalation is the reader's, not the siege's.

entries.name: The Home-Front Novel
entries.description: Fiction in which the condition of being at war is lived by people who are not fighting, and that condition is the book's central pressure.
entries.principle: The form must generate stakes from pressure without event — waiting, rationing, the telegram that has not come, the specific temporality of not knowing — and it fails the moment it imports a combat scene to bail itself out. Nothing happens to the protagonist and the war is still the whole weather.
entries.example: Elizabeth Bowen's The Heat of the Day (1948) makes wartime London a condition of consciousness rather than a backdrop; Henry Green's Caught (1943) finds its material in the interval before the raids; Rose Macaulay's The World My Wilderness (1950) works entirely in the ruins after.
entries.application: Ban the front from the manuscript, then find the book's pressure — if it cannot be found without a combat scene, the subject is not the home front and the book should say so.

entries.name: The Occupation and Collaboration Novel
entries.description: Fiction of life under an enemy administration, where the question is not survival but complicity and its gradations.
entries.principle: Collaboration is a continuum with no clean line, and the novelist's placement of that line is the book's argument. Occupation fiction that supplies heroes and traitors has closed the gap in advance. The second pressure is the enemy's interiority: the occupier is in the kitchen, and declining to render him from inside is a choice with consequences, not a neutral omission.
entries.example: Vercors's Le Silence de la mer (1942) puts a cultivated occupier in the house and holds the refusal; Irène Némirovsky's Suite française, written in 1941–42 and published in 2004, renders occupier and occupied at the same depth; Louis Begley's Wartime Lies (1991) makes survival itself the morally compromised act.
entries.application: Draw the collaboration gradient explicitly before drafting and place every named character on it — including the ones the book approves of, who are the test.

entries.name: The Resistance Novel
entries.description: Fiction of organised armed opposition from within an occupied or repressed society, where the cost is borne by people who did not volunteer.
entries.principle: Every resistance action is paid for by civilians who were not consulted, and a resistance novel that does not stage that bill is propaganda regardless of its politics. The form's honesty is measured entirely by whether reprisal appears as arithmetic rather than as tragedy that befalls.
entries.example: Vasil Bykaŭ's Сотнікаў (1970) puts the cost on the page and refuses to resolve who was right; Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o's A Grain of Wheat (1967) distributes complicity across a community rather than assigning it; John Steinbeck's The Moon Is Down (1942) was written as morale work and is the tradition's most useful deliberate teaching failure.
entries.application: Write the reprisal before writing the operation. If the operation still reads as worth it, the book has earned its politics; if the reprisal had to be softened to keep the operation heroic, the book has chosen.

entries.name: The Displacement Novel
entries.description: Fiction of the civilian expelled by war, where the condition of being displaced — not any destination — is the subject.
entries.principle: Displacement has no resolution structure: arrival is not an ending and return is usually impossible, so the form must find shape in the road, the camp, the document and the queue. Its default cheat is to supply an arrival and call it a resolution. Its second problem is that displacement is experienced statistically and statistics cannot be interiorised.
entries.example: Ghassan Kanafani's Rijāl fī al-shams (1963) ends without arrival and makes that the argument; Elias Khoury's Gate of the Sun (1998) builds a structure out of accumulated telling because no single account can close; Viet Thanh Nguyen's The Refugees (2017) works the aftermath in which displacement has become permanent.
entries.application: If the book has an arrival, test whether it is functioning as an ending — and if it is, either remove it or make the reader feel it as the non-ending it was.

entries.name: The Child's War
entries.description: Fiction of war observed and endured by a non-combatant child, where the child's incomprehension is the book's formal device.
entries.principle: A child narrator makes atrocity legible by not understanding it, at no cost to the writer, which is exactly why it is the genre's most reliable route to both sentimentality and to the aestheticising of suffering. The device is not illegitimate; it is unpaid for by default, and the card exists so the bill can be seen.
entries.example: J. G. Ballard's Empire of the Sun (1984) uses a child's misreading of the war without softening what is misread; Günter Grass's Die Blechtrommel (1959) makes the refusal to grow the formal argument; Nosaka Akiyuki's Hotaru no haka (1967) holds the device to an outcome it cannot console; Markus Zusak's The Book Thief (2005) is the tradition's clearest sentimentality case.
entries.application: Ask what the child's incomprehension is buying and who is paying — if the effect is that the reader feels the horror more keenly while feeling less implicated in it, the device has been used as an anaesthetic.

entries.name: The War-Memoir Novel and the Fictionalised Memoir
entries.description: Fiction that borrows the authority of testimony — the author's own war, thinly or thickly fictionalised — and is read as if it were true.
entries.principle: The form claims the epistemic privilege of testimony while retaining the licence of fiction, and the reader cannot audit which is operating in any given sentence. That unauditability is the form's central fact, and a book either makes it the subject or takes the privilege without paying for it.
entries.example: Ernst Jünger's In Stahlgewittern (1920) presents the war as experience without narrative apology; Frederic Manning's The Middle Parts of Fortune (1929) fictionalises to reach what memoir could not say; Tim O'Brien's The Things They Carried (1990) makes the impossibility of auditing it the book's explicit subject.
entries.application: Decide what the book is claiming about its own truth and say so in the text rather than the jacket copy — an authority claim made only in the paratext is one the prose has not paid for.

entries.name: The Captivity and POW Novel
entries.description: Fiction of the soldier removed from the war and held, where the pressure is time, powerlessness and the collapse of the soldier role.
entries.principle: Captivity removes agency, which removes plot; the form either invents an escape, becoming adventure and closing the gap, or holds the reader in duration. Its second decision is the perpetrator: the guard is present daily, and every captivity novel makes a choice about his consciousness whether or not it notices making it.
entries.example: Richard Flanagan's The Narrow Road to the Deep North (2013) carries the captivity and the guards' later lives in one structure; Pierre Boulle's Le Pont de la rivière Kwaï (1952) turns captivity into a contest of competence and shows what that costs; J. G. Ballard's Empire of the Sun (1984) holds civilian internment in duration without supplying release.
entries.application: Write the duration before writing any escape attempt, and if the escape is doing structural work the duration could not, the book has chosen adventure — which is a legitimate choice only if it is a choice.

entries.name: The Genocide and Atrocity Novel
entries.description: Fiction whose central subject is the organised mass killing of a civilian population as policy, not as an incident of combat. Real events, real dead, and living descendants: the analysis here is of published works only.
entries.principle: This is the pack's hardest form, because every technique that makes the material readable is a candidate falsification — plot, redemption, a survivor whose survival means something, a perpetrator with a coherent inner life. Both failure modes are live at once and pull in opposite directions, so a solution to one is usually a concession to the other.
entries.example: Imre Kertész's Sorstalanság (1975) refuses the survivor's retrospective wisdom; Boubacar Boris Diop's Murambi, le livre des ossements (2000) distributes narration across perpetrators and victims; Jonathan Littell's Les Bienveillantes (2006) grants a perpetrator full interiority and is disputed on exactly that ground; Jerzy Kosiński's The Painted Bird (1965) is a contested-provenance case the pack marks as contested and does not adjudicate.
entries.application: Name the material plainly in the opening pages rather than building toward a revelation of it, and treat every readability technique as something to be justified individually rather than assumed.

entries.name: The Child-Soldier Novel
entries.description: Fiction narrated by or centred on a combatant below the age of consent to combat.
entries.principle: The child-soldier narrator is victim and perpetrator simultaneously, and the language chosen for him — broken, lyrical, marked as authentic — is the book's entire ethical argument. The form also carries the sharpest market pressure in the genre: a documented Anglophone appetite for these narratives shapes what is published and translated, which is a condition of the work and not an accusation against any author.
entries.example: Ahmadou Kourouma's Allah n'est pas obligé (2000) uses a deliberately unstable register that refuses to be read as authenticity; Ken Saro-Wiwa's Sozaboy (1985) invents a language for the position; Uzodinma Iweala's Beasts of No Nation (2005) sustains a present-tense voice through acts the narrator commits.
entries.application: Interrogate the invented voice before anything else — if its brokenness is producing lyricism the character could not produce, the book is aestheticising the child rather than rendering him.

entries.name: The Return and Veteran Novel
entries.description: Fiction of the soldier after, where the war is over and is still the generating pressure.
entries.principle: The pressure is entirely internal and entirely retrospective, so the form must decide how much war to flash back to — and every flashback risks converting aftermath into a delivery mechanism for combat scenes. It is also the genre's largest cliché reservoir: the jumpy veteran, the uncomprehending spouse, the redemptive animal.
entries.example: Rebecca West's The Return of the Soldier (1918) works entirely in the domestic aftermath; Larry Heinemann's Paco's Story (1986) makes the narrating voice itself the wound; Phil Klay's Redeployment (2014) distributes return across many roles rather than resolving it in one.
entries.application: Count the pages of flashback combat against the pages of aftermath. If the war scenes are where the book comes alive, it is a combat novel with a frame, and the frame should either be cut or made load-bearing.

entries.name: The Satiric and Absurdist War Novel
entries.description: Fiction that takes the bureaucratic and logical absurdity of organised violence as its formal principle, refusing tragic register as a matter of technique.
entries.principle: Once the register is comic, every death must decide whether to break it, and that decision is the form's whole craft. The failure mode is precise: the joke becomes an anaesthetic and the reader is entertained by the deaths rather than implicated in them.
entries.example: Jaroslav Hašek's Osudy dobrého vojáka Švejka (1921–23) makes evasion the only sane position and never resolves it; Joseph Heller's Catch-22 (1961) breaks its own register once, deliberately, and structures the novel around the break; Kurt Vonnegut's Slaughterhouse-Five (1969) takes the opposite route and refuses to break register at all; Louis-Ferdinand Céline's Voyage au bout de la nuit (1932) is carded as a work by an author later disgraced for documented antisemitic writing, which the pack states and does not adjudicate.
entries.application: Decide in advance whether the comic register will break and where — an unplanned break reads as a failure of nerve, and no break at all is a position that must be sustained to the last page to work.

entries.name: The Military Procedural and Technothriller
entries.description: Fiction whose engine is the accurate operation of military systems — platforms, intelligence, doctrine — at or near the level of the present.
entries.principle: In this form glorification is structural rather than incidental. The pleasure on offer is the system working, and the reader is placed at the console rather than under the ordnance; nothing in the form's machinery generates a cost, so any cost must be added against the grain. It also dates faster than any other war form, and the overtaken prediction is a legitimate object of study rather than a joke.
entries.example: Tom Clancy's The Hunt for Red October (1984) is the template for competence as narrative reward; John Hackett's The Third World War: August 1985 (1978) is the dated-prediction case, written as plausible extrapolation and now readable as a document of its assumptions; Elliot Ackerman and James Stavridis's 2034 (2021) applies the form to a war the authors argue against.
entries.application: Locate where in the book the system fails at a cost to someone rendered from inside — if there is no such scene, the novel is an advertisement for a capability, whatever its stated politics.

entries.name: The Military-Adventure Series
entries.description: Long-running series fiction in which a recurring soldier protagonist moves through a war or campaign sequence, with the reading pleasure in continuity and competence.
entries.principle: The protagonist cannot die, which removes the genre's central fact, and the form compensates by killing supporting characters on a schedule — a schedule that is an argument about whose lives are expendable. The most interesting solutions in the tradition are the ones that make the protagonist unworthy of the survival the form guarantees him.
entries.example: Bernard Cornwell's Sharpe sequence, from Sharpe's Eagle (1981), delivers battle from the ranks with the survival guarantee intact and visible; George MacDonald Fraser's Flashman (1969) answers the problem with a protagonist who is a coward and a scoundrel; Patrick O'Brian's Aubrey–Maturin sequence (1969–2004) spends its supporting cast slowly enough that the attrition registers.
entries.application: Chart which characters die across the series and what they have in common — if the expendable are consistently the unnamed, the foreign, or the recently introduced, that pattern is the series' actual position on the war.

entries.name: The Alternate-War and Counterfactual Novel
entries.description: Fiction that changes the outcome or conduct of a real war and follows the consequence, where the counterfactual is an argument about the actual war.
entries.principle: The point of divergence must be load-bearing, and the counterfactual must be about the reader's real war or it is decoration. There is a hard line at systematic world-building: where the extrapolation becomes a built system with its own rules, the work belongs to the science-fiction pack, and this card names that line rather than blurring it.
entries.example: Robert Harris's Fatherland (1992) uses the changed outcome to make the suppression of evidence its subject; Len Deighton's SS-GB (1978) works the occupation the actual war did not produce in Britain; Philip Roth's The Plot Against America (2004) diverges domestically and keeps the war offstage.
entries.application: State the divergence in one sentence and then test whether removing it would leave the book intact — if it would, the counterfactual is scenery, and the book is a thriller wearing a premise.

entries.name: War and the Historical Record (hand-off)
entries.description: Hands off to the historical-fiction pack, which owns the question of what claim a book makes about the past; this card names the specifically war pressure that remains here.
entries.principle: This card hands off to historical-reference, which owns the record, the archive and the question of who is permitted to narrate a war from which side's surviving papers. The specifically war pressure is different: what combat, command and supply were actually like inside the event, and whether a scrupulous reconstruction closes the gap by making a battle legible in a way no participant could have experienced it.
entries.example: Michael Shaara's The Killer Angels (1974) sits in both packs and is read differently in each — historical-reference asks whose account survived to be dramatised, and this pack asks whether two commands' interiority can be rendered without granting either a clarity the day did not contain.
entries.application: Establish which question the book is finally answerable to. If the difficulty is the record's silence, work from the historical pack; if the difficulty is that the event resists representation at all, work from here — and expect serious books to need both.

entries.name: The Literary War Novel (hand-off)
entries.description: Hands off to the literary-fiction pack, which owns the formal and interpretive contract; this card names the obligation the literary pack does not carry.
entries.principle: This card hands off to literary-reference, which asks what the form does that a summary would destroy. This pack asks the same question about one specific thing the form is trying to carry — the event that resists representation — and adds an obligation the literary contract does not include: what is owed to the people it happened to.
entries.example: Kurt Vonnegut's Slaughterhouse-Five (1969) is a formal experiment and a testimony problem at once, and reading it only as the first leaves its refusal to narrate the firebombing directly looking like technique rather than an answer to a debt.
entries.application: Where the book's difficulty is formal and its subject happens to be a war, work from the literary pack; where the formal difficulty exists because the subject will not hold still to be represented, work from here.

entries.name: Military SF and the Future War (hand-off)
entries.description: Hands off to the science-fiction pack, which owns extrapolation; this card names the test a future war still has to pass.
entries.principle: This card hands off to sf-reference, which asks whether the extrapolation is rigorous. The war question survives the hand-off intact: whether the invented war still obeys the things that make war war — friction, attrition, supply, the limits of command — or whether the future has been used to exempt it from them.
entries.example: Joe Haldeman's The Forever War (1974) keeps attrition and the return problem load-bearing while extrapolating; the tradition's weaker instances grant a technology that removes friction and then narrate the resulting engagements as though they were still costly.
entries.application: Strip the speculative element and ask whether the remaining conflict still costs what war costs. If the invented technology has quietly abolished supply, distance or the information horizon, the book has written a war with the war removed.

entries.name: The Spy and Wartime Thriller (hand-off)
entries.description: Hands off to the mystery, crime and thriller pack, which owns the puzzle and the investigation; this card names what changes when killing is already lawful.
entries.principle: This card hands off to mystery-crime-thriller-reference, which asks whether the puzzle and the investigation are fair. The war pressure is that intelligence in war is partial, late and wrong, and is acted on anyway — so a wartime thriller that renders intelligence as a solvable problem with an answer at the end has described a genre convention rather than a war.
entries.example: Graham Greene's wartime and post-war intelligence fiction keeps the information bad and the decisions consequential; the espionage tradition's weaker instances supply an answer the historical record almost never supplied to anyone in time to use it.
entries.application: Decide whether the book's information will ever become reliable. If it does, the book is a thriller set in a war; if it does not and people die on the strength of it anyway, the book is working here.

entries.name: Battle in Secondary-World Fantasy (hand-off)
entries.description: Hands off to the fantasy pack, which owns world and magic coherence; this card names the failure mode fantasy does not police.
entries.principle: This card hands off to fantasy-reference, which asks whether the world and its systems cohere. The war question is whether the army coheres — whether it eats, marches, routs and is commanded by someone with an information horizon — and battles fought without friction, logistics or a command horizon are a recurring failure the fantasy pack's own tests do not catch.
entries.example: The tradition's stronger battle writing gives its armies supply, weather and a chain of command that degrades under pressure; its weaker battle writing stages a set-piece with no rear echelon behind it and no reason any formation holds or breaks when it does.
entries.application: Ask where the food is coming from and who told which formation to move, and answer both before writing the engagement — the questions are the same in an invented world, and the specialist collection in this pack applies unchanged.

entries.name: War as Horror (hand-off)
entries.description: Hands off to the horror pack, which owns fear as a delivered payload; this card names what the supernatural register costs.
entries.principle: This card hands off to horror-reference, which asks what the fear is of and how the dread is delivered. The war question is whether the horror on the page is the war's own — the specific, documented, industrial and frequently boring kind — or whether a supernatural or splatter register has been borrowed to make it bearable, and in the borrowing has relieved the human perpetrator of responsibility.
entries.example: The strongest work in the overlap keeps the atrocity human and lets the supernatural comment on it rather than explain it; the weaker instances supply a monster and thereby answer the question of who did this with something other than people.
entries.application: Remove the supernatural element and see whether the atrocity still has an author. If the horror was doing the work of explanation, the book has offered its perpetrators an alibi.

entries.name: The Wartime Romance (hand-off)
entries.description: Hands off to the romance pack, which owns the central promise; this card names what a war does to a guarantee.
entries.principle: This card hands off to romance-reference, which asks whether the central promise is paid. The war question is what the war is actually doing in the book: whether separation and return are the engine driving the relationship, or whether the war is a pressure the relationship is measured against and can legitimately lose to — which the romance guarantee does not permit and this pack does.
entries.example: The overlap's stronger work lets the war set terms the relationship cannot meet; the weaker work uses the war as an obstacle course whose difficulty is calibrated to make the reunion feel earned.
entries.application: Ask whether the war in the book is capable of producing an outcome the romance contract forbids. If it is not, the war is machinery, and the book belongs to the romance pack.

entries.name: The Commander's Picture Is Always Old
entries.description: A commander acts on a picture of the battle that has already expired, and a competent one knows it.
entries.principle: Command runs on information that is contradictory, partly false and largely uncertain, and always describes a situation that has moved on. The commander is therefore not reacting to the battle; he is reacting to a report of the battle, at whatever lag his communications impose.
entries.example: Clausewitz's discussion of intelligence in war states the case at its source — a great part of the information received in war is contradictory, a greater part false, and the greatest part uncertain — and it has survived every subsequent change in technology.
entries.application: Fix the lag in minutes or hours before writing any command scene, and let the commander act on the stale picture. A commander who responds to events as they happen has been given the reader's omniscience by accident.

entries.name: Friction Is Not Error
entries.description: The gap between what was ordered and what happened is mostly the resistance of the medium, not anyone's mistake.
entries.principle: In war everything is simple and the simplest thing is difficult, and the difficulty is structural rather than attributable. Units get lost, orders arrive late, fuel does not, weather closes in, and none of it requires a fool or a traitor to explain it.
entries.example: Clausewitz's account of friction in On War distinguishes war on paper from war in practice, and is the origin of the term the whole subject is now organised around.
entries.application: Before assigning a failure to a character's incompetence, test whether friction alone accounts for it. Fiction that makes every failure someone's fault has substituted a plot device for a war.

entries.name: The Plan Synchronises the First Hours and Then Stops Being a Plan
entries.description: A plan's real function is to get everyone moving in a coordinated direction at H-hour; after contact it is superseded by the intent behind it.
entries.principle: The plan is not a blueprint that is either executed or goes wrong; it is a synchronisation device with a short half-life. What survives contact is the commander's intent, and units that understood the intent can improvise usefully while units that only received the plan cannot.
entries.example: The Normandy airborne drops of June 1944 scattered units across the Cotentin far from their drop zones, and those units fought to effect because the intent was understood at a level below the plan — the standard maxim about plans and first contact is widely paraphrased in a form its supposed author did not write, so the pack cites the case and not the quotation.
entries.application: Give subordinates the intent in the briefing scene, then break the plan. If the book's units become useless the moment the plan fails, the book has said something about that army's command culture — make sure it meant to.

entries.name: Orders Degrade Systematically in Transmission
entries.description: An order arrives altered, and the alteration follows the geometry of who could see what — not random chance and not a single fool.
entries.principle: Orders are written by someone with one view of the ground and read by someone with another, and the discrepancy between those two views is where the degradation happens. It is a systematic product of position, not an accident of wording.
entries.example: At Balaclava in 1854 the order that sent the Light Brigade forward was written from a height that showed the writer guns the receiving commanders could not see from the valley floor; the historiography continues to dispute the apportionment of blame, and the pack states the mechanism without adjudicating the blame.
entries.application: Establish what each party to an order can physically see before writing the order, and let the misreading follow from the difference. A garbled order played as comedy or as one man's stupidity has skipped the part that is actually instructive.

entries.name: The Medium Sets the Tempo of Command
entries.description: Command runs at the speed of its communications, and each era's technology produces its own characteristic failure.
entries.principle: The available medium determines not only how fast orders move but what kind of command is possible at all. Each communications technology produces its own characteristic failure, and no rule derived under one transfers to another.
entries.example: Napoleonic courier and semaphore, the 1916 telephone line cut by shellfire, the 1944 divisional radio net and satellite reachback in 2003 are four different command systems producing four different failures. Martin van Creveld's Command in War (1985) traces the relationship across eras and is the standard framework; any specific delay figure drawn from it is bound to the army and period it describes and does not generalise.
entries.application: Name the army and the year before setting any communication delay, and derive the failure from that medium. Universal-radio fiction, in which every era's commander can reach anyone, is the most common anachronism in the genre.

entries.name: Staff Is an Organism With a Throughput Limit
entries.description: A headquarters is an information-processing system that can be saturated, and it degrades under load in observable ways.
entries.principle: Command above the smallest unit is exercised through a staff that receives, filters, collates and issues, and that apparatus has a finite capacity. Under sustained crisis its output falls in quality before it falls in volume, which is why the worst orders often arrive during the busiest hours.
entries.example: Van Creveld's Command in War contrasts the Prussian and German general-staff system with the ad-hoc staffs of the 1914 armies, and the difference in sustained output under crisis is the clearest available demonstration.
entries.application: Put the staff on the page. Fiction consisting of a general, a map and a radio has removed the organ that actually converts a decision into a movement, and with it every interesting failure available at that level.

entries.name: Mission Command Is an Institution, Not a Temperament
entries.description: Devolved initiative is a system with prerequisites — common training, shared doctrine, accepted risk — and centralised control is a different system with different costs, not a failure. Contested: see the note below.
entries.principle: Where subordinates act on intent rather than instruction, that capacity was built by an institution over years and can be withdrawn; it is not a quality individual officers happen to possess. The centralised alternative is also a choice with a real record of success, not evidence of stupidity or authoritarianism.
entries.example: The German Führen mit Auftrag tradition is the usual reference point, and its Anglophone reception is disputed — Ricardo Herrera in Military Review (2022), and Robert Citino and Antulio Echevarria elsewhere, argue that the familiar Auftragstaktik story is substantially a post-1945 construction, while the doctrinal literature that adopted the concept continues to treat it as a recoverable historical practice. The pack records the dispute and takes no side. Against it, David Glantz's work on Soviet operational art from 1943 onward describes a centralised, artillery-heavy and prescriptive system achieving results at a scale decentralised armies did not.
entries.application: Decide which system your army is running and pay its costs consistently. The free-thinking maverick whose initiative is a personality trait rather than an institutional product is the genre's most common command anachronism.

entries.name: The Decision Under Time Pressure Is Not a Comparison of Options
entries.description: Experienced commanders under time pressure generate one workable course of action and mentally test it, rather than weighing alternatives.
entries.principle: Expertise under pressure works by recognition rather than comparison: the situation is matched to a pattern, one course of action is produced and simulated forward, and if it survives that check it is executed. Weighing parallel options is a planning activity time does not permit.
entries.example: Gary Klein's recognition-primed decision model in Sources of Power (1998), developed from studies of fireground commanders and extended to military decision-makers, is the standard account; how far it transfers to sustained high-stress combat is disputed in degree rather than in kind.
entries.application: Write the commander producing one option and testing it. The scene in which three courses of action are laid out and debated during a crisis is a staff process relocated into a moment that could not hold it.

entries.name: The General Who Cannot See the Battle Is the Normal Case
entries.description: For most of the modern period, commanders above a certain level have been unable to observe the fighting at all, and that is the ordinary condition rather than a failure.
entries.principle: Smoke, dispersion, range and scale removed the commander from the visual field of his own battle, and everything after that point is mediated by runners, wire and radio. A commander's ignorance is therefore a structural property of his position, not a deficiency of character.
entries.example: John Keegan's The Face of Battle (1976) sets the change out directly: at Agincourt the commanders were inside the fighting, at Waterloo they could see fragments, and on the Somme they could see nothing and depended on runners and telephone lines that were cut.
entries.application: Establish what the commander can physically observe, then hold him to it for the whole battle. The panoramic hilltop general survives in fiction for a century after gunpowder smoke and dispersion made him impossible.

entries.name: Intelligence Fails at Interpretation, Not at Collection
entries.description: The decisive fact is usually already in the system; what fails is the filter that assigns it meaning against a prevailing expectation.
entries.principle: After the event the signals are visible in the record, which is why intelligence failure looks like negligence in retrospect and was not. The indicators arrive inside noise and are interpreted through a governing concept, and it is the concept that fails.
entries.example: Roberta Wohlstetter's Pearl Harbor: Warning and Decision (1962) established the signal-and-noise account; Richard Betts argued in World Politics (1978) that such failures are structurally inevitable rather than aberrant; the Israeli konzeptzia before October 1973 is the second standard case.
entries.application: Put the fact in the file early and let it be read wrongly for good reasons. The thriller model in which the missing piece is the problem inverts what actually happens and removes the tragedy from it.

entries.name: The Estimate That Fits the Plan Is the Dangerous One
entries.description: An intelligence assessment consistent with what a headquarters already intends to do receives far less scrutiny than one that obstructs it.
entries.principle: Motivated reasoning at the staff level does not usually take the form of suppression. Reports that fit the plan are integrated quickly; reports that threaten it attract questions about sourcing, are referred upward, and arrive after the decision. The mechanism is procedural rather than conspiratorial.
entries.example: The handling of reports of armour near Arnhem before Market Garden in 1944 is the standard case; how firm the reporting was and how far it was suppressed remain disputed in the historiography, and the pack states the mechanism rather than settling the case.
entries.application: Write the inconvenient report being processed correctly and slowly. Playing it as a scene of villainous suppression is both less true and less frightening than the version in which everyone follows procedure.

entries.name: The Reserve Is the Commander's Only Freedom, and Spending It Ends It
entries.description: An uncommitted reserve is the one thing a commander still controls once the battle has begun; committing it converts freedom into consequence.
entries.principle: Every other element is engaged, positioned or moving under orders already given. The reserve is the sole remaining variable, which makes its commitment the decision the whole battle turns on — and irreversible, because a reserve cannot be recalled from contact.
entries.example: Clausewitz treats the reserve as a distinct instrument of command; Trevor Dupuy's combat verities record its role in restoring a broken line, and the Imperial Guard's late commitment at Waterloo remains the most-analysed instance.
entries.application: Establish the reserve early and make the reader aware it is uncommitted. Reinforcements that arrive as a matter of timing rather than as a decision with a price have removed the battle's only real choice.

entries.name: Relief of Command Is an Instrument of Tempo
entries.description: Removing a commander is a routine, systemic act used to change the speed of an organisation, not primarily a punishment or a career drama.
entries.principle: Armies under pressure relieve commanders in numbers, quickly, and often without a specific failure to point to, because replacing a slow subordinate is faster than retraining him. The act is administrative in character and brutal in effect, and it is a normal part of how a campaign is run.
entries.example: The US Army's relief of divisional and regimental commanders in North Africa during 1942–43, including Fredendall after Kasserine, is documented in the official histories and in Rick Atkinson's An Army at Dawn; the British Eighth Army's serial reliefs are the parallel case.
entries.application: Treat relief as weather rather than as scandal. The officer whose removal is the emotional centre of a chapter is being given a significance the system did not attach to it.

entries.name: Command Reasons From a Sample That Is Not Random
entries.description: The evidence in front of a headquarters has been selected by survival, by reporting incentives and by what could physically get back — and reasoning confidently from it is a known failure.
entries.principle: What reaches a commander is what survived to be reported. Units that were destroyed do not report, patrols that failed to return contribute nothing, and subordinates report what they believe is wanted. Any inference drawn from the returning evidence is therefore drawn from a biased sample.
entries.example: Abraham Wald's 1943 work for the Statistical Research Group on returning bombers established the form of the error: armour belongs where the aircraft that came back were not hit, because the aircraft hit there did not come back.
entries.application: Ask what did not return before letting a commander draw a conclusion. Confident reasoning from present evidence is fiction's default mode for showing competence, and in war it is the standard way of being wrong.

entries.name: A Firefight Is Mostly Noise, Mostly at Nobody in Particular
entries.description: The great majority of rounds fired in an infantry engagement are not aimed at an identified person and do not hit anyone.
entries.principle: Fire in contact is directed at areas, at suspected positions, and at where the noise came from. Aimed shooting at a visible individual is a small fraction of what happens, and the ratio of rounds expended to casualties inflicted is enormous by any civilian intuition.
entries.example: The US Operations Research Office's wartime and Korean casualty surveys, published as Operational Requirements for an Infantry Hand Weapon (ORO-T-160, 1952), established the pattern; David Rowland's The Stress of Battle (2006) quantified how far fire effectiveness falls when the firer is himself under fire, though the specific degradation factors remain disputed.
entries.application: Write the volume of fire honestly and let it produce almost nothing. The aimed-shot firefight makes a real ammunition load look absurd and makes every hit a matter of individual skill.

entries.name: Fire Is for Suppression, and Suppression Is What Takes Ground
entries.description: The purpose of most fire is to stop the enemy from firing effectively, so that someone else can move; casualties are a by-product.
entries.principle: Ground is taken by a group that fires while another group moves, and the firing element's job is to make the defenders keep their heads down rather than to kill them. This is why ammunition expenditure is vast and why an engagement can be won without either side hitting much.
entries.example: The fire-and-movement doctrine derived from 1917–18 practice and carried into every modern infantry manual encodes the principle; Rowland's work quantifies the effect of incoming fire on outgoing accuracy, while the magnitude of suppression effects is contested in the operational-analysis literature.
entries.application: Give the fire a job other than hitting. A scene in which shooting is only for killing cannot explain why anyone carries that much ammunition or why the position was abandoned without casualties.

entries.name: Engagement Ranges Are Far Shorter Than Weapon Capability
entries.description: Infantry fight at a small fraction of their weapons' effective range, and past a few hundred metres hits become substantially a matter of chance. Period-bound and theatre-bound: see the qualification below.
entries.principle: What limits the range of an engagement is not the weapon but the ground and the eye. Beyond a few hundred metres hit probability approaches randomness even for trained marksmen, and where the hits land is governed by exposure rather than by marksmanship.
entries.example: The ORO casualty analysis (ORO-T-160, 1952) found almost all rifle hits on Bougainville at under about 75 yards, most Korean hits at little over 100 yards and nearly all under 300, with British data placing roughly 80 per cent of effective rifle and light-machine-gun fire under 200 yards. These figures are bound to those armies and theatres — Afghan valley fighting after 2006 produced markedly longer average engagement ranges and a live doctrinal argument about small-arms calibre as a result.
entries.application: Set the range from the ground and the visibility, not from the weapon's specification, and name the theatre you are borrowing the figures from. A marksman protagonist whose skill scales with distance is running on statistics that no survey supports.

entries.name: Cover Stops Rounds; Concealment Only Stops Being Seen
entries.description: The distinction is elementary, universally taught, and universally confused by people under fire.
entries.principle: Cover is material that will stop a projectile; concealment merely breaks line of sight. Under fire the instinct is to get behind something rather than behind something adequate, and the error is so reliable that every modern army teaches the distinction explicitly.
entries.example: The distinction appears in the infantry field manuals of every modern army precisely because the mistake is universal rather than because it is subtle.
entries.application: Let characters take concealment and believe it is cover, and let the material behave as material. The hero behind a car door, a plasterboard wall or a sofa is a physics error the genre repeats more often than any other.

entries.name: Visibility, Not Range, Is the Binding Constraint
entries.description: On most ground, the distance at which anything can be seen is far shorter than the distance at which weapons work.
entries.principle: Terrain, vegetation, smoke, dust and light close the battlefield down to a fraction of weapon range, and it is that closed distance that governs how the fighting goes. The clear field of fire is the exception and generally has to be created.
entries.example: The ORO terrain-visibility studies took thousands of line-of-sight readings across theatres and found sight lines consistently far shorter than the ranges the weapons were designed for.
entries.application: Establish the sight line before staging the engagement. The wide, clear, evenly lit battlefield is a convention of the war film, and it silently makes every other element of a fight behave wrongly.

entries.name: Combat Is Deafening, and the Deafness Takes the Command Net First
entries.description: Noise at combat levels removes voice control at exactly the moment a unit most needs it.
entries.principle: Weapon and blast noise produces immediate temporary hearing loss as well as permanent damage, and the first casualty is the spoken order. Control passes to gesture, to physical contact, to pre-arranged signals and to whatever radio survives, which is why drills exist.
entries.example: Accounts of the collapse of voice command at company level in 1916 and in Normandy describe the effect directly, and the modern audiology literature on blast-induced temporary threshold shift supplies the mechanism; Richard Holmes's Acts of War collects the experiential evidence.
entries.application: Remove speech from the firefight and make the unit work by drill and signal. Conversational dialogue across ten metres in contact is the single clearest marker that the writer has not thought about sound.

entries.name: Most Casualties Are Inflicted by People Who Never See Them
entries.description: Fragments — from artillery, mortars, mines and bombs — have caused the majority of wounds in twentieth-century conflicts; small arms a minority. Specific percentages are disputed.
entries.principle: The dominant casualty agent in modern war is indirect and impersonal, which means the characteristic experience of being hurt in war is being hurt by someone who did not know you were there. This is the fact most at odds with how the genre stages its violence.
entries.example: The US Army Borden Institute's volumes on conventional warfare wound ballistics and weapons effects, together with the Army Medical Department official histories, establish the pattern across conflicts. The specific percentages vary widely by conflict and by counting rule — whether killed-in-action are included, how multiple-agent wounds are attributed — and the pack reports the pattern rather than a number.
entries.application: Distribute the book's wounds the way the surveys do, not the way the scenes want them. A rifle-centric battle is not merely inaccurate; it converts an impersonal industrial process into a series of personal encounters, which is the glorification failure at its most structural.

entries.name: The Last Hundred Metres Is a Separate Problem
entries.description: The final approach of an assault is governed by different rules from everything preceding it, and it is where supporting fire has just stopped.
entries.principle: Supporting fire must lift before the assaulting troops arrive, and in that interval the defence recovers. Everything the attack achieved beforehand is spent there, and the assault becomes a matter of what the defenders can do in the seconds they were given back.
entries.example: Keegan's analysis of 1 July 1916 in The Face of Battle sets it out at its worst — the barrage lifts, the wire is uncut in places, and the advance becomes a walk into machine guns that were never suppressed.
entries.application: Time the lift and the arrival separately and let the gap between them do the killing. The assault written as one continuous charge has removed the specific mechanism by which assaults fail.

entries.name: The Ambush Is Decided in the First Twenty Seconds
entries.description: An ambush is resolved almost immediately, by drilled reaction rather than by decision, and then it is over. Period-bound to modern small-unit doctrine.
entries.principle: The ambusher has surrendered surprise the moment he opens fire, and the ambushed party's survival depends on immediate violent movement — into the killing zone or out of it — executed before anyone has assessed anything. Deliberation in that window is fatal, which is why the response is trained as a reflex.
entries.example: The near and far ambush drills of modern infantry doctrine, derived substantially from Vietnam-era experience, prescribe immediate action precisely because the interval available for judgement is measured in seconds.
entries.application: Resolve the ambush fast and let the aftermath carry the weight. The ambush that becomes an extended running battle has turned a doctrinal event into a set piece, and the drill — not the protagonist's decision — is what should determine who lives.

entries.name: Night Does Not Equalise, and Which Way It Tilts Inverts Across the 1980s
entries.description: Darkness advantages whoever has trained and equipped for it, and the answer to who that is changes completely with night-vision technology. Period-bound in the strongest sense in this collection.
entries.principle: Before widespread image intensification and thermal imaging, night meant confusion and fratricide risk for everyone, favouring whoever would accept that chaos. After it, night is an asymmetric advantage for the equipped force. The rule does not shift across that boundary; it reverses.
entries.example: Pre-1970s night operations are documented as confusion and fratricide risk on both sides; US operations in Desert Storm and after, conducted under thermal and image-intensification superiority, produced the doctrine of owning the night.
entries.application: Name the year and the equipment before writing a night action, and derive the advantage from them. The timeless claim that night favours the attacker, or the defender, is false in both directions and depends entirely on a technology date.

entries.name: Urban Fighting Fragments Command Downward and Compresses Range to Metres
entries.description: A city breaks a battle into hundreds of separate small fights that no headquarters can see or coordinate.
entries.principle: Buildings sever line of sight, block radio, and cut a formation into room-sized engagements fought by whoever is present. Effective command devolves to junior ranks by physical necessity, and the higher headquarters loses the ability to know, let alone direct, what is happening.
entries.example: Stalingrad in 1942–43, Hue in 1968, Grozny in 1994–95 and Fallujah in 2004 are the standard sequence, and the RAND urban-operations studies analyse the command fragmentation directly.
entries.application: Break the command structure before staging the city fight, and keep the senior commander ignorant. A city written as a set — a backdrop for the same engagement that would have happened in a field — has skipped the only thing that makes urban combat distinct.

entries.name: Urban Combat Is Catastrophic for Civilians; Its Cost to the Attacker Is Disputed
entries.description: Two separate findings that are routinely collapsed into one: cities are lethal for the people who live in them, and whether they are unusually lethal for attacking troops is contested.
entries.principle: These are two rules, not one. The civilian toll of urban offensives is very large and well evidenced. The military claim — that urban fighting is a meat grinder for the attacker — is not established and is contradicted by some of the historical battle data.
entries.example: ICRC analysis of Syria and Iraq between March 2017 and July 2018, across four governorates, associated urban offensives with roughly eight times the conflict-related civilian fatalities of other fighting, around 6,485 deaths and some 78 per cent of the total in the areas studied. Against that, the Dupuy Institute's historical battle databases indicate attacker daily casualty rates in urban operations that are on average lower than in open terrain — a finding Christopher Lawrence sets out in War by Numbers and which remains disputed. The pack records both and adjudicates neither.
entries.application: Decide which of the two claims the book is making and support that one. Using the civilian catastrophe as evidence for the attacker's suffering is the most common way this material is misused, and it quietly redirects the reader's sympathy.

entries.name: Being Shelled Without the Ability to Reply Is the Most Reliably Morale-Destroying Experience Recorded
entries.description: Passivity under fire breaks people far more consistently than active fighting does, and bombardment degrades the un-hit on a curve entirely separate from the one that kills.
entries.principle: What destroys endurance is not danger but the absence of agency within it. Psychiatric casualty data across four wars associates breakdown with enforced passivity under fire rather than with exposure as such, which makes courage a function of what a person is permitted to do.
entries.example: The US Army's Second World War neuropsychiatry official history and Lord Moran's The Anatomy of Courage (1945) both record the pattern; the trench bombardments of the First World War, the German experience under Allied air and artillery in Normandy, and Grozny supply the cases.
entries.application: If the book wants to break a character, take away their ability to act rather than increasing the danger. Courage written purely as a response to danger level misses the variable the evidence actually identifies.

entries.name: The First Casualty Stops the Unit
entries.description: One wounded man reorganises a section's entire behaviour, whatever its orders were.
entries.principle: Treating and extracting a casualty consumes people, time and attention out of proportion to the single loss, and it happens whether or not the mission permits it. A unit that has taken one casualty is a different unit with a different plan, and the effect is immediate rather than cumulative.
entries.example: The pattern is recorded consistently across small-unit combat reporting and in Holmes's collected accounts, though it is better documented as an observed behaviour than as a quantified effect.
entries.application: Make the first wound cost the unit its momentum. Casualties written as counters — the section continues, one man lighter — remove the mechanism by which small actions actually stall.

entries.name: Supply Is Not a Constraint on Operations; It Is the Shape of Them
entries.description: What can be moved decides what can be attempted, and commanders who override that are not bold — they are about to stop.
entries.principle: Logistics does not limit a plan at its edges; it determines which plans exist. The direction of an advance, its depth, its timing and the point at which it ends are set by tonnage and transport before anyone chooses them.
entries.example: Martin van Creveld's Supplying War (1977) surveys the problem from Wallenstein to Patton and finds the pattern recurring across four centuries, though several of its specific readings are disputed in the later literature.
entries.application: Work out what the force can move before deciding what it does. Supply that appears only when the author wants a crisis is a plot device wearing a quartermaster's uniform.

entries.name: The Horse-Drawn Army Ran on Fodder
entries.description: In animal-transport armies the dominant tonnage requirement was feed for the animals, not food or ammunition for the men. Period-bound to pre-railway warfare.
entries.principle: A horse consumes an order of magnitude more than a man and cannot forage in winter, so an army's movement, its campaigning season and its route were governed by grass and grain. The transport that carried the supplies was itself the largest consumer of them.
entries.example: John Lynn's Feeding Mars (1993) makes the argument in detail; his high estimate of fodder's share of total requirement is disputed as seasonally inflated, and van Creveld's account of local requisition is disputed by the same volume, but the direction of the finding is not in question.
entries.application: For any army before the railway, work out the animals first. The pre-modern army whose logistics amount to a wagon of bread has left out the majority of its own supply problem.

entries.name: The Culminating Point Is a Real Place on the Map
entries.description: An advance has a calculable distance beyond which it cannot be sustained, and reaching it has nothing to do with whether the enemy is beaten.
entries.principle: As an advance lengthens, a growing share of what is moved forward is consumed by the act of moving it, until the force at the front is being supplied by a system that spends everything on its own transit. That point can be computed in advance and does not care about momentum.
entries.example: The German advance in 1941 outran its railhead conversion; Rommel in North Africa in 1942 was consuming the fuel the front needed to cover the distance from Tripoli and Benghazi to the front. Van Creveld's specific reading of the Rommel case is contested; the concept it illustrates is not.
entries.application: Fix the culminating point before writing the pursuit. The advance that continues because the enemy is broken is the genre's most common logistical error, and it is usually the moment a real campaign stopped.

entries.name: The Tail Is Bigger Than the Teeth, and It Grows
entries.description: Most of a deployed force does not fight, and the proportion that does has fallen steadily with mechanisation.
entries.principle: An army is a machine for putting a small number of people in contact with the enemy, and the ratio of supporters to fighters worsens as equipment gets heavier and more complex. The people in the rear are not surplus; they are the reason the front exists at all.
entries.example: The twentieth-century decline in the fighting proportion of deployed strength is well established in direction, but tooth-to-tail ratios are computed differently by different authorities and figures from separate sources are not comparable — the pack states the direction, not a number.
entries.application: Populate the rear. Fiction in which an army is its riflemen has removed nine-tenths of the organisation and every constraint that comes with it.

entries.name: Ammunition Expenditure Per Casualty Is Enormous
entries.description: The quantity of ordnance consumed to produce one casualty is vast, rises with industrialisation, and is nothing like fiction's economy of fire. The famous per-kill statistics are unsourceable.
entries.principle: Fire is expended on suppression, on area, on suspicion and on nothing at all, so the ratio of rounds and shells to bodies is enormous. That ratio is the reason logistics dominates modern operations, and it is why an infantryman's load is mostly ammunition.
entries.example: The week-long preparatory bombardment before the Somme in 1916, set against the German dead it produced, is the standard illustration. The widely quoted figures of so many thousand rounds per kill are contested and largely untraceable to a primary source — the pack states the pattern and declines to reproduce a number it cannot source.
entries.application: Make the ammunition supply a constraint the characters feel. An economy in which every magazine matters and every round is aimed cannot support a realistic firefight, and cannot explain the supply chain behind it.

entries.name: Fuel Is Consumed by Not Fighting
entries.description: Unlike ammunition, fuel is spent continuously — idling, repositioning, waiting — and a mechanised force burns it whether or not anything happens. Period-bound to mechanised warfare from 1939.
entries.principle: Ammunition is consumed by events; fuel is consumed by time. A stationary armoured formation is still drawing down its stocks, which is why fuel states drive decisions that look tactically inexplicable from outside.
entries.example: The Ardennes offensive of December 1944 was planned around capturing Allied fuel dumps because the operation could not be sustained otherwise, and the failure to take them determined the offensive's limit more directly than any engagement did.
entries.application: Track the fuel state across waiting as well as movement. Vehicles that consume fuel only when driving toward the plot have been given a property no engine has.

entries.name: March Rates Are Set by the Road and the Slowest Element
entries.description: A formation moves at the speed of its worst component and its traffic control, never at the speed of a fit soldier or a good engine. Any specific figure must name its army and its manual.
entries.principle: Foot columns are governed by the slowest unit, the halt regime and the road surface; motorised columns are governed by road capacity and traffic control rather than by vehicle speed. In both cases the constraint is organisational, not physical.
entries.example: Every army's field service regulations set planning factors for a day's march and for column movement, and those factors differ by army and by period — a figure lifted from one manual and applied to another army is an invented statistic.
entries.application: Find the planning factor for the specific army and year, or write the movement without a number. Fiction routinely moves whole formations at the speed of a single courier, which is the fastest thing in the theatre and the least representative.

entries.name: Casualty Evacuation Is a Chain, and Each Period's Chain Has a Different Fatal Link
entries.description: Whether a wound kills depends on the era's evacuation system far more than on the era's surgery. Period-bound per conflict, with figures that must not be summed.
entries.principle: A wound's survivability is a property of the chain from the point of injury to a surgical facility — who applies what in the first minutes, how the casualty moves, and how long it takes. Change the chain and the same wound becomes survivable or fatal.
entries.example: US data give case fatality of roughly 19.1 per cent in the Second World War, 15.8 in Vietnam and 9.4 in Iraq and Afghanistan; the proportion killed before reaching a medical facility runs around 20.2, 20.0 and 13.8 per cent respectively. The authors of the standard analysis note explicitly that these measures use different denominators and cannot be added together. The improvement is attributable to the helicopter, the tourniquet and blood products rather than to better surgeons.
entries.application: Set the survivability from the year's chain, not from a general sense of medicine. A wound written as survivable in 1944 because it would be survivable now is an anachronism that changes who lives in the book.

entries.name: A Rising Died-of-Wounds Rate Can Mean the System Is Working
entries.description: When more casualties reach a hospital alive, more of them die in hospital — and the overall death rate falls at the same time.
entries.principle: Casualty statistics are outputs of a system and cannot be read naively. A better evacuation chain moves deaths from the field into the facility, which raises the died-of-wounds figure while lowering total case fatality. The metric that looks like deterioration is evidence of improvement.
entries.example: In Iraq and Afghanistan the died-of-wounds proportion rose against the Second World War and Vietnam figures while overall case fatality fell substantially, precisely because casualties who would previously have died in the field were arriving alive.
entries.application: If the book has anyone reading casualty returns, let them read them wrongly, or let someone explain why the bad number is the good one. It is the clearest available demonstration that war generates statistics no one can interpret at the time.

entries.name: Individual Replacement Produces Trained Strangers; Unit Rotation Produces Untrained Units
entries.description: Both systems for keeping formations at strength have costs, and the choice between them shapes what the war feels like. Period-bound to the US Army in the European and Mediterranean theatres, 1943–45.
entries.principle: Feeding trained individuals into existing units preserves the formation and destroys its cohesion; withdrawing and reconstituting whole units preserves cohesion and removes the formation from the line. There is no third option, and every army's replacement policy is a standing decision about which cost it prefers.
entries.example: US Army Ground Forces Study No. 7 records that by 1943 in Italy only about 34 per cent of infantrymen in line companies had come overseas with their units; Stephen Ambrose judged the individual-replacement policy wasteful of life, and that causal judgement is disputed even where the description is not.
entries.application: Decide the replacement policy before writing the arriving soldier. The new man treated as a character beat rather than as the output of a system misses that the system produced his isolation deliberately.

entries.name: Disease and Non-Battle Causes Have Killed More Soldiers Than Combat
entries.description: For most of military history the enemy was a minority cause of death, and non-battle injury still dominates the medical workload on operations.
entries.principle: Camps concentrate people, water supplies fail, and the resulting sickness has historically outproduced the enemy. Even in modern operations with the pattern reversed for deaths, disease and non-battle injury remain the dominant reason people are evacuated.
entries.example: The American Civil War, the Crimean War and the Spanish-American War are the standard cases, documented in the Army Medical Department official histories; systematic reviews of disease and non-battle injury in deployed forces establish the modern evacuation pattern. Specific war-by-war ratios vary by counting rule and are not reproduced here.
entries.application: Let the book lose people to sickness, accident and water. A war novel in which everyone lost is lost to the enemy has described a war that has never happened.

entries.name: Attrition Is an Exchange, and the Exchange Rate Is What Victory Costs
entries.description: Battles are settled by relative loss and remaining capacity, not by possession of the ground — and the winner is frequently the more damaged party.
entries.principle: What matters after an engagement is who can continue, which is a function of losses against replaceable strength rather than of who held the field. A formation's fighting strength also falls faster than its casualty list, because sickness, detachment and straggling remove people the returns still count.
entries.example: Trevor Dupuy's combat verities record average divisional engagement casualty rates on the order of one to three per cent per day for the Second World War armies studied — a figure bound to that period and that army set — and the routine gap between ration strength and trench strength in both wars' returns is the ordinary condition rather than an anomaly.
entries.application: Do the accounting after the battle and let it contradict the outcome. Fictional casualty rates are almost always either negligible or total, and both remove the exchange that actually decides campaigns.

entries.name: Whether Men Fire, and Whether Killing Is Innately Resisted, Are the Two Least Secure Claims in This Field
entries.description: The two most quoted findings about combat behaviour — that most soldiers do not fire, and that humans innately resist killing — are both under sustained methodological attack. Contested; the pack states the argument and takes no side.
entries.principle: These claims are attractive to novelists precisely because they are humane and dramatic, and they are the collection's weakest ground. A book may use either, but should know it is using a disputed finding rather than an established one.
entries.example: S. L. A. Marshall's Men Against Fire (1947) reported that only around 15 to 25 per cent of infantrymen fired their weapons in engagements. Roger Spiller argued in the RUSI Journal (1988) that the ratio appears to have been an invention — the stated sample varies between accounts, the interview schedule was incompatible with the time available, and the surviving field notebooks contain no fire-ratio tabulations; Fredric Smoler extended the critique in American Heritage (1989). Robert Engen tested the question against Canadian battle-experience questionnaires in Canadians Under Fire (2009) and found the pattern absent. Defenders hold that Marshall's qualitative observations match combat experience whatever the number's status. Dave Grossman's On Killing (1995) builds an innate-resistance thesis on Marshall's ratio; Engen argues it inherits the evidentiary problem wholesale, and other critics contest its research process, its sourcing and its extension to media violence, while its defenders point to its reach and to clinicians who find the phenomenology accurate. What is not disputed is Marshall's large influence on post-war training doctrine.
entries.application: If the book turns on soldiers who will not shoot, put the dispute inside the book rather than asserting the finding — a character who has been trained on the basis of a contested study is more interesting than a narrator who repeats it.

entries.name: Cohesion Has Been Redefined Twice Since Men Fight for the Men Beside Them Was First Said
entries.description: The primary-group explanation is the most repeated claim in the field and the most revised. Contested; the positions are named below.
entries.principle: The classic finding has been successively narrowed, tested and reinterpreted, and what survives is not what the popular version says. Treating small-group loyalty as the explanation for combat endurance is using a 1948 conclusion that the intervening literature has substantially rebuilt.
entries.example: Edward Shils and Morris Janowitz argued in 1948, from Wehrmacht prisoners, that German endurance rested on the face-to-face primary group rather than on ideology, and Stouffer's The American Soldier (1949) is cited alongside it.
