entries.example: The command form exists because the loneliness of the senior position is structural — the decision cannot be discussed with anyone present — and that is a fact about the hierarchy rather than about the commander's personality.
entries.application: Establish what each character may say to each other character, and let the constraint generate the dialogue. Fiction that writes a unit as a group of friends with different insignia has removed the system that produces most of its available drama.

entries.name: The NCO, the Officer and the Specialist
entries.description: Three distinct professional positions with different relationships to the institution, routinely collapsed into a single competence hierarchy.
entries.principle: The non-commissioned officer's authority comes from practice and from the men; the officer's comes from the institution and is exercised at a distance; the specialist's comes from a skill the hierarchy needs and cannot supply. These are different kinds of power that fail in different ways.
entries.example: The relationship between a competent NCO and an inexperienced officer is the genre's most reliable engine precisely because it is a collision between two legitimate authorities rather than between competence and incompetence.
entries.application: Write the three as different systems rather than as points on a scale. The version in which the sergeant is simply better at the job than the lieutenant is the cliché that results from treating all three as the same kind of authority.

entries.name: Profanity, Register and the Sanitised Mouth
entries.description: How soldiers actually speak is a documented register, and both cleaning it up and reproducing it wholesale are failures.
entries.principle: Military speech is profane, technical, heavily abbreviated and full of humour that reads as callous from outside. Sanitising it produces characters nobody has met; transcribing it produces prose that is exhausting and, past a point, self-parodic. The register has to be represented rather than reproduced.
entries.example: The satiric tradition demonstrates the upper limit by going past it deliberately, which is a different act from a naturalistic novel losing control of its own vernacular.
entries.application: Establish the register early at full strength and then thin it, so the reader continues to hear what the page no longer reproduces. Note that the pack's own house rule against extended quotation applies to the sources, not to a character's mouth.

entries.name: The Unit's Private Language
entries.description: Every unit generates vocabulary that no one outside it uses, and the reader's exclusion from it is a resource.
entries.principle: Nicknames, in-jokes, local terms for places and equipment, and the shorthand that makes a whole story out of three words are how belonging is signalled. A reader who does not understand a phrase and can tell that everyone present does has been shown the boundary of the group from outside it.
entries.example: The small-unit form runs on this, and the arrival of a replacement is the standard device for making the private language audible — he does not know the words, so the reader learns what they cost.
entries.application: Invent a small vocabulary and never explain it. The urge to gloss is the urge to let the reader inside, and keeping them outside is more useful to the book.

entries.name: The Non-Combatant Protagonist
entries.description: A central character who does not fight — a civilian, a medic, a chaplain, a correspondent, an interpreter — changes what the book can see and what it must supply.
entries.principle: A non-combatant protagonist has access to the war's whole social range and no access to its central act, which solves the interiority problem and creates a structural one: the book must generate pressure from a position with no agency in the fighting.
entries.example: The home-front and occupation forms are built entirely from this position, and they demonstrate that the pressure comes from constraint, waiting and complicity rather than from action.
entries.application: If the protagonist does not fight, resist giving them a weapon in the third act. The moment they act militarily the book has conceded that the position could not carry the novel, which is the opposite of what it set out to show.

entries.name: The Child, the Interpreter and the Borrowed Eye
entries.description: Three narrators the genre uses to see a war from an angle its own participants cannot — and each buys its clarity from someone else's position.
entries.principle: A narrator who does not fully understand what they are seeing supplies defamiliarisation at no cost, and the cost is transferred to the person whose incomprehension is being used. The interpreter is the sharpest case: their position is a real and morally loaded one, and using it purely as a window is the failure.
entries.example: The child's-war form makes the mechanism visible because the device is so efficient — incomprehension renders atrocity legible while relieving the reader of the obligation to have understood it.
entries.application: Give the borrowed eye its own stake in what it is watching. A narrator whose only function is to see is not a character but a lens, and the position they occupy is one somebody actually held.

entries.name: Giving the Enemy a Voice
entries.description: Rendering the adversary in his own language and terms is the strongest available correction to the interiority ledger, and it has two characteristic failure modes.
entries.principle: The first failure is the mirror — an enemy whose interiority is the protagonist's with different equipment, which flatters the reader with an easy symmetry. The second is the study — an enemy rendered with such analytic care that he becomes a specimen rather than a person. The workable position grants him his own frame without endorsing it.
entries.example: Deighton's Bomber (1970) is the structural solution: the enemy is not given a speech but is given a section of the book, and the equivalence is made by the form rather than asserted in the prose.
entries.application: Give the enemy scenes rather than sympathetic lines. Structural interiority is harder to fake and harder to dismiss than any statement a character can be made to deliver.

entries.name: Propaganda Analysed as Craft
entries.description: Work made to serve a war effort is a legitimate object of craft study, and the study is of its technique rather than of its politics.
entries.principle: Propaganda is competent writing directed at an effect, and analysing how it achieves that effect is instructive precisely because the techniques are the ones the genre uses generally. A pack that treats it only as a category to condemn has forfeited the most concentrated available demonstration of how the gap gets closed.
entries.example: John Steinbeck's The Moon Is Down (1942) was written as morale work for occupied Europe and is a useful teaching case because it is skilful, avowed and demonstrably effective, which makes its mechanisms legible.
entries.application: Study the technique and name the purpose in the same breath. Analysing propaganda's craft is not endorsement; refusing to analyse it leaves the writer using its methods without recognising them.

entries.name: The Memoir's Truth-Claims and the Composite
entries.description: Compression, conflation and the composite character are standard memoir techniques and each one moves the text further from the report it claims to be.
entries.principle: A memoir that compresses three patrols into one, or builds a composite from four men, has produced something truer to the experience and less true to the record. That trade is defensible and it is a claim the book makes on the reader, which means it has to be visible somewhere.
entries.example: The war-memoir novel exists because writers have repeatedly found the fictional frame more honest than the testimonial one, which is itself evidence about what the testimonial form cannot carry.
entries.application: Disclose the method rather than the individual departures. A reader who knows the book composites can read every scene correctly; a reader who discovers it afterwards re-reads the whole book as a different kind of document.

entries.name: The Atrocity Committed by the Viewpoint Side
entries.description: The hardest scene in the genre is the one in which the people the reader has been attached to do something unforgivable. Sensitive material, named plainly and analysed as craft.
entries.principle: Reader attachment is an asset the book has spent chapters building, and this scene spends it. The two evasions are to have the act committed by a character the reader was never attached to, and to supply mitigation in the same scene — both preserve the attachment at the cost of the book's claim.
entries.example: Ernest Hemingway's For Whom the Bell Tolls (1940) stages atrocity committed by the side the novel is sympathetic to, and does not resolve it for the reader afterwards.
entries.application: Have it done by someone the reader likes, and do not explain it in the same chapter. The distance between the act and any account of it is where the scene does its work.

entries.name: Writing the War Your Country Is Currently Fighting
entries.description: An ongoing war has no settled record, living participants with immediate stakes, and a reading public inside the argument.
entries.principle: The material is unfinished, the archive is closed, the casualty figures are contested and provisional, and everything the book says enters a live political argument. The additional obligation is not to wait but to write in a way that will survive the record arriving.
entries.example: The counterinsurgency and contemporary veteran traditions were largely written in these conditions, and the works that have held up are those that did not stake themselves on contested factual claims that later evidence could overturn.
entries.application: Keep the book's weight on what is directly witnessed and structural rather than on disputed specifics. A novel whose argument depends on an unresolved factual question has bet the book on an archive it cannot see.

entries.name: The Entertainment Problem
entries.description: War fiction is consumed for pleasure, and the pleasure is produced by the same techniques that produce the falsification.
entries.principle: Suspense, competence, spectacle and the satisfactions of narrative shape are what make the book readable and are also the mechanisms by which violence becomes enjoyable. There is no version of the form that removes them, so the question is not whether the book gives pleasure but what the pleasure is attached to.
entries.example: The argument that the medium itself makes combat exciting is long-running and is usually cited in a paraphrased form its supposed author did not write — the pack records the argument as an argument and attributes it carefully.
entries.application: Identify what the book is pleasurable for and check that it is not the violence itself. The competence and the prose can carry the pleasure; when the killing is carrying it, no amount of framing will recover the scene.

entries.name: The Game's Version of the Same Problem
entries.description: Interactive war forms make the reader an agent, which sharpens every question in this collection and adds one the prose forms do not face.
entries.principle: A player does not witness the violence but performs it, receives feedback for performing it well, and is free to replay. Skill, reward and repeatability are the medium's native properties, and each one works directly against holding the gap open — while the same properties make possible a demonstration of complicity no novel can stage.
entries.example: The forms that engage the problem honestly place the player in positions the genre's prose rarely occupies — the civilian under siege, the person who cannot fight — and let the failure states carry the argument rather than the cutscenes.
entries.application: If the work is interactive, ask what the player is rewarded for and what they are permitted to repeat. A war work that lets the player replay an atrocity until it goes well has answered this collection's central question by accident.

entries.name: The Institutional Relationship and the Unproven Effect
entries.description: War fiction has a documented cooperative relationship with military institutions, and a contested and largely unevidenced relationship with recruitment. The two are separate claims and the pack keeps them apart.
entries.principle: Access to equipment, locations and personnel has historically been exchanged for a degree of editorial consultation, and work produced under that arrangement operates within a constraint its audience cannot see. Whether such work measurably drives enlistment is a different question, and the honest answer is that nobody has established it in either direction.
entries.example: The documented instances are specific: required script changes to The Green Berets (1968) as a condition of Department of Defense cooperation, the US Navy holding final approval of the cut on Act of Valor (2012), and America's Army (2002) as a game developed and published by the Army itself. The defence of the arrangement is also named and published: Lawrence Suid's Guts and Glory frames it as mutual exploitation and rejects the censorship characterisation on the ground that no filmmaker is compelled to request assistance; Marcus Schulzke, writing in Games and Culture in 2013, sorts the critical literature into strands and concludes that critics judge military games more harshly than the evidence warrants; and Philip Strub, as director of the Department's entertainment media office, is on the record seeking an accurate portrayal rather than a sugarcoated one. On the recruitment claim specifically, the widely repeated surge figure attributed to Top Gun traces to a single unsourced assertion and is contradicted by the service's own recruiting data for the period, and no peer-reviewed causal study of entertainment on enlistment could be located.
entries.application: Separate the two claims before making either. The cooperation is a documented condition of production and can be stated as fact; the recruitment effect is an argument in which the strong version is unproven on both sides, and a book or a card that asserts it has taken a position the evidence does not currently support.

entries.name: Analysing the Work, Never the War
entries.description: The pack's standing discipline, stated as a craft card: the subject of analysis is always the published work and its handling of the material, never the real event, its victims or the accused.
entries.principle: A craft reference has no standing to adjudicate a disputed massacre, assign responsibility for an atrocity or resolve a casualty figure, and attempting it converts a craft judgement into a historical verdict the form cannot support. Where a work depicts a contested event, the analysis is of the depiction.
entries.example: The genocide and atrocity form makes this unavoidable, and the practice is the same one the library applies to true-crime-derived fiction: the case is not the subject, the book is.
entries.application: Name the material plainly, mark the dispute as a dispute with its range and its disputants, and keep the analysis on the page rather than on the event. This is the discipline that lets the pack handle the material at all rather than omitting it.

entries.name: Sentimentality and the Redemptive Reflex
entries.description: The genre's default emotional settlement — that suffering produced something worth having — installs itself during revision rather than during drafting.
entries.principle: Sentimentality is unearned emotion, and in war fiction it takes one characteristic form: the suggestion that the experience conferred wisdom, bonds or moral seriousness. It arrives late, because revision moves toward emotional resolution and the redemptive reading is the most available one.
entries.example: The return form is where it concentrates, since aftermath invites summary and summary invites meaning; the child-narrator forms are where it is hardest to detect, because tenderness toward a child reads as decency rather than as a settlement.
entries.application: Compare the ending of the final draft with the ending of the first. If the war has acquired a meaning it did not have at the start, revision has installed it, and the diagnostic block's first question should be run again on the new version.

entries.name: The Last-Page Consolation
entries.description: The closing image is where a book most often concedes what the whole preceding text refused.
entries.principle: Endings want to resolve, and a final image of continuity, renewal or peace can undo four hundred pages of refusal in a paragraph. The reader takes the last page as the book's verdict, whatever the rest of it argued, which makes the closing image disproportionately load-bearing.
entries.example: The displacement form's rule — that arrival is not an ending — generalises here: any closing image that functions as arrival has supplied a resolution the material does not contain.
entries.application: Read the last page as though it were the only page and ask what it claims. If it says something the book spent its length denying, it is the ending that is wrong, not the book.

entries.name: The Epigraph and the Borrowed Gravity
entries.description: Quoted authority at the front of a war novel imports a seriousness the book has not yet earned and frequently misattributes it.
entries.principle: An epigraph asks the reader to begin in a register the prose must then sustain, and it borrows the credibility of the quoted source. The genre's stock quotations are also among its most misattributed texts, which means the borrowing is often from someone who did not say it.
entries.example: The most-quoted lines in war writing — on the nature of war, on the impossibility of representing it, on the dead — circulate in paraphrased and reattributed forms, and the pack's verification standard applies to an epigraph exactly as it applies to an award.
entries.application: Verify the attribution against the source text or cut it. An epigraph is the first factual claim the book makes, and a wrong one tells the informed reader everything about the research behind what follows.

entries.name: The Final Pass Against Both Traps
entries.description: The last read, run explicitly against the two symmetrical failures the pack's organising claim names.
entries.principle: The two traps are not opposites to be balanced but the same failure taking opposite forms, and a manuscript corrected against one drifts toward the other. The final pass runs both audits separately and accepts that a book can commit both — glorifying its own side while consuming the suffering of everyone else.
entries.example: The pattern is common enough to be predictable: a book that has scrupulously removed heroism from its protagonists frequently retains an escalating intensity in what it shows happening to civilians.
entries.application: Run the meaning audit and the intensity audit as two separate reads with time between them. Both failures survive a single pass, because each looks like the correction of the other.

entries.name: The Gap Screen
entries.description: Run at outline stage and again on the finished draft. This is the pack's primary screen and the one the other fifteen descend from; it tests whether the book knows the distance between the event and its representation. Any single no is a stop, not a note.
items: Can you state in one sentence what this book cannot reach, and is that sentence still true of the finished draft?
Does the reader finish a battle scene understanding it better than any participant could have — and if so, was that a decision?
Is there anywhere in the book where the difficulty of representing this is visible to the reader, rather than only to you?
Has revision made the war more coherent than the first draft had it? Compare the two directly rather than from memory.
If a participant read this, would they recognise the shape of the experience, separately from whether they recognise the facts?

entries.name: The Interiority-Budget Screen
entries.description: Run after a complete draft, with the manuscript in front of you and a page count. It tests the distribution of interior access rather than the presence of sympathy, and it is a counting exercise before it is a judgement.
items: Count the pages of interior access by position — own side, enemy, civilian, prisoner, dead. Is the distribution what you intended?
Which of the four under-rendered positions gets no interiority anywhere in the book, and what has the book asserted by that?
Where a character is rendered only from outside, is that a choice you made or one you arrived at?
Does any group appear solely as a condition of the environment — bombed, displaced, occupied, endured?
If you granted the enemy interiority, does it mirror the protagonist's, and does that mirroring make a symmetry the book has not argued for?

entries.name: The Non-Combatant Screen
entries.description: Run at outline and again at first draft, before the combat scenes are polished. The pack's claim is about the people it happened to, and most of those people were not fighting; this screen exists because the genre's own vocabulary selects against them.
items: Were the civilian scenes drafted first, in the civilian's terms, or written into a world already built for soldiers?
Does any civilian in the book have a war of their own — their own objectives, knowledge, risk and defeats — rather than a relationship to someone else's?
Is the civilian material structurally load-bearing, or could it be cut without changing the book?
Where a civilian suffers, does the scene belong to them or to the combatant witnessing it?
Does a non-combatant ever know something the soldiers do not, and act on it?
If the book has a home front, does it generate its own pressure without importing a combat scene?

entries.name: The Aestheticisation Screen
entries.description: Run late, on a clean read, ideally after time away from the manuscript. It tests what the prose does to the reader at the worst moments, and it is a craft screen rather than a question of taste.
items: Find the most admired sentences about the worst material. What does the reader leave that passage feeling?
Is any suffering in the book rendered more beautifully than the character experiencing it could have perceived it?
Where a child, a naif or an outsider narrates, is the lyricism theirs or yours?
Does the intensity of what is shown rise across the book, and if so, did the material require that or did the effect?
Strip one such passage to plain statement. Is anything lost that the book actually needed?

entries.name: The Atrocity Screen
entries.description: Run on any scene depicting mass killing, massacre, genocide, or organised violence against civilians. Real events, real dead, and frequently living descendants — the material is in scope and is named plainly rather than avoided.
items: Is the material named plainly at the opening of the scene, rather than built toward as a revelation?
Which readability technique is doing most work here — plot, a redemptive arc, a meaningful survivor, a coherent perpetrator — and can you justify that one specifically?
Is any disputed element of the real event presented as settled, and does the book state the dispute where one exists?
Is the scene answerable to someone who survived this, or to their descendants?
Does the book adjudicate responsibility for a real event anywhere, and should it?

entries.name: The Our-Side Screen
entries.description: Run wherever the viewpoint side commits an act the reader would condemn. This is the hardest scene in the genre and the one most likely to have been softened in revision without anyone deciding to soften it.
items: Is the act committed by a character the reader is attached to, or by one introduced for the purpose?
Is mitigation supplied in the same scene, and what would happen if it were moved or removed?
Does the book explain the act, and does the explanation function as an excuse?
Is the victim of this act rendered from inside anywhere in the book?
Compare this scene in the first and final drafts. Has it become easier to read?

entries.name: The Standing Screen
entries.description: Run once, at outline stage, and revisit only if the book's method changes. It tests whether the book has located itself in a live and genuinely disputed argument, not whether it has permission.
items: Where does this book sit in the dispute about who is entitled to write war, and does the text carry that position rather than the jacket copy?
What is the book claiming about its own relationship to the material — invention, reconstruction, testimony, or a mixture — and is that claim visible inside the book?
If the prose adopts the register of testimony, has it earned that register or borrowed it?
Is any authority being claimed in the paratext that the prose does not support?
Have you verified every biographical claim about service or combat exposure that the book or its publicity makes?

entries.name: The Real-Unit Screen
entries.description: Run wherever the book names a real formation, operation, ship, squadron or engagement. Naming attaches invention to identifiable people and to a record that can be checked.
items: Is the unit, operation and date correct, verified as you would verify a publication date?
Does the book attribute invented conduct to a real formation, and will the record bear it?
Are any of the people who served in this formation alive, and does the depiction take that into account?
Would an invented designation cost the book anything real, or only atmosphere?
Does the author's note specify where the record ends and the invention begins, in enough detail to be checked?

entries.name: The Living-Reader Screen
entries.description: Run before drafting the scenes that would matter most to the people they concern. This is the screen that distinguishes war fiction's position from historical fiction's — the archive problem is silence, and this one is presence.
items: Who is still alive to read this book — veterans, survivors, their children, the community it happened to?
Which scene would matter most to them, and is it the scene you have taken the most care over?
Where the book depicts a disputed event, is the dispute marked as a dispute with its range and its disputants named?
Has a reader from the position depicted seen the manuscript, and were their procedural corrections separated from their interpretive objections?
Is any living person identifiable from a fictionalised character, and has that been considered rather than assumed away?

entries.name: The War-Record Screen
entries.description: Run on every factual claim taken from military documents. After-action reports, citations, unit histories and casualty returns are dense sources that deform the record in known and different directions.
items: What was this document written for, and how does that purpose deform what it records?
Is a casualty figure taken at face value from a return that had an interest in it?
Where a citation supplies a scene, has the dramatised version been checked against any other account?
Is a unit history being used as a source when it was written by survivors for survivors?
Is the absence of a document being read as the absence of an event?
Has any claim traceable only to a single memoir been given the weight of a record?

entries.name: The Who-Could-Know Screen
entries.description: Run across the whole manuscript, scene by scene, tracking information rather than plot. Most command implausibility in fiction is an information error rather than a judgement error.
items: What can each character physically see, and for how long has their picture been out of date?
Does anyone act on information that could not have reached them at that speed, given the year's communications?
Does the narration grant the reader knowledge a character has just been denied, and is that transition marked?
Where a decision looks stupid, is the reader's hindsight doing the work?
Is any intelligence in the book reliable in a way the period's intelligence was not?

entries.name: The Supply-and-Distance Screen
entries.description: Run at outline stage on the campaign's geography and again when a movement or advance is written. Most implausible operations in fiction are logistics failures the book never notices.
items: Where is the food, fuel, water and ammunition coming from, and who is moving it?
Has the advance passed a point where it could not be supplied, and does the book acknowledge it?
Is the formation moving at the speed of its slowest element and its roads, or at the speed of a courier?
Is the ammunition economy consistent with the volume of fire the scenes describe?
Does anyone in the book lose people to sickness, weather, accident or the rear?
If the period has animals, has their forage been accounted for?

entries.name: The Combat-Plausibility Screen
entries.description: Run on every action scene. It tests the mechanics rather than the drama, and most of its questions have answers in the specialist collection.
items: At what range is this happening, and is the range set by the ground and the visibility rather than by the weapons?
Is anyone taking concealment and believing it is cover, and does the material behave as material?
Can the characters hear each other, and if they are speaking in contact, why?
Who is inflicting the casualties in this book, and does the distribution resemble the wound-agent record?
Does the unit keep moving after its first casualty?
Is the scene's timing precise, narrated from inside, by someone who could not have known how long it took?

entries.name: The Technical-Detail Screen
entries.description: Run in revision, on the research-heavy passages. It separates detail that characterises from detail that instructs, and it usually removes more than expected.
items: Would a competent person actually notice this detail in this moment, or is it here because you know it?
Is any equipment described by specification where the character's attention would have been on weight, noise or malfunction?
Does any character explain a term to another character who already knows it?
Which scenes exist because you researched something rather than because the book needs them?
Cut the technical material by two-thirds. Is the passage weaker, or only shorter?

entries.name: The Ongoing-War Screen
entries.description: Run if the book concerns a conflict that is unfinished, recent, or still politically live. The archive is closed, the figures are provisional, and the readership is inside the argument.
items: Does the book's argument depend on a factual claim the record may later overturn?
Are casualty or responsibility figures stated as settled where they are provisional and disputed?
Is the book's weight on what is directly witnessed and structural, rather than on contested specifics?
Would this book survive the archive opening, and which parts would not?
Are the participants in a position to be harmed by identification, and has that been weighed?

entries.name: The Final Pass
entries.description: Run last, as two separate reads with time between them. The two failures the pack's claim names are not opposites to be balanced, and a manuscript corrected against one drifts toward the other.
items: Read once for meaning: what does each death in this book buy, and does the war end up having produced something worth having?
Read again for intensity: does the suffering escalate across the book, and did the material require it?
Has the ending acquired a resolution the first draft did not have?
Does the last page claim something the rest of the book spent its length denying?
Is every epigraph, attribution and award claim in the manuscript verified against its source?
Are both traps now absent, or has correcting one produced the other?

entries.name: Before the Novel: The War-Tale and the Epic
entries.description: War narrative predates prose fiction by millennia, and the epic settled several conventions the novel is still arguing with.
entries.principle: The oldest surviving war narratives establish the catalogue of warriors, the single combat as the decisive event, the intervention of powers beyond the fighters, and the lament for the dead as the form's closing register. Each is a convention rather than an observation, and each is still operating.
entries.example: The Iliad supplies the named-warrior catalogue and the funeral lament; the Heike monogatari supplies the fall of a house told as the fall of a world; the chansons de geste supply the doomed rearguard. All three are read by later war fiction as models rather than as history.
entries.application: Know which of these conventions your book is inheriting. The single combat that decides an engagement is an epic device, and using it in a modern setting imports a theory of war along with it.

entries.name: The Soldier's Account as a Form
entries.description: Before war fiction there was war memoir, and the memoir's conventions shaped the fiction that followed it.
entries.principle: The participant's account established the expectation that a war narrative is answerable to experience, and it set the terms — the eyewitness claim, the corrective impulse against official versions, the tension between what the writer saw and what the campaign was. The novel inherited all of it.
entries.example: Caesar's commentaries write the campaign as its commander wished it read; the memoir literature that followed the Napoleonic wars supplied a mass of ranker and junior-officer accounts that later fiction drew on directly.
entries.application: Recognise that the memoir is the older form and the more trusted one. A novel competing with it has to offer something the account cannot, which is the argument at the root of the whole genre.

entries.name: Stendhal and the Battle Nobody Can See
entries.description: The decisive early move in war fiction was to narrate a battle from inside the incomprehension of one participant.
entries.principle: Rendering an engagement as a sequence of unexplained events experienced by someone who never learns what happened established the possibility that a novel could refuse the panoramic account. It made the battle a problem of perception rather than of description.
entries.example: La Chartreuse de Parme (1839) puts a young man at Waterloo who cannot tell whether he has been in the battle, and the episode became the reference point for every later attempt to write combat from inside.
entries.application: Study the episode for what it declines to supply. Its power is entirely in the withheld overview, and it demonstrates the technique nearly a century before the wars that made the technique necessary.

entries.name: Tolstoy and the Argument Against the Great Man
entries.description: The nineteenth century's largest war novel is also an argument that battles are not commanded and history is not steered.
entries.principle: The claim is structural rather than stated: by rendering the same events at the level of the staff and at the level of the man in the line, and letting the two accounts fail to match, the novel argues that command is a retrospective fiction imposed on chaos.
entries.example: War and Peace (1869) sets the commander's picture against the participant's throughout, and the historical-fiction pack cards the same novel for a different question, about the book's claim on the past.
entries.application: Note that the technique and the argument are the same thing. Any book that alternates between the map and the mud is making Tolstoy's argument whether or not it means to.

entries.name: Crane and the Combat Novel Without the War
entries.description: The American canon's founding combat novel was written by a man who had seen no combat, and the fact is central to the genre's argument about standing.
entries.principle: The Red Badge of Courage demonstrated that phenomenological accuracy about fear, confusion and self-deception could be reached by imagination and reading rather than by experience, which is why the standing dispute has never been settled by pointing at examples.
entries.example: The Red Badge of Courage (1895) narrates a battle its protagonist never comprehends and was written by an author born after the war it describes.
entries.application: Hold this case alongside the memoir tradition when locating your own position. It is the strongest available evidence against the experience requirement, and it is a single case rather than a rule.

entries.name: 1914–18 and the Break
entries.description: Industrial war broke the conventions the genre had run on, and the forms that replaced them are the ones still in use.
entries.principle: Mass artillery, the machine gun and the trench removed the individual's agency in his own survival, made the panoramic view impossible, and destroyed the connection between courage and outcome. Every convention that assumed those connections became unwritable, and the genre had to rebuild.
entries.example: The war produced a body of poetry before it produced its novels, and the delay is itself evidence — the material took a decade to find prose forms adequate to it.
entries.application: Date your conventions. A book set after 1916 that runs on pre-1914 assumptions about individual agency in battle is making a claim about war that the war it depicts had already refuted.

entries.name: The Memoir and Novel Boom of the Late 1920s
entries.description: A decade after the armistice, the war's prose arrived in a concentrated wave across several countries at once.
entries.principle: The delay is the interesting fact. The generation needed distance, the reading public needed a decade, and the resulting cluster of books established the conventions of the modern war novel more or less simultaneously in several languages.
entries.example: The years around 1928 to 1930 produced a concentration of war prose across Germany, Britain, France and beyond, including work that had been written years earlier and could not find a readership until the wave arrived.
entries.application: Expect the same lag in contemporary material. A war's fiction generally arrives on a delay that has nothing to do with how quickly it is written.

entries.name: Remarque and the International Bestseller
entries.description: The war novel became a global commercial form with a single book, and the reaction to it shaped what followed.
entries.principle: Im Westen nichts Neues established that a war novel could sell internationally, be adapted immediately, and be treated as a political act by the state whose army it depicted. Commercial reach and political consequence arrived together, and the genre has carried both since.
entries.example: Im Westen nichts Neues (1929) was translated widely and adapted for the screen almost immediately, and was subsequently banned and burned in the country of its origin.
entries.application: Note that the book's reception is part of its history and not separate from it. The genre's political exposure is not a modern development.

entries.name: Jünger and the Other Answer
entries.description: The same war produced a body of work that found the experience clarifying rather than annihilating, and the genre contains both.
entries.principle: A tradition exists in which industrial war is rendered as an intensification rather than a destruction of the self, written by participants with the same claim to authority as those who reached the opposite conclusion. The pack cards it because its existence is a fact about the genre and because its techniques are the same ones.
entries.example: In Stahlgewittern (1920) presents the war as experience without the anti-war frame the Anglophone canon treats as native to the material.
entries.application: Read the opposing tradition for technique rather than for agreement. The pack takes no position on the politics and notes that the two traditions draw on identical craft.

entries.name: Hašek and the Satiric Line
entries.description: A third answer to the same war: refuse the tragic register entirely and make absurdity the formal principle.
entries.principle: The satiric war novel treats the bureaucratic and logical incoherence of organised violence as the subject, and its evasive protagonist is a structural position rather than a character trait. It descends into the twentieth century as a continuous line and generates a distinct set of technical problems.
entries.example: Osudy dobrého vojáka Švejka (1921–23), left unfinished at its author's death, established the mode and its central device of survival by apparent idiocy.
entries.application: If the book is comic, know which line it belongs to. The satiric tradition has its own conventions and its own failure mode, and it is not a tonal variation on the tragic one.

entries.category: The Interwar and the Second World War
entries.name: Spain and the Committed Novel
entries.description: The Spanish Civil War produced a literature written by participants who had chosen the war on political grounds, which changed what the fiction was for.
entries.principle: Volunteer combatants writing about a war they went to on principle produced work in which the political question and the combat question are inseparable, and in which disillusionment is a betrayal of a commitment rather than a discovery about violence.
entries.example: The war generated fiction and reportage in several languages, much of it by foreign volunteers, and the resulting body of work is the clearest case in the genre of writing produced by people who chose their war.
entries.application: Distinguish the conscript's disillusionment from the volunteer's. They are different emotional structures and the genre routinely conflates them.

entries.category: The Interwar and the Second World War
entries.name: The Big American War Novel
entries.description: The Second World War produced an American form: the long, socially panoramic novel using a unit as a cross-section of the nation.
entries.principle: The form's ambition is to make a platoon carry a society, and its characteristic device is the ensemble assembled to represent regions, classes and origins. It delivered scale and produced the demographic-argument problem the craft collection treats as a standing failure.
entries.example: The Naked and the Dead (1948) and From Here to Eternity (1951) established the pattern, and its influence on the American war novel outlasted the war it described by decades.
entries.application: Recognise the form when you are writing inside it. The cross-section platoon is not a neutral structure and it arrived with a specific mid-century ambition attached.

entries.category: The Interwar and the Second World War
entries.name: The German and Japanese Reckonings
entries.description: The defeated powers produced war literature answering a question the victors' literature did not have to ask.
entries.principle: Writing from the losing side of a war of aggression means writing about complicity as well as suffering, and the resulting fiction developed techniques for holding both — the grotesque, the unreliable narrator, the deliberately compromised witness.
entries.example: Ōoka Shōhei's Nobi (1951) and Ibuse Masuji's Kuroi ame (1965) work the Japanese case; the German post-war novel developed the grotesque and the compromised narrator as its characteristic instruments.
entries.application: Note that these techniques were developed for a specific problem and have since been borrowed by writers who do not have it. Using the compromised narrator without the complicity is using the form without its content.

entries.category: The Interwar and the Second World War
entries.name: The Soviet War Novel and the Censor
entries.description: A vast war literature produced under a state that determined what the war had meant, and whose best work circulated late or not at all.
entries.principle: Where the war's meaning is state property, the fiction's history is a publication history. The significant works are frequently those written in one decade and published in another, and the gap between composition and publication is part of what they are.
entries.example: Vasily Grossman's Жизнь и судьба was completed by 1959, suppressed, and published in Switzerland in 1980; the Belarusian and Ukrainian traditions carry equivalent cases.
entries.application: Date these works by composition, not publication, and treat the delay as evidence. The pack cites original-language years and records the publication history where it is part of the work's meaning.

entries.category: The Interwar and the Second World War
entries.name: The Camp and the Limits of Representation
entries.description: The literature of the camps forced the genre's central question into the open: whether some material can be represented in fiction at all.
entries.principle: The argument that fictionalising industrial murder is impermissible, or possible only in specific registers, was made by survivors and by critics, and it has never been settled. It is the sharpest form of the pack's own claim and it originates here rather than in criticism of war fiction generally.
entries.example: Primo Levi's testimony and Imre Kertész's Sorstalanság (1975) take different positions on what form the material permits, and both are the work of survivors. The dispute over permissibility is live and the pack does not resolve it.
entries.application: Know that this argument exists before entering the material. Sensitive material of this kind is in scope for the pack, named plainly, analysed as craft, and never adjudicated as history.

entries.name: The Absurdist Turn
entries.description: Two decades after the Second World War, the American novel returned to it through absurdity and broken chronology rather than realism.
entries.principle: The delay allowed a formal freedom the immediate post-war novels could not take, and the resulting books treat the war as a system rather than an experience — the bureaucratic loop, the unstuck timeline, the refusal of a sequential account.
entries.example: Catch-22 (1961) makes the mission count the moral architecture; Slaughterhouse-Five (1969) refuses to narrate its central event directly and structures the novel around that refusal.
entries.application: Note that both are formal solutions to a representation problem rather than stylistic choices. The unstuck chronology is an answer to the question of how to write something the writer will not describe.

entries.name: Vietnam and the American Reordering
entries.description: A war without a national consensus produced a literature organised around unreliability, and it reset the American genre.
entries.principle: Where the war's justification was contested at home while it was being fought, the fiction turned to the question of whether any account could be trusted, and produced a body of work in which the reliability of testimony is the subject rather than the medium.
entries.example: Michael Herr's reportage, Tim O'Brien's fiction and Gustav Hasford's The Short-Timers (1979) established the register; O'Brien's later work made the unreliability explicit and structural.
entries.application: Recognise how much contemporary war writing runs on conventions established here. The distrust of one's own account is a Vietnam-era inheritance rather than a general property of war writing.

entries.name: Decolonisation and the War Novel From the Other Side
entries.description: The wars of decolonisation produced a literature in which the counterinsurgent is the antagonist and the insurgent has interiority.
entries.principle: These novels invert the vantage the Anglophone and European traditions assume, and they raise the question of who the genre's default reader is. They also supply the child-soldier form, the emergency and the anticolonial struggle as major subjects with their own conventions.
entries.example: Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o's A Grain of Wheat (1967) distributes complicity across a community under emergency; Assia Djebar's work engages the Algerian war and its archive; Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie's Half of a Yellow Sun (2006) carries the Biafran war.
entries.application: Read against the vantage you were trained on. A genre that treats these as regional variants of a Western form has mistaken its own default position for neutrality.

entries.name: The Vietnamese, Korean and Chinese Traditions
entries.description: The wars whose Anglophone literature is best known also produced literatures in the languages of the people they were fought among.
entries.principle: For several major twentieth-century wars there are two or more national literatures that rarely cite one another, and the Anglophone canon of a war is frequently the canon of one participant. Reading only one produces a genre that mistakes a partial record for the record.
entries.example: Bao Ninh's Thân phận của tình yêu (1990) is the standard case: a novel of the same war as the American canon, written from the other side, and read in the Anglophone world as a corrective rather than as part of the same conversation.
entries.application: For any war the book depicts, find out whether the other side produced a literature and what it is. The answer is usually yes, and it is frequently unavailable in translation, which is itself a fact worth knowing.

entries.name: The Commercial Market: Series, Adventure and the Technothriller
entries.description: A large and continuous popular market runs alongside the literary tradition and rarely intersects with it.
entries.principle: The military-adventure series and the technothriller sustain the genre commercially, operate on different conventions, and are read by a partly military readership with expectations about accuracy that the literary tradition does not face. The two markets have different failure modes and the pack cards both.
entries.example: The long-running campaign series and the systems-accurate thriller are the two dominant commercial forms, and their conventions — serial survival, competence as pleasure — are treated in the subgenre cards for each.
entries.application: Know which market a book is written for, because the same technical error costs differently in each. Accuracy is a genre requirement in one and an optional virtue in the other.

entries.name: The Screen Takes the Genre's Centre
entries.description: For most of the post-war period the dominant war narratives have been films and, later, television, and the prose tradition has been in conversation with them.
entries.principle: Once the screen became the form in which most people encountered war narrative, prose began to write against screen conventions — the establishing shot, the coherent battle, the scored climax — and readers began arriving with screen-formed expectations the novel has to negotiate.
entries.example: The war film's conventions are sufficiently dominant that a novel's refusal of them registers as a technique, which is a reversal of the relationship the genre had before the war film existed.
entries.application: Assume the reader's default battle is a filmed one. Much of what a war novel does now is corrective work against a visual grammar the reader did not choose either.

entries.name: The War Game as a Mass Form
entries.description: Interactive war narrative reaches audiences larger than the prose and screen traditions combined, and it engages the genre's questions in a medium where the audience acts.
entries.principle: The game makes the audience a participant, which sharpens every question the pack asks and adds the problems of reward, skill and replay. It is genre-constitutive rather than adjacent, and the craft conversation now includes it whether or not the prose tradition acknowledges it.
entries.example: The form spans the systems-model of command, the campaign as narrative, the moral-choice architecture and the civilian-perspective game, and the pack cards examples across that range including deliberate teaching failures.
entries.application: Treat the interactive tradition as part of the genre rather than as a market. The questions the craft collection asks about interiority and consumption apply to it directly and in some cases more sharply.

entries.name: The Global War on Terror and the Veteran-Writer Cohort
entries.description: The most recent Anglophone war literature was produced substantially by participants writing while the conflicts continued, many through formal writing programmes.
entries.principle: A cohort of participant-writers reaching publication quickly, and often through institutional writing programmes, produces a literature with a characteristic register and a shared set of formal solutions — the linked story collection, the compressed timeline, the deployment-and-return diptych.
entries.example: Phil Klay's Redeployment (2014), Kevin Powers's The Yellow Birds (2012) and Elliot Ackerman's fiction are the standard reference points, and the linked-collection form recurs across the cohort.
entries.application: Note both the speed and the institutional route. This literature did not wait the decade the First World War's did, and the difference in lag is visible in the work.

entries.name: From the National Epic to the Witness Problem
entries.description: The arc of the genre, stated as one movement: from war narrative as a nation's account of itself to war narrative as a problem about representation and obligation.
entries.principle: The form began as the story a people told about its own arms and has become a set of questions about who may tell it, what the telling does to the people it happened to, and whether the experience can be represented at all. Every earlier stage survives in the contemporary field rather than being replaced by it.
entries.example: The catalogue of warriors and the funeral lament are still in use; so is the national epic, in the commercial market and in state-supported production. What has changed is that the genre's serious centre now treats its own possibility as the question.
entries.application: Locate the book on this arc deliberately. A novel that writes a national epic in the contemporary field is making a choice, and the pack's claim is that the choice has to be answerable rather than unconscious.

entries.name: Why Readers Go to War Fiction
entries.description: The genre's audience includes people seeking to understand, people seeking excitement, and people who were there — and the same book serves all three.
entries.principle: A war novel is read simultaneously as moral inquiry, as adventure and as testimony, and the writer cannot control which reading a given reader performs. The techniques that satisfy one frequently serve another, which is why the entertainment problem cannot be solved by intention.
entries.example: The same battle sequence delivers comprehension to one reader, excitement to another and recognition or offence to a third, and nothing in the prose distinguishes them.
entries.application: Write knowing all three readers are present. A book calibrated only for the moral reader will be consumed as adventure by a large part of its audience regardless.
entries._label: Psychology of Command, Fear and Aftermath

entries.name: Vicarious Witness and the False Claim to Have Been There
entries.description: Fiction can produce a powerful sense of having understood an experience, and that sense is not knowledge.
entries.principle: Immersive narrative generates a felt familiarity with events the reader has not undergone, and the feeling is strongest where the prose is best. The risk is a reader who leaves the book believing they now know what it was like, which is a claim the book cannot underwrite.
entries.example: The most immersive combat writing produces the strongest version of this effect, which is why technical excellence and epistemic overreach tend to arrive together.
entries.application: Leave the reader something they cannot reach. A book that closes the distance entirely has handed the reader an unearned authority they may go on to use.
entries._label: Psychology of Command, Fear and Aftermath

entries.name: Why Atrocity Compels Attention
entries.description: Extreme suffering attracts attention reliably, and the genre depends on that attraction while being obliged to work against it.
entries.principle: Attention to horror is not a moral failing in the reader; it is a stable property of attention. The consequence for the writer is that the material carries its own pull, and any escalation will be rewarded by engagement regardless of whether it was warranted.
entries.example: The escalation pattern the craft collection screens for succeeds commercially, which is the reason it has to be screened for rather than left to the writer's judgement.
entries.application: Assume escalation will be rewarded and treat that as a reason for suspicion rather than encouragement. The market signal and the craft signal point in opposite directions here.
entries._label: Psychology of Command, Fear and Aftermath

entries.name: The Aesthetic Response Displaces the Moral One
entries.description: A beautifully rendered horror produces admiration, and admiration occupies the space the material's actual demand would fill.
entries.principle: The two responses compete for the same attention. A reader struck by the writing is, at that moment, not struck by what is being written about, and the more accomplished the prose the more reliably the substitution occurs.
entries.example: This is the mechanism underneath the aestheticisation screen: the problem is not impropriety but displacement, and it is measurable by asking what the reader is left holding.
entries.application: Test the worst passages for what they leave behind. If it is chiefly the sentence, the sentence has taken the place of the subject.
entries._label: Psychology of Command, Fear and Aftermath

entries.name: Fear Is Not the Only Wound
entries.description: Combat produces at least two distinct injuries — one from threat and one from moral violation — and they present differently.
entries.principle: Threat-based injury and the injury caused by having done, witnessed or been ordered into something that violated one's moral framework are separable, and conflating them produces characters whose aftermath does not match what happened to them.
entries.example: The moral-injury literature developed from clinical work with veterans locates the second injury in betrayal of what is right by a legitimate authority; its boundary with post-traumatic stress disorder remains disputed in the clinical field.
entries.application: Decide which injury the character has, and let the symptoms follow. Writing all aftermath as fear removes the category that applies to characters who did something rather than survived something.
entries._label: Psychology of Command, Fear and Aftermath

entries.name: Courage Is a Resource, Not a Character
entries.description: Endurance under fire is expended and only partly restored, which makes courage a state rather than a trait.
entries.principle: A soldier's capacity to keep functioning draws on a finite reserve depleted by exposure. The observable consequence is that the bravest are frequently those with the least remaining, and that the point of exhaustion arrives well before it becomes visible to others.
entries.example: The clinical accounts written from regimental medical service treat courage explicitly as capital that is spent, and the specialist collection carries the operational version of the same rule.
entries.application: Track the reserve rather than assigning a level of courage. The brave man who breaks is the normal case and the standard war-fiction character types make it look like a reversal.
entries._label: Psychology of Command, Fear and Aftermath

entries.name: Agency Governs Endurance More Than Danger Does
entries.description: What breaks people is the inability to act within danger, not the amount of danger.
entries.principle: Enforced passivity under fire is associated with breakdown far more consistently than active exposure is, which means the psychological cost of a situation is better predicted by what a person is permitted to do than by how dangerous it is.
entries.example: Psychiatric casualty patterns across several twentieth-century wars record bombardment without the ability to reply as the most reliably destructive combat experience, and the specialist collection carries the operational statement of it.
entries.application: To break a character, remove their options rather than increasing the threat. It is both truer to the evidence and harder to write, which is why fiction reaches for danger instead.
entries._label: Psychology of Command, Fear and Aftermath

entries.name: The First Kill and What Fiction Assumes About It
entries.description: The genre treats killing as a threshold event with a predictable aftermath, and the evidence for that model is weaker than its ubiquity suggests. Contested.
entries.principle: The claim that killing produces a characteristic and severe psychological reaction, rooted in an innate resistance, is a specific and disputed position rather than an established finding. Reactions in the record vary widely, including indifference and satisfaction, and the variation is itself the more defensible datum.
entries.example: The specialist collection sets out the dispute over the resistance-to-killing thesis and its evidentiary base in full; the pack states the argument on both sides and adopts neither.
entries.application: Do not write the first kill as an automatic trauma without knowing that this is a contested model. The more interesting scene is frequently the one in which the expected reaction does not arrive.
entries._label: Psychology of Command, Fear and Aftermath

entries.name: Habituation and the Loss of the Ordinary Response
entries.description: Sustained exposure produces a flattening that is adaptive in the situation and disabling outside it.
entries.principle: The responses that make a person functional under repeated horror — reduced affect, black humour, treating bodies as objects — are adaptations rather than damage while the exposure continues. They become the problem at the point of return, which is why aftermath and combat require different psychological registers.
entries.example: The characteristic humour of units under sustained exposure reads as callousness from outside and as function from inside, and both readings are correct in their own context.
entries.application: Let the adaptation be genuinely adaptive in the war and genuinely disabling after it. Writing the flattening as damage throughout removes the reason anyone develops it.
entries._label: Psychology of Command, Fear and Aftermath

entries.name: The Small Group and What It Actually Supplies
entries.description: The unit provides something real, and what it provides is better described as obligation and shared competence than as love. Contested.
entries.principle: Small-group attachment is real and load-bearing, and the popular account of what it is — affection producing endurance — is the weakest version of it. The evidence favours commitment to a shared task, mutual dependence and the intolerability of being seen to fail in front of the others.
entries.example: The specialist collection sets out the cohesion literature and its revisions in detail, including the finding that surveyed soldiers named group solidarity far less often than the theory built on their responses would suggest.
entries.application: Build the unit on obligation and competence rather than on affection, and let the affection follow. The shame of failing in front of these particular men is a stronger and better-evidenced motive than love for them.
entries._label: Psychology of Command, Fear and Aftermath

entries.name: Command Loneliness
entries.description: The decision that spends lives cannot be discussed with anyone present, which makes command a structurally isolated psychological position.
entries.principle: A commander cannot express doubt to subordinates without degrading their performance, cannot express it to superiors without inviting relief, and has no peer in the room. The isolation is a property of the position rather than of the person, and it is the reason the command novel exists as a distinct form.
entries.example: The command tradition's recurring device — the commander's interiority rendered for the reader and for nobody in the book — is a technical response to this structural fact.
entries.application: Give the commander no one to talk to and let the reader hold what he cannot say. A confidant relieves the pressure that makes the position worth writing about.
entries._label: Psychology of Command, Fear and Aftermath

entries.name: Responsibility at a Distance
entries.description: Ordering deaths and causing them produce different psychological outcomes, and the difference is not simply a matter of degree.
entries.principle: Decision-makers whose orders kill experience the responsibility abstractly, through numbers and reports, and the aftermath they carry is characteristically different from that of the people who executed the order. Neither is a lesser burden; they are unlike.
entries.example: The moral-injury literature distinguishes the injury of the person who acted from that of the person who ordered, and the specialist collection's material on the commander's information horizon supplies the mechanism for the abstraction.
entries.application: Do not write the commander's guilt as the soldier's guilt at greater volume. The abstraction is the specific feature, and a commander who feels each death individually has been given a psychology the position does not permit.
entries._label: Psychology of Command, Fear and Aftermath

entries.name: Decision Under Uncertainty and the Retrospective Verdict
entries.description: Commanders are judged on outcomes and act on expectations, and the gap is the source of most of what looks like incompetence.
entries.principle: The decision is made from a partial and stale picture, and it is assessed afterwards against a complete one. Hindsight makes the reasoning look absent when it was present, which is why so much command history reads as a catalogue of obvious errors.
entries.example: The specialist collection sets out both halves — the commander's information horizon and the biased sample he reasons from — and the law's insistence that proportionality is judged prospectively encodes the same distinction.
entries.application: Write the decision from inside the picture available at the time. A reader given the full picture first will read every subsequent decision as stupidity, and the book will have made an argument about that commander it did not intend.
entries._label: Psychology of Command, Fear and Aftermath

entries.name: Obedience, Diffusion and the Order That Is Not Given
entries.description: Compliance in hierarchies is produced more by ambiguity and shared responsibility than by explicit direction.
entries.principle: The explicit unlawful order is rare; what produces the act is usually a permissive climate, an ambiguous instruction and a distribution of responsibility in which no individual holds the decision. This makes the mechanism institutional rather than a matter of individual obedience.
entries.example: The specialist collection's cards on the manifestly unlawful order and on the administrative pattern of concealment set out the legal and institutional forms of the same finding.
entries.application: Write the ambiguity and the climate rather than the explicit order. The scene in which someone is told plainly to commit an atrocity is the version that lets every other character off.
entries._label: Psychology of Command, Fear and Aftermath

entries.name: Why Ordinary People Do It
entries.description: Atrocity is generally committed by unremarkable people, and which conditions produce it is exactly what scholars dispute. Contested; the pack states the argument and adopts neither position.
entries.principle: Both available shortcuts are unsupported. The monstrousness account is contradicted by the evidence about who the perpetrators were; the situational account is a specific scholarly position disputed by scholars working from the same records.
entries.example: The specialist collection sets out the exchange between the situational and the ideological accounts of the same police battalion in detail, drawn from the same postwar interrogation records, and the pack does not adopt a mechanism.
entries.application: Choose a mechanism knowingly, because a novel cannot avoid implying one. The choice is the book's most consequential psychological claim and it should not be made by default.
entries._label: Psychology of Command, Fear and Aftermath

entries.name: The Civilian's War Is a Different Psychology
entries.description: Enduring war without fighting it produces its own conditions, and they are not a milder version of the combatant's.
entries.principle: The civilian under war experiences danger without training, without a role, without a unit and frequently without information, and the resulting psychology is organised around powerlessness and uncertainty rather than around exposure and function. The differences are structural.
entries.example: The home-front and occupation forms are built on this material, and their characteristic pressures — waiting, rationing, the news that does not come — have no combatant equivalent.
entries.application: Do not model the civilian on the soldier with the weapon removed. The absence of a role is the defining condition and it changes everything downstream of it.
entries._label: Psychology of Command, Fear and Aftermath

entries.name: Waiting, Rumour and the Information Vacuum
entries.description: Populations without reliable information generate their own, and the rumour economy is a documented feature of war rather than a failure of character.
entries.principle: Where official information is absent, censored or disbelieved, rumour fills the space and behaves predictably — it moves fast, favours the catastrophic, and is corrected slowly. It is the civilian population's substitute for intelligence and it shapes behaviour as effectively as fact.
entries.example: The rumour dynamics of besieged and occupied populations are consistently recorded, and the specialist collection carries the military parallel in its account of how rout begins.
entries.application: Give the civilian characters an information environment rather than a knowledge state. What they believe and how they came to believe it is more revealing than what is true.
entries._label: Psychology of Command, Fear and Aftermath

entries.name: Complicity as a Gradient
entries.description: Life under occupation is a continuous series of small accommodations, and the psychology is one of gradual position rather than of decision.
entries.principle: Nobody chooses collaboration as an act; people make successive small accommodations, each defensible, and arrive somewhere they would not have chosen. The absence of a decisive moment is the characteristic feature and the reason the moral gradient is so hard to render.
entries.example: The occupation form's central technical problem is exactly this: fiction wants a moment of choice, and the experience does not supply one.
entries.application: Remove the decisive moment and write the accumulation. A character who chooses collaboration in a scene has been given a clarity the position specifically denies.
entries._label: Psychology of Command, Fear and Aftermath

entries.name: Displacement and the Loss of the Future
entries.description: Being displaced removes not only place but the capacity to plan, and the resulting condition has no resolution built into it.
entries.principle: Displacement suspends the ordinary structure of a life — the expectation of continuity, the ability to make commitments, the assumption of return — and the psychological condition is organised around indefinite suspension rather than around loss. There is no arrival that resolves it.
entries.example: The displacement form's structural refusal of arrival is a formal rendering of this psychological fact rather than a stylistic choice.
entries.application: Write the suspension rather than the grief. Grief has a shape and displacement's characteristic feature is that it does not.
entries._label: Psychology of Command, Fear and Aftermath

entries.name: The Child Under War
entries.description: Children experience war without the frameworks adults use to organise it, and the effects are distinctive rather than simply more severe.
entries.principle: A child lacks the political, historical and causal frameworks that make an adult's war intelligible, so the experience is organised around the immediate and the sensory, and around the behaviour of the adults present. The long-term effects run through developmental disruption rather than through the adult trauma model.
entries.example: The child's-war form uses the missing framework as a literary device, and the craft collection screens for the cost of using it that way.
entries.application: Render the missing framework rather than a small adult's understanding. And note that the device the book gains from it is charged to the child, which is the craft collection's objection.
entries._label: Psychology of Command, Fear and Aftermath

entries.name: The Return and the Missing Structure
entries.description: Coming home removes the structure that made the war survivable, and the removal is itself a shock.
entries.principle: The war supplies role, hierarchy, purpose, unit and an unambiguous set of demands. Return removes all of them simultaneously and replaces them with a civilian life that requires initiative and offers no equivalent clarity. The difficulty is frequently the absence of pressure rather than the memory of it.
entries.example: The return form's recurring subject — the veteran who cannot find a use for himself — is a description of this structural removal rather than of trauma in the clinical sense.
entries.application: Write what the character has lost as well as what they carry. The missing structure explains behaviour the trauma model does not, including the wish to go back.
entries._label: Psychology of Command, Fear and Aftermath

entries.name: Survivor Guilt and Its Arithmetic
entries.description: Surviving where others did not produces a distinctive and durable condition organised around unearned outcome.
entries.principle: The condition is not primarily grief; it is an unresolvable arithmetic in which the survivor's continued existence is felt as having been taken from someone else. It responds poorly to consolation because the consolation addresses a loss and the condition is about an allocation.
entries.example: The literature of the camps and the small-unit tradition both supply the material, and the two produce recognisably the same structure from very different situations.
entries.application: Resist supplying consolation. The condition's defining feature is that it cannot be argued with, and a scene that resolves it has described something else.
entries._label: Psychology of Command, Fear and Aftermath

entries.name: Inherited War
entries.description: The children of participants and survivors carry a relationship to events they did not experience, and it shapes them in describable ways.
entries.principle: A war is transmitted across a generation through silence, through fragments, through the behaviour of a parent who does not explain it. The inheritor's relationship to the event is mediated and incomplete, and it is a distinct condition rather than a diluted version of the original.
entries.example: The concept was developed in relation to the children of Holocaust survivors and has been extended to other atrocities and to veterans' families; the historical-fiction pack carries the general version of the same material.
entries.application: Write the transmission through the gap rather than through the story. What is not said, and the child's construction of what it must have been, is the actual material.
entries._label: Psychology of Command, Fear and Aftermath

entries.name: National Memory and the Usable War
entries.description: Societies construct accounts of their wars that serve present purposes, and war fiction operates inside and against those accounts.
entries.principle: A nation's war memory is selective, and the selection is a live political process rather than a settled inheritance. Fiction is one of the instruments by which it is constructed, which means a war novel is intervening in national memory whether or not it intends to.
entries.example: The good war, the lost cause and the great patriotic war are three constructions whose relationship to their events is documented and contested, and each has a fiction that maintains it and a fiction that contests it.
entries.application: Identify the national account your book is written inside. A novel that reproduces the received version is making a political intervention as surely as one that attacks it.
entries._label: Psychology of Command, Fear and Aftermath

entries.name: The Veteran's Account and Its Reliability
entries.description: Testimony from participants is unreliable in known directions, and the unreliability is a property of memory rather than of honesty.
entries.principle: Combat memory compresses and dilates time, reorders sequence, and consolidates around whichever version has been told before. A veteran's account is therefore a record of how the event was survived and retold rather than of how it occurred, and treating it as a transcript misuses it.
entries.example: The specialist collection records that nobody in a firefight knows how long it lasted, and combat-interview practice has treated this as a known property of the source since the method began.
entries.application: Treat contradiction between two accounts of one action as material rather than as an error. The disagreement usually locates what mattered to each of them.
entries._label: Psychology of Command, Fear and Aftermath

entries.name: What Fiction Can and Cannot Do Here
entries.description: The pack's closing psychological card: what a war novel is realistically able to accomplish for a reader, and what it cannot.
entries.principle: Fiction can extend the range of situations a reader has imaginatively occupied, and it cannot transfer experience. It can complicate a national account, and it cannot settle a historical dispute. It can hold a gap open, and it cannot close one. Claiming more is the failure the whole pack is organised against.
entries.example: The genre's most durable works are consistently those that decline the largest claims — refusing to narrate the central event, refusing to resolve the standing question, refusing an ending.
entries.application: Set the book's ambition at what the form can actually do. A novel that promises to convey what it was like has undertaken the one thing the pack's organising claim says is not available.
entries._label: Psychology of Command, Fear and Aftermath

entries.name: The Rifleman's Horizon
entries.description: The war narrated strictly from what one soldier in the line can see, hear and be told, with no access to the wider action.

examples.text: Crane holds the horizon so tightly that the protagonist cannot establish whether he has been in the battle, and the reader is denied the orientation that would settle it.
