Ledig fragments the horizon further by rotating among men who each see only their own metre of the line, refusing any composite the reader could assemble.
The multi-strand structure repeatedly promises the soldier's horizon and then supplies the map view, so the restriction reads as a texture rather than a constraint.

entries.name: The Battle Nobody Can See
entries.description: An engagement rendered as a set of unexplained events, in which no character — and often no narrator — ever assembles what happened.

examples.text: Stendhal's Waterloo established the device a century before the wars that required it, and it remains the purest instance: the battle is a series of encounters whose relation to each other is never supplied.
Jones distributes the engagement across a company so that the reader accumulates fragments the characters never reconcile.
The panoramic reconstruction is spectacular and inverts the trope entirely, which makes it a useful contrast case rather than an instance.

entries.name: The Green Narrator
entries.description: A newly arrived soldier whose ignorance supplies the reader's education, and whose learning curve structures the opening.

examples.text: Marlantes uses a new lieutenant's incomprehension to introduce a system the novel then holds him inside for four hundred pages.

examples.work: All Quiet on the Western Front
examples.text: The adaptation opens on induction and equipment reissued from the dead, making the green arrival a statement about supply rather than about innocence.
The new crewman's education is delivered largely through set-pieces staged for his benefit, so the device becomes a delivery mechanism rather than a limitation.

entries.name: The Veteran Narrator Looking Back
entries.description: The war told years later by a survivor whose retrospection colours everything, and whose reliability is part of the subject.

examples.text: O'Brien makes the retrospection audibly unstable, revising his own stories inside the book and refusing to settle which version stands.
Kertész withholds the retrospective wisdom the form invites, so the adult voice reports without the consolation of having understood.
The framing device supplies retrospection as sentiment at the beginning and end without letting it operate on the material between.

entries.name: The Enemy's Chapter
entries.description: A structural section given to the other side, granting interiority the rest of the book withholds.

examples.text: Deighton runs the same raid from the aircraft and from the German town beneath it, and the structural equivalence does moral work no statement could.
Buchheim's crew are the enemy in the tradition most of his readers inherited, and the novel simply declines to treat them as such.
The companion-film structure is the trope at feature scale, and the separation into two films lets each audience keep its own side intact.

entries.name: The Civilian Who Watches the Battle Arrive
entries.description: An engagement seen by someone with no role in it, from a house, a field or a cellar.

examples.text: Némirovsky, writing in 1941–42, renders the collapse of 1940 as traffic, hunger and abandoned possessions seen by people fleeing through it.
The war reaches a Belarusian boy as a series of arrivals he cannot interpret, and the film refuses to explain them for him.
The Dunkirk sequence is observed rather than inhabited, and the continuous take makes the observation an achievement of the camera rather than of a consciousness.

entries.name: The Unit Speaking as We
entries.description: First-person plural narration in which the group rather than an individual holds the point of view.

examples.text: Hasford's collective register absorbs individuals into a shared voice and lets the reader feel the cost when it does.
Hašek's narration speaks for and against the army simultaneously, so the collective voice becomes the institution's rather than the men's.
The ensemble is rendered with great fidelity but the point of view remains distributed among individuals rather than becoming genuinely collective.

entries.name: The Interpreter Between Two Armies
entries.description: A character who moves between languages and sides, and whose position is itself a moral problem rather than a convenience.

examples.text: Nguyen's narrator is a translator in every sense and the novel refuses to let the position be neutral.
Ackerman narrates entirely from the Afghan side, so the translation runs the other way from the reader's expectation.
The role becomes a thriller mechanism, and the specific ethical exposure of the position is not engaged.

entries.name: The Correspondent Who Cannot Look Away
entries.description: A journalist or photographer whose access to the war is total and whose stake in it is compromised.

examples.text: Greene's narrator is a correspondent whose claim to detachment is dismantled by the plot he is reporting.
Herr writes the correspondent's compromised position as the subject, including the appetite that brought him there.
The correspondent's guilt is real and is resolved by the film in a way the historical record around it does not support.

entries.name: The Narrator Who Was Not There
entries.description: A book that announces its own distance from the war it describes, making the absence of witness part of the method.

examples.text: Vonnegut opens by describing his failure to write the book, and the refusal to narrate the firebombing directly is the structural consequence.
Satrapi narrates a war she experienced as a child from an adult exile's distance, and the drawn line carries the gap.
The device of a non-human narrator supplies distance without cost and produces consolation the material does not contain.

entries.name: Basic Training as Unmaking
entries.description: The opening movement in which a civilian is systematically dismantled and reassembled as a soldier.

examples.text: Hasford's opening section renders the process as a technical procedure with an intended output, and shows it working.
Klay's collection assumes the transformation and examines it from the far side, which is the harder and less used approach.
The unmaking is rendered as a romantic obstacle course whose completion confers worth, which is the trope's most sentimental available form.

entries.name: The Instructor Who Is Making Something
entries.description: The training NCO as a craftsman with a product in mind, rather than as a sadist or a comic figure.

examples.text: The instructor is played as a professional executing a syllabus, and the film's first half is the syllabus working exactly as designed.
Myrer's professional soldiers train men as an institutional task, and the novel treats the competence as competence.
The comic register removes the purpose, leaving the figure without the function that makes him frightening.

entries.name: The Arrival at the Front
entries.description: The transition from rear to line, in which the war becomes physically present and the training's inadequacy is exposed.

examples.text: Graves renders the arrival as a set of practical instructions about not being seen, which is the version that treats the front as a workplace with rules.
The arrival is rendered as logistics — mud, rain, radios, the hill — rather than as a moment of recognition.
The arrival compresses into an orientation lecture, so the transition is stated rather than experienced.

entries.name: The First Bombardment
entries.description: The soldier's first experience of sustained shelling, which the genre uses as the point at which the war becomes unarguable.

examples.text: The passage renders bombardment as an assault on the capacity to think rather than as danger, which is the finding the psychiatric literature supports.
Jünger describes the same experience reaching an opposite conclusion, and the pack cards the divergence rather than resolving it.
The continuous-take construction converts bombardment into an obstacle to be traversed, which is a decision about pace rather than about the experience.

entries.name: The First Kill
entries.description: The moment the protagonist kills, treated by the genre as a threshold with a predictable aftermath. Contested: the underlying model is disputed.

examples.text: Bao Ninh's killing is unremarkable in the moment and returns later without a clean causal line, which matches the record better than the threshold model.
Sledge records reactions across a range including numbness and satisfaction, and declines to arrange them into a progression.
The film organises its protagonist's killing around competence and burden simultaneously, and the resulting structure makes the count itself a source of tension.

entries.name: The First Corpse
entries.description: The dead body as an object of attention, and the point at which the genre most often converts a person into description.

examples.text: Mailer's dead retain the specificity of who they were, which makes the patrol's indifference to them legible as a change in the living.
Ōoka's corpses are the novel's central problem rather than its scenery, and the book follows the logic to where it goes.
The dead are staged for atmosphere at scale, and the scale is what removes them from the reader's attention.

entries.name: The Veteran Who Will Not Learn Your Name
entries.description: Experienced soldiers withholding attachment from replacements, treated as callousness and functioning as a documented survival behaviour.

examples.text: The behaviour is shown as a rational institutional adaptation rather than as a character flaw.
Caputo records the practice as universal and explains its arithmetic without softening it.
The series shows the behaviour and then repeatedly overrides it, because the ensemble form needs the replacements to become known.

entries.name: The Talisman and the Ritual
entries.description: Superstition, charms and fixed routines as the observed psychological response to uncontrollable risk.

examples.text: O'Brien's inventory of carried objects makes the talismans an index of what each man cannot say.
Orr's rituals and the mission count are the same mechanism, and the novel treats both as rational under the circumstances.
The rituals are catalogued as texture without the risk that produces them ever fully arriving.

entries.name: The Letter Home That Lies
entries.description: Correspondence that conceals the war from its recipients, and the gap between the two accounts.

examples.text: Japrisot builds the novel out of letters and official notifications, so the gap between what was written and what happened is the plot rather than a scene.
Brittain works the correspondence from the receiving end, where the omissions are legible only in retrospect.
The Bixby letter frames the film with an official consolation whose authenticity has itself been questioned, and the frame accepts it entirely.

entries.name: The Photograph of the Enemy's Family
entries.description: The dead adversary's personal effects revealing him as a person, staged as the moment of recognition.

examples.text: Remarque's shell-hole sequence stages it at length and lets the recognition fail to change anything.
The device appears in compressed form and does the work of a whole argument in a few seconds.
The recognition is deployed as a beat inside a romance structure, and its function is to reassure the audience about the protagonists' decency.

entries.name: The Order That Cannot Be Obeyed
entries.description: An instruction that is impossible on the ground, and the question of who is destroyed by carrying it out.

examples.text: The impossible attack and the subsequent prosecution of its survivors are staged as one continuous institutional process.
Forester's protagonist issues the impossible order without malice, and the novel holds him inside the limitations that produced it.

examples.work: The Charge of the Light Brigade
examples.text: The satire is aimed at individuals, which converts a geometry of vision into a story about fools.

entries.name: The Commander Who Cannot See
entries.description: A senior officer directing a battle he has no visual access to, dependent on reports that are already old.

examples.text: Shaara keeps both commands inside their information horizons and lets the reader feel the lag.
The adaptation sustains the same restriction across an entire documented engagement, which is rare at feature length.
The commander sees his battle whole from a height, which is an epic convention imported into a film claiming reconstruction.

entries.name: The Relieved Commander
entries.description: An officer removed from command, staged by the genre as personal tragedy and functioning institutionally as tempo management.

examples.text: Wouk makes the removal a legal and institutional process and lets the reader's sympathies fail to settle.
The film treats command as a consumable resource and the relief as the system working rather than failing.
Relief is rendered as an injustice done to a great man, which is the reading the institutional record does not support.

entries.name: The Staff Officer at the Front
entries.description: A headquarters officer visiting the line, used to stage the distance between the two worlds.

examples.text: Manning renders the encounter without caricature, so the gulf reads as structural rather than as a matter of individual vanity.
Sherriff's dugout receives its instructions from an authority that never appears, which is the more accurate version of the relationship.
The staff officer as preening idiot is the trope's most influential comic form, and its influence on popular understanding of the war is larger than its intent.

entries.name: The Intelligence Nobody Believes
entries.description: Accurate warning that fails to be acted on because it does not fit the prevailing expectation.

examples.text: The armour reports before Arnhem are staged as a procedural failure rather than as villainy, which is the more instructive version.
Grossman's bureaucratic scenes show information being processed correctly into the wrong conclusion.
The intelligence work becomes a puzzle solved by a brilliant individual, which inverts what the interpretive-failure literature describes.

entries.name: The Reserve Committed Too Late
entries.description: The last uncommitted force released at the point where it can no longer change the outcome.

examples.text: The novel makes the reserve a decision with a price rather than a matter of arrival timing.
The Guard's commitment is staged as the moment the commander's remaining freedom is spent.
Reserves function as reinforcement arriving on schedule, which removes the decision entirely.

entries.name: The Attack Postponed
entries.description: Waiting for an operation that is repeatedly delayed, and what the delay does to the people holding at readiness.

examples.text: The whole play-turned-novel is the interval before an attack, and the tension is entirely a function of the waiting.
Monsarrat's escort work is a sustained readiness with intermittent violence, which is the naval version of the same shape.
The weather delay is present as a plot fact rather than as a condition the men are held inside.

entries.name: The Casualty Estimate Accepted in Advance
entries.description: An operation authorised with expected losses stated as a number, and the number becoming people.

examples.text: Jones runs the arithmetic at the command level and then delivers the individuals it converts.
The novel places the calculation and the calculated in the same structure without editorialising the join.
The expenditure of men is staged as a single spectacular sequence, which makes it an atrocity rather than a policy.

entries.name: The Mutiny That Is Not Called One
entries.description: Collective refusal that stops short of open revolt, and the institution's careful avoidance of the word.

examples.text: The novel is built on whether the word applies, and declines to answer it cleanly.
Cobb's source novel treats the refusal and its punishment as one administrative sequence.
The naval-mutiny tradition tends toward the personal quarrel, which removes the collective character that defines the trope.

entries.name: The Order to Hold at All Costs
entries.description: A position designated as one to be held regardless of loss, and the arithmetic behind the designation.

examples.text: The boat's orders keep it at sea past the point of viability, and the crew's knowledge of that is the novel's pressure.
Vilsmaier's film works the German side of an encirclement held for reasons the men are not given.
The last stand is rendered as a chosen glory, which is the trope's oldest and least examined form.

entries.name: The Squad as a Household
entries.description: The small unit rendered as a domestic arrangement with roles, routines and hierarchies of its own.

examples.text: Manning's rankers organise their lives around food, shelter and each other with an exactness that makes the unit a working household.
The vehicle crews are shown living in a space too small for privacy, and the domestic detail is where the characterisation happens.
The household is real and is also the source of the series' recurring difficulty: its warmth argues that the losses purchased the bond.

entries.name: The Replacement Nobody Expects to Live
entries.description: A new arrival treated as provisional by the men he joins, and the system that produced his isolation.

examples.text: The newly arrived are treated by the veterans as an actuarial category, and the film keeps the calculation unsentimental.
Replacements arriving between campaigns are shown being assessed by veterans on a purely actuarial basis, and the series lets the calculation stand.
The newly attached specialists are protected by the plot's requirements rather than exposed to the position the film says they occupy.

entries.name: The Unit Destroyed and Reconstituted
entries.description: A formation rebuilt to strength after catastrophic loss, wearing the same designation and being a different thing.

examples.text: Myrer follows a formation across two wars and records what is lost when it is rebuilt under the same designation.
Jünger's company is rebuilt repeatedly and he notes the change in it without sentiment.
The series shows reconstitution but keeps its protagonists continuous, so the loss of unit identity is stated rather than felt.

entries.name: The Man Everyone Protects
entries.description: A soldier the unit shields — too young, too slow, too unlucky — and the arithmetic of the protection.

examples.text: Barker's patients are protected by an institution whose purpose is to return them, and the protection is legible as the system's function rather than as care.
Nguyen's account of how war memory selects its innocents illuminates why the figure recurs and what it is for.
The protected figures are shielded by the plot as well as by their comrades, and every loss is converted into a demonstration of the survivors' worth.

entries.name: The Competent Man Who Is Killed Anyway
entries.description: Skill and experience failing to protect, staged against the genre's habit of rewarding competence with survival.

examples.text: The film's crews are shown as highly trained and are lost at a rate their training does not affect, which the command plot treats as the governing fact.
Monsarrat kills competent men on a schedule that has nothing to do with their competence.
Skill is repeatedly shown producing survival, so the deaths read as exceptions to a rule the film has established.

entries.name: The Order to Leave Someone Behind
entries.description: The decision to abandon a casualty or a position, and the unit living afterwards with having made it.

examples.text: Bowden reconstructs the decisions to hold and to withdraw around specific casualties, and declines to resolve who was right.
The decision to leave a man is made under fire and is never resolved for anyone afterwards, which the film declines to relieve.
The decision is framed as a moral test with a right answer, which removes the irresolvability that makes it a trope.

entries.name: The Reunion That Cannot Happen
entries.description: Survivors meeting afterwards, or failing to, and the discovery that the unit was the only place the bond worked.

examples.text: Heinemann's survivor carries the unit alone, and the narrating voice is what remains of it.

examples.work: The Best Years of Our Lives
examples.text: Three men return to a society with no equivalent structure, and the film is honest that the bond does not transfer.
The reunion is supplied as consolation, and the film's closing movement resolves what the material leaves open.

entries.name: The Assault Across Open Ground
entries.description: The advance into unsuppressed fire, the genre's most-staged action and its clearest test of the legibility problem.

examples.text: Keegan's reconstruction of the Somme's first morning is the analytical source most subsequent fictional versions are working from.
The attack is staged as an administrative event with a predetermined outcome, and the camera refuses to make it exciting.
The final advance is powerful and is also constructed to deliver a single emotional stroke, which simplifies the mechanism that produced it.

entries.name: The Ambush
entries.description: The engagement decided in seconds by drilled reaction, frequently written as an extended running battle.

examples.text: Ackerman writes the ambush from the side laying it, where the waiting is nearly all of it and the contact is over before it is understood.
O'Brien's contacts are short, unresolved and impossible to reconstruct afterwards.
The contacts extend well past the interval doctrine and experience describe, because the form needs the duration.

entries.name: The House-to-House Fight
entries.description: Urban combat as a sequence of room-sized engagements that no headquarters can see.

examples.text: The Hue sequence reduces the war to a street and a single unlocated shooter, and the platoon's command structure dissolves into whoever can see.
Vilsmaier renders the fragmentation without supplying an overview to relieve it.
The urban and close fighting is staged as continuous spectacle with a clear field of view, which is what a city removes.

entries.name: The Sniper's Patience
entries.description: Killing at distance by a specialist, and the genre's ambivalence about the skill it depicts.

examples.text: Galloway gives the counter-sniper the waiting and withholds the satisfaction of the shot.
The role is written as a duel between specialists, which is the tradition's default and has little relation to how the task is actually employed.
The kill count functions as a scoreboard, and the film's tension is organised around whether it will rise.

entries.name: The Air Raid From Below
entries.description: Bombardment experienced by the people underneath it, without access to the aircraft or the decision.

examples.text: The bunker sequences render the raid as sound and structural failure rather than as visible attack.
Ōe's reporting works the aftermath at the level of individual survivors and their treatment.
The attack is rendered from the attacking ordnance's point of view, which is the aesthetic this trope exists to refuse.

entries.name: The Patrol That Finds Nothing
entries.description: The operation that produces no contact, no result and no narrative event, and is the majority of the war.

examples.text: The novel's realist frame is a patrol structure that generates nothing, and the fantasy is what the mind does with it.
The documentary form allows the empty patrol to be shown at its real frequency.
Each operation is made to produce an event, so the film's rhythm is the opposite of the deployment it depicts.

entries.name: The Sealed Compartment
entries.description: Combat inside a machine, where the enemy is an instrument reading and death is a failure of the hull.

examples.text: Petersen makes sound the only channel and the hull's integrity the entire plot, and the film's tension is almost wholly auditory.
Beach writes the submarine interior as a set of stations with tasks, and the enemy exists only as a bearing and a sound.
The enclosure is used for suspense while the crew retain freedom of action the form does not permit.

entries.name: The Weapon That Fails
entries.description: Equipment malfunction at the decisive moment, the genre's most available irony and its most honest technical detail.

examples.text: Caputo records weapons and radios failing from heat, wet and use as a constant background rather than at moments of crisis.
Sledge records malfunction as a constant background condition of the Pacific campaign.
Failures are staged at points of maximum tension, which converts a chronic condition into a series of reversals.

entries.name: The Supply That Does Not Arrive
entries.description: The absent resupply as the actual determinant of an operation's outcome.

examples.text: Van Creveld's account of how operations are shaped by what can be moved is the analytical basis for the trope.
The operation is defeated by what does not arrive — relief, radios, resupply — and the film keeps the failure logistical rather than heroic.
The fuel problem is present as a plot objective rather than as a condition governing everything the formation can do.

entries.name: The Rear Echelon
entries.description: The support organisation behind the fighting, usually absent from fiction and comprising most of the army.

examples.text: Heller makes the supply and administrative apparatus the novel's actual subject and the flying its symptom.
The transport operation's own history records a war fought by drivers, which fiction almost never depicts.
The rear is present and is rendered as a place where the war arrives rather than as a place that produces it.

entries.name: The Medical Chain
entries.description: The passage of a casualty from the point of wounding rearward, and the period-specific system that decides whether he lives.

examples.text: Barker works the psychiatric end of the chain and treats the return-to-duty function as the system's actual purpose.
Hemingway's ambulance service renders the chain as transport and paperwork, with the wounded moving through a system that barely registers them.
The hospital sequence is staged for scale and for the protagonist's moral education, and the triage that would structure such a ward is decorative.

entries.name: Disease, Weather and the Enemy That Is Not the Enemy
entries.description: Losses to sickness, cold, heat and accident, historically the majority and rarely the subject.

examples.text: Starvation and disease are the novel's antagonists and the enemy army barely appears.

examples.work: The Narrow Road to the Deep North
examples.text: Flanagan's camp is governed by disease, food and rain, and the guards are one pressure among several.

examples.work: The Bridge on the River Kwai
examples.text: The camp's medical reality is present and subordinated to a contest of wills between two officers.

entries.name: The Number That Becomes People
entries.description: A casualty figure stated at one level and delivered as individuals at another.

examples.text: Barker sets the closing offensive's arithmetic against a single named death, and the join is left for the reader to make.
Barker sets an offensive's stated cost against one named death, and the arithmetic is left visible on the page.
The scale is rendered structurally rather than numerically, which is effective and sidesteps the trope rather than performing it.

entries.name: The Ration, the Cigarette and the Object of Exchange
entries.description: The economy that forms inside armies and camps, where small goods acquire disproportionate value.

examples.text: Hašek's protagonist survives entirely inside an economy of small exchanges, and the novel treats it as the army's real organising system.
Levi describes the camp economy with the precision of someone who survived by understanding it.
The economy becomes a heist plot, which is entertaining and detaches the exchange from the scarcity that produces it.

entries.name: The Machine Outlasts the Men
entries.description: Equipment, formations and institutions persisting while the people in them are replaced.

examples.text: Deighton's aircraft are numbered and reassigned while the crews are replaced around them, and the squadron's continuity is administrative.
Keegan traces how a regimental identity persists across complete replacement of its personnel and what that continuity actually consists of.
The tank as continuous character is the trope, and the film supplies a final stand that gives the machine a death of its own.

entries.name: The Home That Does Not Know
entries.description: A household continuing under a war whose reality it cannot access, receiving only official information and rumour.

examples.text: Bowen renders wartime London as a state of consciousness in which information is unavailable and every relationship is affected by that.
Green's wartime London runs on official information nobody trusts and gossip everybody acts on, in the interval before the raids arrive.
The film was made as morale work and is a useful teaching case: the household knows exactly what it needs to know.

entries.name: The Telegram
entries.description: Official notification of a death, and the machinery that delivers it.

examples.text: Japrisot builds an entire novel on a notification that turns out to be incomplete, and on the bureaucracy behind it.
Brittain records the arrival of notifications repeatedly, and the repetition is the book's structure.
The notification sequence is moving and assigns the delivery to a taxi driver, which converts an administrative failure into a human-interest device.

entries.name: The Queue, the Ration Book and the Administered Life
entries.description: War experienced as bureaucracy, scarcity and forms, which is how most civilians experience most wars.

examples.text: Green writes the wartime service life as administration, waiting and social friction rather than as emergency.
Levi's account of the camp's administrative logic is the extreme case of the same phenomenon.
The administered life is rendered nostalgically through a child's pleasure in it, which is a legitimate choice that removes the pressure.

entries.name: The Cellar
entries.description: Civilians sheltering below ground during bombardment, in a space that becomes a society.

examples.text: Morris keeps a besieged city at the scale of one flat and one life, and the shelter is where the social order is renegotiated.
The below-ground world develops its own hierarchy and its own information environment.

examples.work: All the Light We Cannot See
examples.text: The cellar is a site of coincidence and convergence, which is a structural use rather than a rendering of the condition.

entries.name: The Requisitioned House
entries.description: The occupier billeted in a civilian home, and the daily proximity that occupation actually consists of.

examples.text: Vercors puts a cultivated German in the house and makes the household's silence the entire action.
Némirovsky renders the billeting from both sides at the same depth, which is what the situation requires and rarely receives.
The occupied villa is a space for private histories rather than a site of the occupation's daily pressure.

entries.name: The Road Out
entries.description: The refugee column as a place people live, with its own hierarchies, economies and duration.

examples.text: Kanafani makes the journey the entire subject and refuses the arrival that would resolve it.
Khoury renders displacement as an accumulating social world in which the road and the camp acquire their own hierarchies.
The journey is structured toward arrival, which supplies the resolution the condition does not contain.

entries.name: The Child Who Does Not Understand
entries.description: A civilian child's incomprehension used as the reader's lens, the genre's most efficient and most costly device.

examples.text: Ballard's boy misreads the war continuously and the novel never softens what is being misread.
Nosaka holds the device to an outcome it cannot console, which is what makes the use defensible.

examples.work: The Boy in the Striped Pyjamas
examples.text: The incomprehension is sustained past what the situation permits, and the ending redistributes the material's meaning toward the perpetrator's family.

entries.name: The Ordinary Day Continuing
entries.description: Normal life persisting alongside catastrophe, and the strangeness of the adjacency rather than of the catastrophe.

examples.text: Bowen's characters continue dinner parties and love affairs, and the continuation is the novel's real disquiet.
The novel tracks how a besieged routine forms and what it costs to maintain it.
The maintenance of ordinariness is made deliberate and protective, which is a fable's use of the trope and has been contested on those grounds.

entries.name: The Surrender
entries.description: The moment of giving up, staged by the genre as a decision and governed in practice by the capturing unit's circumstances.

examples.text: Bykaŭ makes capture the beginning of the moral problem rather than its resolution, and refuses to settle which prisoner chose correctly.
The account renders capture as an administrative absorption into a system, and the disputed status of the book itself is part of its record.
Captivity begins after the dangerous interval the trope is actually about, so the surrender itself is offstage.

entries.name: The Guard Who Is Also a Man
entries.description: The captor rendered from inside, and the decision every captivity narrative makes about whether to grant him consciousness.

examples.work: The Narrow Road to the Deep North
examples.text: Flanagan follows the guards into their post-war lives and gives them interiority without offering the reader relief.
The film reverses the positions and makes the custodian's judgement the subject, with the prisoners as boys.

examples.work: The Bridge on the River Kwai
examples.text: The camp commandant is granted a code and a dignity that the contest of wills requires, and the historical record around the case is contested.

entries.name: The Escape That Restores Agency
entries.description: The break-out plot, which solves captivity's structural problem by abolishing the condition it depicts.

examples.text: Renoir uses the escape structure to examine class and nation rather than to supply adventure, and the escape resolves nothing about the war.
The film is the trope's definitive form and converts imprisonment into a project with milestones.
Captivity becomes the first act of an action film, and the powerlessness that defines the condition is removed entirely.

entries.name: The Camp Economy
entries.description: The internal system of exchange, rank and favour that forms in any confined population.

examples.text: Clavell builds the novel on the camp's commercial order and on who is competent inside it.
Ballard's boy survives by understanding the internment camp's economy better than the adults do.
The economy is present as comic business, and the scarcity that generates it is not felt.

entries.name: The Occupier at the Table
entries.description: Daily domestic proximity between occupier and occupied, which is what occupation mostly consists of.

examples.text: Vercors reduces the entire situation to one house, one officer and a refusal to speak.
The series sustains the proximity across seven seasons and lets the accommodations accumulate rather than resolve.
The farce depends on the proximity while removing every consequence attached to it.

entries.name: The Gradual Accommodation
entries.description: Collaboration reached by a series of small defensible steps with no moment of decision.

examples.text: Tan renders accommodation under occupation as a sequence of survivable decisions, and the reckoning arrives only decades afterwards.
Begley's family accommodates continuously and defensibly at every step, and arrives somewhere none of them chose.
Accommodation is a posture the protagonist abandons in a single decisive scene, which is the shape the condition specifically lacks.

entries.name: The Reprisal
entries.description: Civilians killed in response to resistance action, and the arithmetic that every resistance narrative either stages or conceals.

examples.text: Melville stages the internal executions and the civilian exposure as routine administration, and prices neither for the audience.
Barry's soldier is caught between two reprisal economies at once, and the novel refuses to resolve which claim on him is legitimate.
Steinbeck's occupied town is written as morale work, and the reprisal arithmetic is resolved in favour of resistance by construction.

entries.name: The Denunciation
entries.description: The neighbour who informs, and the social system that makes informing possible.

examples.text: Denunciation is shown as an available administrative channel that ordinary grievances flow into.
Begley renders survival as continuous concealment from people who might report, which makes every social encounter a hazard.
The threat of denunciation is present and is repeatedly defused, so the ambient risk does not accumulate.

entries.name: The Resistance Cell and Its Amateurism
entries.description: Clandestine organisation by people with no training for it, and the security failures that follow.

examples.text: Melville renders the work as procedure, exhaustion and internal policing rather than as heroism.
Kanafani renders clandestine movement as improvisation by people with no training for it, and the improvisation is what kills them.
The film is explicitly a fantasy of retribution and is carded here as the clearest case of the mode it belongs to.

entries.name: The Partisan and the Uniform Question
entries.description: Irregular fighters without uniform or protected status, and the consequences the law attaches to that.

examples.text: The film puts the legal and moral status of the irregular at the centre and lets both sides argue it.
Hemingway's guerrilla band operates outside protected status and the novel treats the exposure as their governing condition.
Irregular status confers only advantages, and the legal exposure that defines the position is absent.

entries.name: The Displaced Person Who Cannot Return
entries.description: The end of a war leaving people with nowhere that will receive them.

examples.text: Khoury's camp is decades old and the novel is structured around the impossibility of the return it keeps describing.
Nguyen works the condition after it has become permanent and unremarkable to everyone but the displaced.
The narrative resolves in arrival and possession, which is the ending the condition does not supply.

entries.name: The Liberation That Is Not One
entries.description: The arrival of the liberating force, and the discovery that it does not restore what was taken.

examples.text: Kertész's return is the novel's most disquieting passage precisely because nothing is restored and the narrator declines to perform gratitude.
The end of occupation resolves into a subsequent emergency, and the novel refuses to treat either as an ending.
Escape functions as full resolution, which is the form the trope exists to complicate.

entries.name: The Massacre Reconstructed
entries.description: An atrocity assembled from testimony and record, with the reconstruction's limits part of the work. Real events and real dead; the analysis is of the published work.

examples.text: Klimov stages a village's destruction through a boy who cannot process it, refusing both explanation and spectacle, and the film has no consoling movement anywhere in it.
Diop distributes narration across perpetrators, victims and returnees, so no single account is allowed to stand as the event.
The genocide is organised around one rescuer's competence, which supplies the audience a position inside the event that most people did not have.

entries.name: The Order Nobody Records
entries.description: The instruction that produces an atrocity, given ambiguously and without paper, and the resulting absence of an author.

examples.text: Littell renders the bureaucratic production of mass killing in administrative detail, and the novel is contested on precisely that ground.
The participants describe their own actions without a documented order behind them, and the absence of one is the film's finding.
The film's structure requires attributable decisions, which is a courtroom's requirement rather than the mechanism's shape.

entries.name: The Perpetrator With an Inner Life
entries.description: Granting interiority to someone who commits atrocity, the genre's most disputed technique. Contested.

examples.text: The novel's central technique is exactly this, and the objection to it is a serious critical position the pack records rather than settles.
The perpetrators' domestic ordinariness is rendered without access to their justification, which is a third position between granting and refusing interiority.
The perpetrator's interiority is routed through an incapacity that functions as mitigation, and the novel has been contested on that basis.

entries.name: The Bystander
entries.description: The person who saw, did nothing, and continued — the position most readers actually occupy.

examples.text: The household's proximity to the killing is total and its attention to it is nil, which is the position rendered exactly.
The film's most useful passages are the ones showing an administrative and social world proceeding around the killing without remark.
The film supplies a bystander who becomes a rescuer, which is the historically exceptional case and the one the audience is invited to occupy.

entries.name: The Denial and the Later Exhumation
entries.description: An atrocity denied at the time and established later by physical evidence, and the interval between.

examples.text: The novel is built on the return to a site whose evidence is unavoidable and whose account is still contested.
The film's subject is the recovery of a suppressed memory of proximity to a massacre, and it does not adjudicate responsibility.
The evidence sequence is powerful and the film's resolution is supplied by an individual reunion.

entries.name: The Child Soldier
entries.description: A combatant below the age of consent to combat, simultaneously victim and perpetrator.

examples.text: Kourouma's unstable register refuses to be read as authenticity, which is the form's central technical problem solved.
Saro-Wiwa invents a language for the position rather than transcribing one; the author was executed in 1995, which the pack states as biographical fact.
The performance and the photography are strong and the film's beauty repeatedly works against the material.

entries.name: The Interrogation
entries.description: Coercive questioning, and the genre's persistent claim that it produces information.

examples.text: The interrogation is reconstructed decades later from its consequences, and the film keeps the practice institutional rather than personal.
Morris assembles the practice from its participants' own accounts, and what emerges is procedure rather than extraction.
The film's structure attributes an operational result to coercive interrogation, a causal claim that was publicly contested by senators with access to the underlying record.

entries.name: The Trial That Comes Later
entries.description: The tribunal arriving years afterwards, working on documents, answering a legal question rather than a historical one.

examples.text: Schlink stages the trial as a proceeding that produces a verdict and no understanding, which is the accurate version.
The legal and investigative apparatus arrives generations later and reconstructs something no proceeding could have established at the time.
The trial is made to deliver historical adjudication and moral resolution together, which is what tribunals cannot do.

entries.name: The Order Refused
entries.description: The soldier who declines an unlawful instruction, rare in the record and common in fiction.

examples.text: The refusal is made by a private with no leverage, and the institution's response is the film's subject.
The refusal costs everything and buys nothing, and the novel does not present it as an example.
Refusal is vindicated by a courtroom and produces a demonstrable institutional consequence, which is the outcome the record rarely supplies.

entries.name: The Cover-Up as Paperwork
entries.description: Concealment achieved through routine reporting rather than conspiracy.

examples.text: The account's own contested provenance demonstrates how a war narrative can enter the record and remain there unexamined for decades.
The absence of any concealment at all, decades later, is the film's most disturbing structural fact.
The concealment is personified in a single commanding figure whose confession resolves it.

entries.name: The Weapon Used on People Who Cannot Answer
entries.description: Overwhelming force applied to an undefended population, from the air or at range.

examples.text: Vonnegut declines to narrate the firebombing directly and structures the whole novel around that refusal.
Ōe works the aftermath at the level of individual survivors and their long medical afterlives.
The satire is precise about the system and necessarily abstract about the people underneath it.

entries.name: The Photograph That Circulates
entries.description: An image of atrocity entering public circulation, and the question of what looking at it accomplishes.

examples.text: Sontag's account of what war photography does to its viewers is the standard treatment and revises her own earlier position.
The film's subject is a set of photographs and the institutional context that produced them rather than the acts alone.
The film's images of atrocity circulate as evidence within its own plot, and their effect on the outside world is the one thing it cannot show.

entries.name: The New Weapon
entries.description: A novel capability introduced as decisive, whose second-order effects exceed its direct ones.

examples.text: Hackett's speculative capabilities are laid out as doctrine, and the book now reads as a document of its own assumptions.
Clancy's premise is a capability whose existence changes what everyone else must do, which is the accurate shape of the effect.
The wonder weapon works exactly as promised, which is the form the historical pattern never takes.

entries.name: The Kill at Distance
entries.description: Remote killing, and the genre's competing claims about what it does to the operator.

examples.text: The film distributes a single strike decision across a chain of people, none of whom is in the country concerned.
The occupational conditions — the shift, the commute, the domestic compression — are the film's actual subject.
The operator's injury is written on the ground-combat model, which the survey evidence on remote crews does not support.

entries.name: The Insurgent Who Is Not a Character
entries.description: An adversary present only as a threat, and the argument the absence makes.

examples.text: Both organisations are given command structures and deliberations, so neither side is available to the audience purely as a threat.
Coetzee's barbarians are never rendered and the novel makes that absence its explicit subject rather than its method.
The adversaries function almost entirely as a count, and the one village granted specificity is granted it for its usefulness to the protagonists.

entries.name: The Technological Advantage That Does Not End the War
entries.description: Overwhelming material superiority producing tactical success and political failure.

examples.text: Greene's American arrives with resources and a theory and produces consequences neither can control.
The documentary records a year of materially dominant operations that alter nothing, and the outpost is abandoned afterwards.
Bowden's reconstruction is meticulous at the tactical level and the political frame around it is largely outside the book's scope.

entries.name: The Simulation and the Briefing Room
entries.description: War rehearsed, modelled and gamed before it is fought, and the gap between the model and the event.

examples.text: Ackerman and Stavridis write a war as a sequence of modelled escalations, and the model's failure is the plot.
The film's subject is the difference between a simulation and a decision, which it states directly.
The simulation-as-reality device is the science-fiction pack's material, and it inverts the relationship this trope describes.

entries.name: The Contractor and the Privatised War
entries.description: Armed personnel outside the military chain of command, with different legal exposure and different incentives.

examples.text: Powers's deployment is populated by the commercial and administrative apparatus attached to it, which the novel treats as part of the war rather than adjacent to it.
Swofford records the commercial and media apparatus attached to a deployment as part of its daily texture.
The contractor sequence is a well-made set-piece and the structural questions the position raises are not engaged.

entries.name: The Ongoing War With No Ending
entries.description: A conflict that continues past every point that would conventionally end a narrative.

examples.text: Powers finds shape in repetition and aftermath because the deployment provides none.
Coetzee's frontier war has no beginning, no enemy that appears and no conclusion, which is the point.
The serial form supplies escalating crises with resolutions, which is the opposite of the condition.

entries.name: The Veteran of a War Nobody Names
entries.description: The returning participant of a conflict the home society does not recognise as a war.

examples.text: Fountain's soldiers are celebrated by a public that has no idea what they did or where.
Buzzati's officer spends a career waiting for a war that would give his service meaning.
The unrecognised veteran becomes an action premise, and the recognition problem is resolved through violence.

entries.name: The Homecoming That Does Not Land
entries.description: Physical return without any corresponding arrival, and a society with no structure to receive it.

examples.work: The Best Years of Our Lives
examples.text: Three returns are followed in parallel and none of them resolves into the life the men left.
Hemingway's story is the compact founding instance and its refusal of event is the technique.
The return sequences are powerful and the film's structure supplies a communal resolution the material resists.

entries.name: The Question Nobody Should Ask
entries.description: Civilians asking a veteran what it was like, or whether they killed anyone, and the impossibility of the answer.

examples.text: Klay opens with the question and lets the answer fail in several directions across the collection.
The novel is a sustained rendering of civilians asking, and of the performance required to answer.
The disconnection is stated in voice-over rather than worked through any relation the film dramatises.

entries.name: The Nightmare and the Flashback
entries.description: Intrusive recollection as the genre's standard signifier of aftermath, and the most conventionalised material in the pack.

examples.text: Heinemann relocates the intrusion into the narrating voice, so it is a property of the telling rather than a scene.
West's shell-shocked officer is treated by a system whose stated aim is restoration to his prior life, and the novel questions what that would mean.
The flashback is the mechanism that licenses the action, which converts a symptom into a plot device.

entries.name: Moral Injury Without a Wound
entries.description: Aftermath caused by what was done rather than by what was survived.

examples.text: The protagonist's injury is entirely about having failed to prevent something, and the film keeps it there.
Nguyen's narrator is damaged by his own actions and by his knowledge of them, not by threat.
The aftermath is rendered almost entirely as fear and damage, with what the characters did while there left largely outside the account.

entries.name: The Family That Receives Him
entries.description: The household absorbing a returned participant, and the second war conducted inside it.

examples.text: West works the entire book inside the domestic reception and makes the household the site of the war's continuation.
Barry's returning soldier finds a home that has changed its politics in his absence, so the return is doubly impossible.
The household absorbs the return without friction, and the war becomes one episode in a life rather than a condition the home must accommodate.

entries.name: The Second Generation
entries.description: Children carrying a war they did not experience, transmitted through silence and fragments.

examples.text: Spiegelman makes the transmission itself the book's subject, including the son's failure to receive it and his discomfort at making a work from it.
Satrapi's narrator inherits a revolution and a war partly through what her family will not say.
The inherited search is structured toward a discovery that resolves it, which is the shape the condition lacks.

entries.name: The Commemoration
entries.description: Public memory of a war, and fiction's relationship to the account a nation settles on.

examples.text: Nguyen examines how a war's memory is produced and by whom, on both sides of the same conflict.
Sontag's account of public looking is directly about what commemoration does and does not accomplish.
The film renders a national account structurally and elegantly, and the commemorative function is built into the form rather than examined by it.

entries.name: The War That Will Not Close
entries.description: The conflict that remains unresolved in a society for generations, and the fiction written inside that condition.

examples.text: Bao Ninh's novel is written from inside a victory and finds no closure in it, which is why it was suppressed and then read as the war's essential account.
Nguyen writes people for whom the war ended decades ago and has not concluded, and the collection declines to supply an ending for any of them.
The war is absorbed into a national biography that resolves it, which is the version of national memory the trope exists to describe.

entries.name: Homer
entries.description: The founding text of the Western war canon, and the founding statement of the interiority problem.
entries.meta: Greek, traditionally dated to the eighth century BCE; the attribution and the singular authorship are both long-contested and the pack states that rather than settling it.
entries.knownFor: The Iliad, and the convention set that later war narrative is still arguing with.
entries.signature: The signature is the granting of a father, a city and a death to the man about to be killed by the protagonist, which is the earliest surviving instance of the interiority budget being spent on the enemy.

works.title: Iliad
works.note: traditional dating; composition and authorship contested

works.title: Odyssey
works.note: the return narrative, and the aftermath's founding text

entries.name: Thucydides
entries.description: The war history that is also a work of tragic form, and the ur-text of command under necessity.
entries.meta: Greek, c. 460 – c. 400 BCE. An Athenian general exiled after a command failure, who wrote the war he had fought in.
entries.knownFor: The History of the Peloponnesian War, and the Melian Dialogue's account of what power says when it is not pretending.
entries.signature: The signature is the composed speech — arguments reconstructed as they must have been made — which is a fictional technique deployed inside a work claiming to be a record.

entries.name: Xenophon
entries.description: The retreat narrative, and the earliest sustained small-unit account in the Western tradition.
entries.meta: Greek, c. 430 – 354 BCE. A participant in the march he describes, who wrote it in the third person and under another name.
entries.knownFor: The Anabasis, and the long withdrawal of a mercenary army through hostile country.
entries.signature: The signature is the logistical particular — food, distance, water, whether the men will follow — treated as the substance of the narrative rather than as its background.

works.title: Anabasis
works.note: published under the name Themistogenes of Syracuse

entries.name: Stendhal
entries.description: The novelist who first put a reader inside a battle nobody in it can understand.
entries.meta: French, 1783–1842. Marie-Henri Beyle served in Napoleon's administration and saw the retreat from Moscow, and published under a pen name.
entries.knownFor: The Waterloo sequence of La Chartreuse de Parme, the founding scene of the legibility problem.
entries.signature: The signature is withheld orientation — the protagonist is given events without their relation, and the narration declines to supply the overview that would make the day cohere.

entries.name: Leo Tolstoy
entries.description: The great argument that battles are not commanded and history is not steered.
entries.meta: Russian, 1828–1910. An artillery officer at Sevastopol who wrote the siege while it was under way.
entries.knownFor: War and Peace, and the Sevastopol sketches that preceded it by a decade.
entries.signature: The signature is the structural rebuttal: the same events rendered at staff level and at the level of the man in the line, with the two accounts left conspicuously unreconciled.

entries.name: Ambrose Bierce
entries.description: The Civil War short story built as a machine for destroying consolation.
entries.meta: American, born 1842; disappeared in Mexico in late 1913 or early 1914 and was never traced. He fought at Shiloh and Chickamauga and was severely wounded at Kennesaw Mountain.
entries.knownFor: Tales of Soldiers and Civilians, and the refusal of any redemptive reading of combat.
entries.signature: The signature is the withheld reversal — a story constructed so that its final sentence retrospectively removes whatever meaning the reader had been assembling.

entries.name: Stephen Crane
entries.description: The combat novel written by a man who had never been in one, and the standing question's founding counter-example.
entries.meta: American, 1871–1900. He wrote The Red Badge of Courage before witnessing any war, and only afterwards worked as a correspondent in Greece and Cuba.
entries.knownFor: The Red Badge of Courage, and the phenomenological accuracy of a battle he reached entirely by imagination and reading.
entries.signature: The signature is sustained restriction to one frightened consciousness that never learns what happened, with the prose refusing every opportunity to explain the day to the reader.

works.title: The Open Boat and Other Tales of Adventure

entries.name: Henri Barbusse
entries.description: The first major combatant novel of the war, written and published while it was still being fought.
entries.meta: French, 1873–1935. He enlisted at forty-one, served in the infantry, and wrote the novel from the line and from hospital.
entries.knownFor: Le Feu, which took the Prix Goncourt in 1916 while the war had two years to run.
entries.signature: The signature is the squad rendered as a collective voice in its own vernacular, with the narration distributed across the group rather than centred on a protagonist.

entries.name: Erich Maria Remarque
entries.description: The definitive statement that the patriotic war novel was no longer writable, and the genre's first global bestseller.
entries.meta: German, 1898–1970. His own front-line service was brief — conscripted in November 1916, at the front from June 1917, wounded on 31 July 1917 and hospitalised until the Armistice, roughly six weeks in the line — a fact the popular account of the book routinely overstates.
entries.knownFor: Im Westen nichts Neues, its immediate international success, and its banning and burning in Germany.
entries.signature: The signature is the flat declarative sentence applied to atrocity, with the withholding of commentary doing the moral work that rhetoric would have undone.

works.title: Zeit zu leben und Zeit zu sterben

entries.name: Ernst Jünger
entries.description: The opposite pole to Remarque: the same war rendered as an experience with value, without repentance.
entries.meta: German, 1895–1998. A much-decorated storm-troop officer, wounded repeatedly, who revised the book across six decades and lived to be a hundred and two.
entries.knownFor: In Stahlgewittern, and a lifelong refusal to disown the experience the Anglophone canon treats as self-evidently disowning.
entries.signature: The signature is precise observational description without moral framing, which produces a text readers have used to argue both for and against war for a century.

works.title: In Stahlgewittern
works.note: revised repeatedly across the author's lifetime

entries.name: Jaroslav Hašek
entries.description: The founding text of the satiric war novel, and its most influential unfinished book.
entries.meta: Czech, 1883–1923. He served in the Austro-Hungarian army, was captured on the Eastern Front, and died with the novel four volumes in and nowhere near done.
entries.knownFor: Osudy dobrého vojáka Švejka, and a protagonist whose apparent idiocy is the only sane position available.
entries.signature: The signature is the digression that never returns — an anecdote inside an anecdote inside an order, which enacts the bureaucracy it describes.

works.title: Osudy dobrého vojáka Švejka
works.note: left unfinished at the author's death

entries.name: Frederic Manning
entries.description: The ranker's war in the ranker's language, suppressed in its unexpurgated form for forty years.
entries.meta: Australian-British, 1882–1935. He served as a private in the ranks — not, as is often stated, as an officer — and published the novel anonymously.
entries.knownFor: The Middle Parts of Fortune, and its expurgated edition Her Privates We, which was the only text available for decades.
entries.signature: The signature is the rendering of soldiers' actual speech at full strength, including the profanity whose removal produced the expurgated text, and the treatment of the unit as a working household.

entries.name: Robert Graves
entries.description: The memoir written as a demolition of the entire culture that produced the war.
entries.meta: British, 1895–1985. A Royal Welch Fusiliers officer, reported dead of wounds in 1916, who left England after the book and did not return to live there.
entries.knownFor: Goodbye to All That, and the deliberate finality of its title.
entries.signature: The signature is the anecdote deployed as evidence — school, regiment, family and war presented as one continuous system of absurdity, with the tone kept dry throughout.

entries.name: Siegfried Sassoon
entries.description: The decorated officer whose public protest against the war was answered with a psychiatric diagnosis.
entries.meta: British, 1886–1967. He was sent to Craiglockhart after his 1917 declaration against the war's continuation, and the episode became the material of a later novel tradition.
entries.knownFor: The Sherston trilogy and the war poems, and the protest itself.
entries.signature: The signature is the double register — a pastoral, mannered surface holding an anger the prose never states directly, which is why the poems and the memoirs read so differently.

entries.name: Ludwig Renn
entries.description: The flat, unliterary combat register, written under a pen name taken from the novel's own narrator.
entries.meta: German, 1889–1979. Born Arnold Vieth von Golßenau, an officer of noble family who became a communist and took his protagonist's name as his own.
entries.knownFor: Krieg, and a deliberately affectless prose that refuses both heroism and protest.
entries.signature: The signature is the removal of interpretation: events are reported in sequence at uniform emphasis, so that the reader supplies every judgement the text declines to make.

works.title: Krieg
works.note: as Ludwig Renn, the narrator's name

entries.name: Arnold Zweig
entries.description: Military justice as the war's clearest self-portrait.
entries.meta: German, 1887–1968. He served in the ranks and later on the Eastern Front press staff, and built a novel cycle around a single judicial killing.
entries.knownFor: Der Streit um den Sergeanten Grischa, in which an army's bureaucracy executes a man everyone knows to be innocent.
entries.signature: The signature is procedural inevitability — the machinery is shown functioning correctly at every stage, and the correctness is the horror.

works.title: Der Streit um den Sergeanten Grischa

entries.name: Emilio Lussu
entries.description: The Alpine front, and the murderousness of one's own command as the book's real subject.
entries.meta: Italian, 1890–1975. An officer of the Sassari Brigade who later became an anti-fascist politician and wrote the book in exile.
entries.knownFor: Un anno sull'Altipiano, and its portrait of commanders spending men on impossible attacks.
entries.signature: The signature is dry comic understatement applied to lethal incompetence, which makes the arithmetic legible without editorialising it.

entries.name: Ford Madox Ford
entries.description: The war placed inside a modernist consciousness rather than reported from a trench.
entries.meta: British, 1873–1939. He served in the Welch Regiment at over forty, was concussed at the Somme, and wrote the tetralogy across the following decade.
entries.knownFor: Parade's End, and the rendering of shell shock from inside the syntax rather than as a described condition.
entries.signature: The signature is the interrupted sentence and the time-shift — the prose fractures where the mind does, so the technique carries the diagnosis.

works.title: The Good Soldier
works.note: not a war novel despite the title

entries.name: Louis-Ferdinand Céline
entries.description: The war as the founding disgust of a whole prose style. The author later wrote antisemitic pamphlets and collaborated; the pack states the record plainly and adjudicates nothing.
entries.meta: French, 1894–1961. Born Louis-Ferdinand Destouches, wounded and decorated in 1914, later the author of antisemitic pamphlets, a collaborator who fled France in 1944, and convicted in absentia before an amnesty.
entries.knownFor: Voyage au bout de la nuit, and a vernacular style that changed French prose.
entries.signature: The signature is spoken-language syntax with ellipsis and interruption, applied to a narrator whose contempt extends to everything including himself.

works.title: Voyage au bout de la nuit

entries.name: C. S. Forester
entries.description: The command novel and the naval series, from a writer who invented both templates.
entries.meta: British, 1899–1966. Born Cecil Louis Troughton Smith; medically rejected for service in the First World War, he wrote its command novel and then the Napoleonic sequence that shaped the genre.
entries.knownFor: The General, and the Hornblower novels.
entries.signature: The signature is command psychology rendered without irony — a limited man executing his duty inside his own limitations, presented for the reader to judge rather than judged by the narration.

entries.category: The Great War: Women and the Home Front
entries.name: Vera Brittain
entries.description: The war as bereavement, written from the position of the woman who survives everyone.
entries.meta: British, 1893–1970. A Voluntary Aid Detachment nurse in London, Malta and France, who lost her fiancé, her brother and two close friends.
entries.knownFor: Testament of Youth, and the transformation of private loss into the era's central civilian document.
entries.signature: The signature is the accumulating notification — the book's structure is the repeated arrival of news, and its power is in the repetition rather than in any single death.

entries.category: The Great War: Women and the Home Front
entries.name: Rebecca West
entries.description: Shell shock seen entirely from the household, in the war's first year of aftermath.
entries.meta: British, 1892–1983. Born Cicily Isabel Fairfield, she published under a pen name taken from an Ibsen character.
entries.knownFor: The Return of the Soldier, published while the war was still being fought.
entries.signature: The signature is the domestic frame holding a clinical subject — the war never appears, and the entire condition is rendered through three women's competing claims on one damaged man.

works.title: The Return of the Soldier
works.note: as Rebecca West, a pen name

entries.category: The Great War: Women and the Home Front
entries.name: Ellen N. La Motte
entries.description: Nurse's sketches so unsparing they were suppressed in wartime Britain and France.
entries.meta: American, 1873–1961. A trained nurse who worked in a French field hospital and published the book in 1916, after which it was banned in both countries until after the war.
entries.knownFor: The Backwash of War, and its refusal to supply any consoling account of the wounded.
entries.signature: The signature is the clinical vignette without frame — short pieces ending exactly where the material stops, with no closing gesture toward meaning.

works.title: The Backwash of War
works.note: suppressed in Britain and France during the war

entries.category: The Great War: Women and the Home Front
entries.name: Mary Borden
entries.description: Formally radical field-hospital prose, written by a woman who funded and ran the hospital.
entries.meta: American-British, 1886–1968. She financed and directed a mobile surgical unit on the French front, and wrote the book from inside it.
entries.knownFor: The Forbidden Zone, and prose that abandons narrative shape in favour of the ward's own rhythm.
entries.signature: The signature is the fragment sequence — sketches, prose poems and dialogues assembled without connective tissue, which renders triage as a form rather than as a scene.

works.title: The Forbidden Zone
works.note: written during the war, published a decade later

entries.category: The Great War: Women and the Home Front
entries.name: Evadne Price
entries.description: Commissioned as a parody of Remarque and delivered instead as the ambulance driver's war.
entries.meta: Australian-British, 1888–1985. Born Eva Grace Price in New South Wales; the widely repeated birth year of 1896 and the claim of birth at sea originate with the author herself and are reproduced in standard reference works.
entries.knownFor: Not So Quiet…, published under the pseudonym Helen Zenna Smith, and its refusal of the commission it was given.
entries.signature: The signature is sustained second-person address and present tense, which puts the reader in the ambulance and denies the retrospective distance the memoir tradition assumes.

works.title: Not So Quiet… Stepdaughters of War

entries.category: The Great War: Women and the Home Front
entries.name: Willa Cather
entries.description: The American war novel written by a non-combatant, awarded the Pulitzer, and criticised for both ever since.
entries.meta: American, 1873–1947. She built the novel partly from a cousin's letters and from the diary of an army doctor, and won the Pulitzer for it in 1923.
entries.knownFor: One of Ours, and the durable argument about whether she was entitled to write it.
entries.signature: The signature is the prairie novel's method applied to the war — the same patient attention to an ordinary interior life, which is precisely what her critics objected to.

entries.name: Norman Mailer
entries.description: The cross-section platoon at its most ambitious, and the American war novel's founding post-war statement.
entries.meta: American, 1923–2007. He served in the Pacific with a reconnaissance platoon and published the novel at twenty-five.
entries.knownFor: The Naked and the Dead, and the ambition to make a platoon carry a society.
entries.signature: The signature is the interpolated biography — the Time Machine sections that stop the war to deliver a man's whole civilian life, which is where the demographic argument enters the form.

entries.name: James Jones
entries.description: The peacetime army and the battle as attrition, from a writer who was at Pearl Harbor and Guadalcanal.
entries.meta: American, 1921–1977. He was wounded on Guadalcanal, and wrote three novels tracking one army from before the war to after it.
entries.knownFor: From Here to Eternity, which took the National Book Award in 1952, and The Thin Red Line.
entries.signature: The signature is the distributed company — attention spread across a dozen men with no protagonist rescued from the arithmetic, so the deaths land as accounting rather than as tragedy.

entries.name: Joseph Heller
entries.description: The bureaucratic loop as the war's real logic, and the satiric tradition's most influential twentieth-century text.
entries.meta: American, 1923–1999. He flew sixty missions as a bombardier in Italy and took thirteen years to write the novel.
entries.knownFor: Catch-22, and a title that entered the language as a description of institutional entrapment.
entries.signature: The signature is comic register broken exactly once, deliberately and late, with the novel's structure built around the break rather than around the plot.

entries.name: Kurt Vonnegut
entries.description: The unwritable book written as its own failure to be written.
entries.meta: American, 1922–2007. Captured in the Ardennes, he survived the firebombing of Dresden in a meat locker as a prisoner of war, and took over twenty years to find a form for it.
entries.knownFor: Slaughterhouse-Five, and the refusal to narrate the bombing directly.
entries.signature: The signature is the unstuck chronology plus the repeated formula after each death, which accretes into an argument about numbness that no single instance could make.

entries.name: Herman Wouk
entries.description: Command, competence and institutional loyalty, argued from inside rather than against.
entries.meta: American, 1915–2019. A Pacific minesweeper officer who lived to a hundred and three and kept publishing into his nineties.
entries.knownFor: The Caine Mutiny, which took the Pulitzer in 1952, and the two-volume war chronicle that followed two decades later.
entries.signature: The signature is the withheld verdict — the reader is invited to condemn a commander and then shown the case for the institution, with neither position finally endorsed.

entries.name: John Hersey
entries.description: The novelist who won a Pulitzer for fiction and then changed the form with a piece of reportage.
entries.meta: American, 1914–1993. A war correspondent who took the Pulitzer for fiction in 1945 and published Hiroshima the following year, filling an entire issue of a magazine.
entries.knownFor: Hiroshima, and its rendering of a nuclear attack through six individual survivors.
entries.signature: The signature is the plain reportorial sentence applied to the unprecedented, with the refusal of rhetoric doing the work that rhetoric would have destroyed.

entries.name: Anton Myrer
entries.description: The career-officer novel, and the most influential war novel inside the American officer corps.
entries.meta: American, 1922–1996. A Marine wounded in the Pacific, whose novel became required reading on professional military lists long after his literary reputation faded.
entries.knownFor: Once an Eagle, and its two-officer structure contrasting the professional soldier with the careerist.
entries.signature: The signature is the paired career — two men followed across fifty years so that institutional virtue and institutional ambition can be compared at every rank.

entries.name: Evelyn Waugh
entries.description: The war as the death of an idea of honour, written by a man who went looking for one.
entries.meta: British, 1903–1966. He served with the Royal Marines and the Commandos, including in Crete and Yugoslavia, and wrote the trilogy across the following decade.
entries.knownFor: Sword of Honour, and its protagonist's progressive discovery that the crusade he enlisted for does not exist.
entries.signature: The signature is comic social observation carrying a tragic argument — the absurdity is rendered as farce while the moral loss accumulates underneath it unremarked.

entries.name: Nicholas Monsarrat
entries.description: The Atlantic convoy war, and command exhaustion rendered as an accumulating condition.
entries.meta: British, 1910–1979. He served in corvettes and frigates on Atlantic escort duty and commanded a frigate by the war's end.
entries.knownFor: The Cruel Sea, and the sea itself as the book's stated antagonist.
entries.signature: The signature is attrition without emphasis — competent men are killed by circumstance on a schedule indifferent to their competence, and the prose declines to mark the deaths as events.

works.title: The Ship That Died of Shame

entries.name: Len Deighton
entries.description: The bomber raid narrated from both ends of it, and the occupation counterfactual.
entries.meta: British, 1929–2026. He died in March 2026; a former RAF photographer and illustrator who researched his war novels to documentary standard.
entries.knownFor: Bomber, which follows one raid from the aircraft and from the German town beneath, and SS-GB.
entries.signature: The signature is structural symmetry as moral argument — the equivalence between bomber crew and bombed civilians is made by the book's architecture rather than asserted in its prose.

entries.name: David Malouf
entries.description: Captivity and its sixty-year aftermath, in a body of work that treats war as something that keeps arriving.
entries.meta: Australian, 1934–2026. He died in April 2026; a poet and novelist whose war fiction runs from the Western Front to the Thai-Burma Railway.
entries.knownFor: The Great World, and Fly Away Peter's rendering of the Western Front from a Queensland bird sanctuary.
entries.signature: The signature is the long retrospect — the war given a few chapters and its consequences given fifty years, so that duration rather than event carries the book's weight.

entries.category: The Second World War: The Home Front and the Blitz
entries.name: Elizabeth Bowen
entries.description: The Blitz as an altered state of consciousness rather than as a series of raids.
entries.meta: Irish-British, 1899–1973. She worked as an air-raid warden in London and reported to the Ministry of Information on Irish neutrality, and wrote the war as it was happening.
entries.knownFor: The Heat of the Day, and short stories in which wartime London is a condition of perception.
entries.signature: The signature is the wartime present tense of consciousness — an atmosphere in which nothing is reliably knowable, applied to a plot that turns on exactly that unreliability.

entries.category: The Second World War: The Home Front and the Blitz
entries.name: Henry Green
entries.description: The home front written during it, by a novelist serving in the wartime fire service.
entries.meta: British, 1905–1973. Born Henry Vincent Yorke, he served in the Auxiliary Fire Service through the Blitz and published under a pen name.
entries.knownFor: Caught, and its rendering of the interval before the raids as the war's actual texture.
entries.signature: The signature is the elided article and the broken idiom — a prose deliberately roughened so that speech and thought arrive without literary smoothing.

works.title: Caught
works.note: as Henry Green, a pen name
