entries.category: The Second World War: The Home Front and the Blitz
entries.name: Olivia Manning
entries.description: War as displacement, tracked across a whole civilian marriage and three countries.
entries.meta: British, 1908–1980. She and her husband fled Romania, then Greece, then to Egypt and Palestine, and she wrote the six novels from that experience across twenty years.
entries.knownFor: The Balkan Trilogy and The Levant Trilogy, following two civilians retreating ahead of a war.
entries.signature: The signature is the marriage as the unit of narration — the war is experienced entirely through what it does to one relationship's daily negotiation.

entries.category: The Second World War: The Home Front and the Blitz
entries.name: Rose Macaulay
entries.description: The ruined city as a psychological condition, written entirely in the aftermath.
entries.meta: British, 1881–1958. She lost her flat and her library to the Blitz, and wrote the ruins as a landscape people came to inhabit.
entries.knownFor: The World My Wilderness, in which bombed London is a wilderness that children colonise.
entries.signature: The signature is ruin as freedom and as damage simultaneously — the wrecked city rendered as a place with its own social order rather than as the absence of one.

entries.category: The Second World War: The Home Front and the Blitz
entries.name: Patrick Hamilton
entries.description: War as accumulated small humiliation in a boarding house, with no front anywhere in sight.
entries.meta: British, 1904–1962. He wrote the wartime English interior as a place of petty tyranny and thwarted lives.
entries.knownFor: The Slaves of Solitude, set in a wartime boarding house outside London.
entries.signature: The signature is social claustrophobia rendered at conversational scale — the war present only as rationing, blackout and the impossibility of privacy.

entries.category: The Second World War: The Home Front and the Blitz
entries.name: Elizabeth Taylor
entries.description: The officer's wife, and the domestic register applied to a war happening entirely elsewhere.
entries.meta: British, 1912–1975. Her first novel is set in wartime lodgings and treats the war as the condition under which an ordinary marriage is conducted.
entries.knownFor: At Mrs Lippincote's, and a body of work that made the domestic interior a serious subject.
entries.signature: The signature is the precisely observed social surface holding an unstated dissatisfaction, with the war supplying the pressure and never the subject.

entries.name: Heinrich Böll
entries.description: The returning soldier and the fatherless household, from the Nobel laureate of the German post-war reckoning.
entries.meta: German, 1917–1985. He served six years in the Wehrmacht on several fronts, was wounded four times, and received the Nobel in Literature in 1972.
entries.knownFor: The Heimkehrer fiction, and a body of work about what the war left in German domestic life.
entries.signature: The signature is the compressed short form — a return, a room, a meal — carrying a national condition without ever describing it directly.

entries.name: Wolfgang Borchert
entries.description: The returning-soldier play written by a dying veteran, first broadcast the day before his death.
entries.meta: German, 1921–1947. Imprisoned twice by the regime for statements against it, invalided from the Eastern Front, he died at twenty-six with the play about to be staged.
entries.knownFor: Draußen vor der Tür, the founding text of German Trümmerliteratur.
entries.signature: The signature is the expressionist compression of a whole return into a single night, with a protagonist who cannot get anyone to admit he has come back.

works.title: Draußen vor der Tür
works.note: broadcast the day before the author's death

entries.name: Gert Ledig
entries.description: The two most physically unbearable German war novels, driven out of print for decades and recovered only in the 1990s.
entries.meta: German, 1921–1999. Severely wounded on the Eastern Front, he wrote two novels that West German readers rejected, and lived to see them recovered as major works.
entries.knownFor: Die Stalinorgel and Vergeltung, and prose that refuses the reader any vantage from which the action would cohere.
entries.signature: The signature is the rotating fragment — the narration moves between men who each see only their own metre of the line, and dies with them mid-scene.

entries.name: Anna Seghers
entries.description: Escape from a camp with the population itself as the terrain to be crossed.
entries.meta: German, 1900–1983. A communist who fled Germany in 1933 and wrote the novel in exile in France and Mexico, later returning to the German Democratic Republic.
entries.knownFor: Das siebte Kreuz, written and published in exile while the camps it described were operating.
entries.signature: The signature is the distributed moral test — a fugitive passes through dozens of ordinary lives, and each person's decision about him is the book's real material.

entries.name: Günter Grass
entries.description: The German war from inside German guilt, by a Nobel laureate whose own war record was disclosed late and became part of the record.
entries.meta: German, 1927–2015. Nobel laureate in Literature in 1999; in 2006 he disclosed that he had served in the Waffen-SS as a teenage conscript, having not stated it publicly for six decades. The disclosure and the controversy following it are stated here as record.
entries.knownFor: Die Blechtrommel, and a career spent insisting that Germany confront its war.
entries.signature: The signature is the grotesque unreliable narrator — a witness whose deformity or refusal to grow makes the national material narratable at all.

entries.name: Lothar-Günther Buchheim
entries.description: The sealed-crew novel's definitive text, from a war correspondent who made the patrol.
entries.meta: German, 1918–2007. He sailed as a war correspondent aboard a U-boat and spent thirty years turning the patrol into a novel.
entries.knownFor: Das Boot, and the enclosure of an entire war inside one hull.
entries.signature: The signature is sound as the only channel — the enemy exists as an instrument reading, and the tension is almost wholly auditory.

entries.name: W. G. Sebald
entries.description: The argument that German literature failed to write its own air war, made by a novelist who then wrote around the gap.
entries.meta: German, 1944–2001. Born in the last year of the war and long resident in England, he delivered the lectures that became Luftkrieg und Literatur and died in a car accident at fifty-seven.
entries.knownFor: The claim that the destruction of the German cities produced almost no adequate literature, and the prose works that circle the century's damage obliquely.
entries.signature: The signature is the digressive documentary manner — photographs, walks and reported testimony assembled so that the catastrophe is approached only from its edges.

entries.name: Isaac Babel
entries.description: The compressed atrocity vignette, by a writer the state that employed him later executed.
entries.meta: Soviet, 1894–1940. He rode with the First Cavalry Army in the Polish-Soviet war as a political journalist, and was arrested, tortured and shot in the Purges.
entries.knownFor: Конармия, and stories that deliver a massacre in two pages without commentary.
entries.signature: The signature is the beautiful sentence placed directly against the atrocity, so that the aesthetic pleasure and the horror arrive together and implicate the reader in both.

entries.name: Mikhail Sholokhov
entries.description: The Don Cossacks through revolution and civil war, in a Nobel-winning epic whose authorship was long disputed.
entries.meta: Soviet, 1905–1984. Nobel laureate in Literature in 1965; the authorship of his major novel was contested for decades, and the pack records the dispute rather than settling it.
entries.knownFor: Тихий Дон, and the rendering of a civil war in which the protagonist changes sides repeatedly.
entries.signature: The signature is the fratricidal structure — a community's men distributed across both sides so that every engagement is a family matter.

entries.name: Vasily Grossman
entries.description: The war correspondent who became the century's great novelist of totalitarian war, and whose manuscript was arrested.
entries.meta: Soviet, 1905–1964. Rejected for military service on medical grounds, he covered the war for Krasnaya Zvezda with an administrative commission rather than as a soldier — a distinction routinely mis-stated. The KGB seized the manuscript of his major novel in 1961.
entries.knownFor: Жизнь и судьба, completed in 1959 and published abroad in 1980, sixteen years after his death.
entries.signature: The signature is the equivalence structure — the two totalitarian systems rendered in parallel scenes at the same depth, which is what made the book unpublishable.

works.title: Жизнь и судьба
works.note: completed 1959; manuscript seized 1961; published in Switzerland

entries.name: Viktor Nekrasov
entries.description: The first honest Soviet Stalingrad novel, by an officer who was there and was later stripped of his citizenship.
entries.meta: Soviet-Ukrainian, 1911–1987. A combat engineer wounded at Stalingrad, awarded the Stalin Prize for 1946, and later expelled from the Party and deprived of Soviet citizenship.
entries.knownFor: В окопах Сталинграда, which established the trench-level register Soviet war fiction was not supposed to have.
entries.signature: The signature is the restricted junior-officer horizon — the battle known only as far as the next position, with the strategic account entirely absent.

entries.name: Viktor Astafyev
entries.description: The late, furious repudiation of the entire Soviet war myth, by a soldier who had spent decades inside it.
entries.meta: Russian, 1924–2001. He served as a private and was severely wounded, and published his angriest war novel in his late sixties as the Soviet Union collapsed.
entries.knownFor: Прокляты и убиты, and its account of the war's treatment of its own conscripts.
entries.signature: The signature is the unmediated fury — a prose that abandons the register of literary retrospection for something closer to accusation.

entries.name: Vasil Bykaŭ
entries.description: The moral-choice partisan novella, and the reprisal problem's canonical solution.
entries.meta: Belarusian, 1924–2003. An infantry officer wounded twice and once reported dead, he wrote in Belarusian and spent his last years in exile.
entries.knownFor: Сотнікаў, in which two captured partisans make opposite choices and the book refuses to award either.
entries.signature: The signature is the two-man moral experiment under conditions of no good option, with the cost always paid by civilians who were not consulted.

entries.name: Ales Adamovich
entries.description: The burned-villages testimony, and the documentary method a later Nobel laureate inherited.
entries.meta: Belarusian, 1927–1994. A partisan as a teenager, he assembled survivor testimony from the destroyed Belarusian villages into a form between document and literature.
entries.knownFor: Я з вогненнай вёскі, compiled with Janka Bryl and Uladzimir Kalesnik, and the screenplay work behind the period's most unsparing war film.
entries.signature: The signature is assembled testimony with the compiler's hand visible but not intrusive, which is the method Alexievich developed into a Nobel-winning form.

works.title: Я з вогненнай вёскі
works.note: with Janka Bryl and Uladzimir Kalesnik

entries.name: Lidiya Ginzburg
entries.description: The siege of Leningrad written as analysis rather than as lament.
entries.meta: Soviet, 1902–1990. A literary scholar who survived the siege and wrote about it in the third person, publishing the work four decades later.
entries.knownFor: Записки блокадного человека, and its refusal of the first person and of pathos.
entries.signature: The signature is the analytic distance — hunger and cold examined as changes in behaviour and cognition, in a register borrowed from criticism rather than from memoir.

entries.name: Svetlana Alexievich
entries.description: Polyphonic oral testimony developed into a literary form, and a Nobel awarded for it.
entries.meta: Belarusian, born 1948. Nobel laureate in Literature in 2015; her book on the Soviet war in Afghanistan drew litigation brought by mothers of dead soldiers, which is part of its record.
entries.knownFor: У войны не женское лицо, and the recovery of the Soviet war as women fought it.
entries.signature: The signature is the edited testimony sequence — hundreds of voices arranged so that the composition is the authorship, which is precisely what her critics have disputed.

entries.name: Victoria Amelina
entries.description: A novelist who became a war-crimes documenter and was killed by the war she was recording.
entries.meta: Ukrainian, 1986–2023. She was fatally wounded in the Russian missile strike on a Kramatorsk restaurant on 27 June 2023 and died on 1 July; at the time she was documenting alleged war crimes for a Ukrainian human-rights organisation. Stated here as biographical record.
entries.knownFor: Her fiction and her documentation work, and the unfinished book about Ukrainian women recording the war.
entries.signature: The signature is the writer-as-recorder position — the literary sensibility turned to evidence-gathering, and the resulting question of what the two forms owe each other.

works.title: Looking at Women Looking at War

entries.name: Ōoka Shōhei
entries.description: The Philippines campaign — capture, starvation, and the question the book will not look away from.
entries.meta: Japanese, 1909–1988. Conscripted at thirty-five, he was captured on Mindoro and held as a prisoner of war, and wrote both a captivity memoir and the novel that followed from it.
entries.knownFor: Nobi, in which a sick soldier is cut loose from any army and follows hunger to where it leads.
entries.signature: The signature is the first-person account whose reliability degrades with the narrator's body, so the reader cannot finally establish what was done.

entries.name: Ibuse Masuji
entries.description: Hiroshima rendered in the register of a village chronicle rather than of catastrophe.
entries.meta: Japanese, 1898–1993. He built the novel from survivors' diaries and documents, serialising it from January 1965.
entries.knownFor: Kuroi ame, and its account of radiation sickness as a social condition affecting marriage prospects and daily life.
entries.signature: The signature is the borrowed diary — documentary text quoted at length inside the novel, so that the fiction defers to the record at its worst moments.

works.title: Kuroi ame
works.note: serialised from January 1965; in book form 1966

entries.name: Hara Tamiki
entries.description: Hiroshima by a survivor who wrote it immediately and took his own life six years later.
entries.meta: Japanese, 1905–1951. He was in Hiroshima on the day, wrote the account within months, and died by suicide in 1951.
entries.knownFor: Natsu no hana, one of the earliest literary accounts of the bombing, delayed in publication by Occupation censorship.
entries.signature: The signature is the present-tense inventory — what is seen, in order, without the retrospective frame that would organise it into an account.

entries.name: Nosaka Akiyuki
entries.description: Two children starving after the firebombing of Kobe, written by a man who lost a sister that way.
entries.meta: Japanese, 1930–2015. He survived the Kobe raids as a teenager and his younger sister died of malnutrition; the story that followed took the Naoki Prize for the second half of 1967.
entries.knownFor: Hotaru no haka, and its refusal of any consolation for the deaths it opens by announcing.
entries.signature: The signature is the announced ending — the reader is told at once that both children die, so the narrative can proceed without suspense and without the possibility of rescue.

works.title: Hotaru no haka
works.note: Naoki Prize for the second half of 1967

entries.name: Kenzaburō Ōe
entries.description: Hiroshima and Okinawa as unfinished national arguments, defended by their author in court.
entries.meta: Japanese, 1935–2023. Nobel laureate in Literature in 1994; he was sued over Okinawa Notes by parties disputing its account of wartime mass suicides, and the case was decided in his favour.
entries.knownFor: Hiroshima Notes, and a career spent contesting Japan's settled version of its own war.
entries.signature: The signature is the reporting essay that refuses the correspondent's detachment — the writer's own moral position is part of the material rather than concealed behind it.

entries.name: Keiji Nakazawa
entries.description: Hiroshima drawn as manga, by a survivor who was six years old on the day.
entries.meta: Japanese, 1939–2012. He was in Hiroshima as a child and lost most of his family, and serialised the autobiographical manga from 1973.
entries.knownFor: Hadashi no Gen, which reached a mass readership including children and was translated worldwide.
entries.signature: The signature is the cartoon idiom applied without softening to the worst material, so that the visual conventions of children's comics carry documentary horror.

entries.name: Primo Levi
entries.description: The definitive account of the camps, and the concept of the grey zone that made complicity discussable.
entries.meta: Italian, 1919–1987. A chemist and briefly a partisan before his arrest and deportation to Auschwitz, he survived and wrote for forty years about it.
entries.knownFor: Se questo è un uomo, and the late essays that revised the survivor's authority downward.
entries.signature: The signature is analytic restraint — a scientist's exactness that lets the material speak without rhetoric, and a refusal to raise his voice that is itself the ethical form.

entries.name: Imre Kertész
entries.description: The camps narrated without retrospective knowledge, which is the formal achievement.
entries.meta: Hungarian, 1929–2016. Nobel laureate in Literature in 2002; deported to Auschwitz and Buchenwald at fourteen, he took thirteen years to write the novel and waited years for its reception.
entries.knownFor: Sorstalanság, and a narrator who reports his own deportation as a sequence of reasonable-seeming steps.
entries.signature: The signature is the withheld hindsight — the narrator is never granted knowledge he did not have at the time, which denies the reader the consolation of a survivor's wisdom.

works.title: Kaddis a meg nem született gyermekért

entries.name: Tadeusz Borowski
entries.description: The camps narrated by a complicit insider, in the flattest and most disturbing voice in the literature.
entries.meta: Polish, 1922–1951. Imprisoned at Auschwitz and Dachau, he wrote the stories immediately after the war and died by suicide at twenty-eight.
entries.knownFor: The Auschwitz stories, narrated by a functionary of the camp who is neither innocent nor apologetic.
entries.signature: The signature is the implicated narrator — a survivor who describes his own participation in the machinery in the same tone as everything else, refusing the reader a clean position.

entries.name: Jorge Semprún
entries.description: Buchenwald, and the twenty-year silence a survivor needed before he could write it.
entries.meta: Spanish-French, 1923–2011. A Spanish exile and French Resistance member deported to Buchenwald, he later served as Spain's culture minister.
entries.knownFor: Le Grand Voyage, and the later book explicitly about the choice between writing and living.
entries.signature: The signature is the deferred narration — the journey told across decades of returns, with the delay in the telling made part of what is being told.

entries.name: Hanna Krall
entries.description: The Warsaw Ghetto Uprising rendered as an interview with its surviving commander.
entries.meta: Polish, born 1935; some sources give 1937 and the pack records the discrepancy. A child survivor in hiding, she became a reporter and developed a documentary form of her own.
entries.knownFor: Zdążyć przed Panem Bogiem, built from conversations with Marek Edelman.
entries.signature: The signature is the interview as literary form — the subject's evasions, corrections and refusals left in place, so the reader watches testimony being produced.

works.title: Zdążyć przed Panem Bogiem i inne

entries.name: Jerzy Kosiński
entries.description: A widely read novel of a child in wartime Poland whose truth-claim and authorship are both publicly contested. Carded as contested; the pack states the dispute and adjudicates nothing.
entries.meta: Polish-American, 1933–1991. He won the National Book Award for Fiction in 1969 for Steps; from 1982 onward journalists disputed both the autobiographical status of his best-known novel and the extent of his authorship of his books, claims he and his defenders rejected. He died by suicide in 1991.
entries.knownFor: The Painted Bird, and the long argument about what kind of document it is.
entries.signature: The signature is the episodic atrocity sequence delivered in a detached child's register, a technique whose power is inseparable from the truth-claim the disputes concern.

entries.name: Bernhard Schlink
entries.description: The second-generation guilt novel, internationally successful and seriously contested.
entries.meta: German, born 1944. A law professor and judge as well as a novelist, he wrote the novel that became the standard second-generation text and the standard second-generation argument.
entries.knownFor: Der Vorleser, and the dispute over whether its central device functions as mitigation.
entries.signature: The signature is the legal frame applied to moral material — a narrator trained to weigh evidence, applying that training to a person he cannot judge and cannot stop judging.

entries.name: Vercors
entries.description: The clandestine novella of occupation, published in secret by a press its author co-founded.
entries.meta: French, 1902–1991. Born Jean Bruller, he wrote under a pen name and co-founded Éditions de Minuit to publish the book clandestinely under the occupation.
entries.knownFor: Le Silence de la mer, in which a household's refusal to speak to a billeted officer is the entire action.
entries.signature: The signature is the withheld voice — resistance rendered as an absence of speech, which makes the occupier's monologues the only sound in the book.

entries.name: Irène Némirovsky
entries.description: The occupation written as it happened, by a novelist who was murdered before she could finish it.
entries.meta: French, of Ukrainian-Jewish birth, 1903–1942. She wrote the first two parts in 1941–42 and was arrested and deported to Auschwitz, where she died; the manuscript was published in 2004.
entries.knownFor: Suite française, and its rendering of occupier and occupied at the same narrative depth.
entries.signature: The signature is the social panorama under invasion — class, property and manners persisting intact through catastrophe, observed without editorial.

works.title: Suite française
works.note: written 1941–1942; published from the manuscript sixty years later

entries.name: Curzio Malaparte
entries.description: The Eastern Front as baroque spectacle, from a witness whose unreliability is the card.
entries.meta: Italian, 1898–1957. Born Kurt Erich Suckert; an early fascist who was later imprisoned by the regime and then reported the Eastern Front, his accounts are widely regarded as partly invented and the pack states that rather than resolving it.
entries.knownFor: Kaputt, and set-pieces whose factual status has been disputed since publication.
entries.signature: The signature is the hallucinatory tableau — atrocity rendered as an aesthetic composition, which is either the book's method or its indictment depending on the reader.

entries.name: Beppe Fenoglio
entries.description: The partisan war without the Resistance myth, by a partisan who wrote it and did not publish it.
entries.meta: Italian, 1922–1963. He fought with the Badogliani partisans in the Langhe and died at forty with his major novel unpublished; it appeared posthumously in 1968.
entries.knownFor: Il partigiano Johnny, and its rendering of partisan warfare as cold, hungry and largely inconclusive.
entries.signature: The signature is the anglicised idiom — an Italian prose deliberately strained through English syntax, which estranges the national material it describes.

entries.name: Italo Calvino
entries.description: The partisan war seen by a child who understands none of it, written by a partisan at twenty-three.
entries.meta: Italian, 1923–1985. He fought with the partisans in Liguria and published his first novel two years after the war.
entries.knownFor: Il sentiero dei nidi di ragno, and a partisan band rendered without political idealisation.
entries.signature: The signature is the uncomprehending child's vantage — the war's politics are invisible to the narrator and therefore have to be assembled by the reader from behaviour alone.

works.title: Il sentiero dei nidi di ragno

entries.name: Bohumil Hrabal
entries.description: The resistance act performed by someone entirely unequipped for it.
entries.meta: Czech, 1914–1997. He worked through the occupation in a series of manual jobs and wrote the novella two decades later.
entries.knownFor: Ostře sledované vlaky, in which a sabotage operation is carried out by a young man preoccupied with something else entirely.
entries.signature: The signature is comic digression that turns lethal without changing register, so the heroic act arrives inside a story that was not about heroism.

entries.category: The Middle East and the Displacement Canon
entries.name: S. Yizhar
entries.description: The 1948 expulsion narrated by a soldier who took part, published within a year and contested ever since.
entries.meta: Israeli, 1916–2006. Born Yizhar Smilansky, he served in 1948 and published the novella the following year; it has been taught in Israeli schools and argued over continuously since.
entries.knownFor: חרבת חזעה, and a first-person account of an expulsion carried out by the narrator's own unit.
entries.signature: The signature is the participant-narrator who objects and complies, with the objection registered inside the action rather than after it.

works.title: חרבת חזעה
works.note: as S. Yizhar, a pen name

entries.category: The Middle East and the Displacement Canon
entries.name: Aharon Appelfeld
entries.description: Catastrophe rendered entirely by what is not said, across a body of work that never depicts the camps.
entries.meta: Israeli, 1932–2018. Born in Bukovina, he escaped a camp as a child and survived alone in the forests before reaching Palestine after the war.
entries.knownFor: באדנהיים עיר נופש, in which a resort's guests are administratively processed toward a destination the book never names.
entries.signature: The signature is the withheld referent — the machinery is described in full and its purpose never stated, so the reader supplies the knowledge the characters lack.

entries.category: The Middle East and the Displacement Canon
entries.name: David Grossman
entries.description: A mother who leaves home so that she cannot be told her son is dead, by a novelist whose own son was killed during the writing.
entries.meta: Israeli, born 1954. His son Uri was killed in Lebanon in 2006 while the novel was being written, a fact the book's reception has never been able to set aside; he received the International Booker Prize in 2017.
entries.knownFor: אישה בורחת מבשורה, and its premise of flight from notification.
entries.signature: The signature is the deferral structure — an entire novel spent avoiding a piece of information, so that the withholding is the plot rather than a technique inside it.

entries.category: The Middle East and the Displacement Canon
entries.name: Ghassan Kanafani
entries.description: The founding text of Palestinian displacement fiction, by a writer assassinated at thirty-six.
entries.meta: Palestinian, 1936–1972. A novelist, journalist and spokesman for the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine with no military service, he was killed by a car bomb in Beirut in 1972 along with his niece.
entries.knownFor: رجال في الشمس, and an ending that refuses the arrival the journey has been driving toward.
entries.signature: The signature is the withheld destination — displacement given no resolution, and a final question the text leaves standing rather than answering.

entries.category: The Middle East and the Displacement Canon
entries.name: Emile Habibi
entries.description: Satire as the only available register for a position with no other language for it.
entries.meta: Palestinian-Israeli, 1922–1996. He remained in Israel after 1948, served in the Knesset, and wrote in Arabic; his acceptance of an Israel Prize in 1992 was itself contested.
entries.knownFor: The Pessoptimist, and a coined word for a condition with no existing name.
entries.signature: The signature is the invented compound — a neologism carrying a whole political position, deployed inside a picaresque that keeps its footing by refusing seriousness.

works.title: الوقائع الغريبة في اختفاء سعيد أبي النحس المتشائل

entries.category: The Middle East and the Displacement Canon
entries.name: Elias Khoury
entries.description: Testimony that cannot be verified and must be told anyway, accumulated across a thousand nights.
entries.meta: Lebanese, 1948–2024. He fought in the Lebanese civil war as a young man and later edited literary journals in Beirut; he died in September 2024.
entries.knownFor: باب الشمس, built as an accumulation of tellings none of which can be confirmed.
entries.signature: The signature is the frame that never closes — a narrator telling stories to an unconscious man, with contradiction between versions left standing as the book's argument.

entries.category: The Middle East and the Displacement Canon
entries.name: Adania Shibli
entries.description: A 1949 incident and its contemporary investigation, in a novel whose German prize ceremony became a documented controversy.
entries.meta: Palestinian, born 1974. The award ceremony for her LiBeraturpreis at the 2023 Frankfurt Book Fair was postponed; the organiser's initial statement that it acted together with the author was subsequently corrected on its own site, and the author has said she was not consulted. Reported here as record.
entries.knownFor: تفصيل ثانوي, and its two-part structure setting a documented incident against a present-day attempt to research it.
entries.signature: The signature is the deliberate asymmetry — a flat, impersonal first part and an anxious first-person second, so that the investigating voice cannot reach the event it is investigating.

works.title: كلنا بعيد بذات المقدار عن الحب

entries.category: The Middle East and the Displacement Canon
entries.name: Sinan Antoon
entries.description: The corpse-washer as the occupation's only constant profession.
entries.meta: Iraqi, born 1967. He left Iraq after the 1991 war and writes in Arabic and English, translating his own work.
entries.knownFor: وحدها شجرة الرمان, narrated by a man who washes the dead of successive Iraqi wars.
entries.signature: The signature is the occupational vantage — a trade that continues through every regime change, so the political history arrives as a change in the volume of work.

entries.name: Chinua Achebe
entries.description: Biafra, from a writer who served the secessionist state as an envoy rather than a soldier.
entries.meta: Nigerian, 1930–2013. He acted as a diplomat and envoy for Biafra, with no military role, and waited four decades to write his account of the war.
entries.knownFor: Girls at War, and the late memoir There Was a Country.
entries.signature: The signature is the compressed story that refuses the epic scale the material invites, and a late nonfiction voice that declines to reconcile.

entries.name: Ken Saro-Wiwa
entries.description: The Nigerian civil war in an invented English, by a writer the state later executed.
entries.meta: Nigerian, 1941–1995. He served the federal side during the civil war as administrator of Bonny and later as a Rivers State commissioner — not, as is sometimes assumed, the Biafran side. He was executed by the Nigerian state in 1995 after a tribunal widely condemned internationally.
entries.knownFor: Sozaboy, subtitled a novel in rotten English, and its invented narrating idiom.
entries.signature: The signature is the constructed language — a deliberately unstable English built for a narrator who has no register in which to describe what happens to him.

entries.name: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie
entries.description: Biafra written by a novelist born seven years after it ended — the standing question's best modern test case.
entries.meta: Nigerian, born 1977. She built the novel from family testimony and research into a war she had not lived, and took the Orange Prize in 2007; the book was later named the Women's Prize Winner of Winners in 2020.
entries.knownFor: Half of a Yellow Sun, and a war carried through the collapse of intimate lives.
entries.signature: The signature is lucid realism used as a stance — clarity maintained deliberately against obscurity, so the horror registers through fully rendered character rather than through style.

entries.name: Ahmadou Kourouma
entries.description: The child soldier who narrates with four dictionaries open beside him.
entries.meta: Ivorian, 1927–2003. He served in the French colonial army before independence and wrote his late novels in exile; the child-soldier novel took the Prix Renaudot and the Prix Goncourt des lycéens in 2000.
entries.knownFor: Allah n'est pas obligé, and a narrating voice that keeps stopping to define its own words.
entries.signature: The signature is the unstable register — a child's French repeatedly interrupted by dictionary glosses, which refuses to be read as authenticity and makes the language itself the subject.

works.title: Allah n'est pas obligé
works.note: Prix Renaudot and Prix Goncourt des lycéens

works.title: En attendant le vote des bêtes sauvages

entries.name: Assia Djebar
entries.description: The Algerian war of independence recovered through women's voices and written in the coloniser's language.
entries.meta: Algerian, 1936–2015. Born Fatima-Zohra Imalayène, she wrote in French, made films in Arabic, and was elected to the Académie française in 2005.
entries.knownFor: L'Amour, la fantasia, which braids colonial military archives with contemporary women's testimony.
entries.signature: The signature is the interleaved archive — French conquest documents set directly against Algerian women's spoken accounts, so the two records interrogate each other on the page.

works.title: L'Amour, la fantasia
works.note: as Assia Djebar, a pen name

entries.name: Boubacar Boris Diop
entries.description: The Rwandan genocide written after a residency that sent African writers to the country to look.
entries.meta: Senegalese, born 1946. He took part in the Rwanda: écrire par devoir de mémoire project, which brought African writers to Rwanda in 1998, and later turned to writing in Wolof.
entries.knownFor: Murambi, le livre des ossements, and its distribution of narration across perpetrators, victims and returnees.
entries.signature: The signature is the refused single account — no narrator is allowed to stand as the event, and the perpetrator's chapters are given the same formal weight as the victims'.

entries.name: Scholastique Mukasonga
entries.description: The Rwandan genocide written by a woman who lost most of her family in it.
entries.meta: Rwandan-French, born 1956. She was exiled as a child and lost twenty-seven family members in 1994; she took the Prix Renaudot in 2012.
entries.knownFor: Notre-Dame du Nil, set in a girls' school in the years before the genocide, and the memoirs that preceded it.
entries.signature: The signature is the anticipatory setting — the machinery of the later catastrophe shown assembling inside an institution that believes itself ordinary.

entries.name: Abdulrazak Gurnah
entries.description: The German colonial wars in East Africa and their unrecorded conscripts, from a Nobel laureate.
entries.meta: Tanzanian-British, born 1948. He left Zanzibar as a refugee after the 1964 revolution and received the Nobel in Literature in 2021.
entries.knownFor: Afterlives, which follows an askari conscripted into the German colonial force, and Paradise.
entries.signature: The signature is the recovered minor life — colonial war narrated through people the imperial record counted but did not name.

entries.category: Asia: China, Korea, Vietnam and South Asia
entries.name: Lao She
entries.description: The occupation of Beijing across one courtyard's four generations, by a writer who died violently in the Cultural Revolution.
entries.meta: Chinese, 1899–1966. Born Shu Qingchun; he was publicly struggled against and beaten at the Temple of Confucius on 23 August 1966 and found dead in Taiping Lake the following day. The official account was suicide by drowning; murder has been argued in the scholarship and the question is unresolved.
entries.knownFor: 四世同堂, following one Beijing courtyard through eight years of Japanese occupation.
entries.signature: The signature is the domestic unit as the occupied nation — collaboration, resistance and survival distributed across one family so that every position is held by someone the reader knows.

entries.category: Asia: China, Korea, Vietnam and South Asia
entries.name: Eileen Chang
entries.description: Wartime Shanghai and Hong Kong, with occupation rendered as social atmosphere rather than as event.
entries.meta: Chinese, 1920–1995. Born Zhang Ailing, she wrote her best-known stories under the Japanese occupation of Shanghai and later emigrated to the United States, where she died alone in Los Angeles.
entries.knownFor: 傾城之戀, in which the fall of a city resolves a courtship, and the late espionage novella.
entries.signature: The signature is catastrophe as a social solvent — the war's function in the fiction is to rearrange the marriage market, which is a colder account than any battle scene.

entries.category: Asia: China, Korea, Vietnam and South Asia
entries.name: Mo Yan
entries.description: The anti-Japanese war stripped of its official heroic register, by a Nobel laureate who served in the army that maintained it.
entries.meta: Chinese, born 1955. He served in the People's Liberation Army and received the Nobel in Literature in 2012, an award that was itself contested on political grounds.
entries.knownFor: 红高粱家族, and a resistance war rendered through bandits, distillers and family grievance.
entries.signature: The signature is the sensory excess — colour, smell and appetite pushed past realism, so the official war narrative cannot survive contact with the prose.

entries.category: Asia: China, Korea, Vietnam and South Asia
entries.name: Ha Jin
entries.description: The Korean War prisoner-of-war camp from the Chinese side, written in English by a former soldier.
entries.meta: Chinese-American, born 1956. He served in the People's Liberation Army as a teenager, left China after 1989, and writes in English; he has twice received the PEN/Faulkner Award, in 2000 and 2005.
entries.knownFor: War Trash, a fictional memoir of a Chinese prisoner in a United Nations camp.
entries.signature: The signature is the plain second-language English — a deliberately unadorned prose that reads as translated testimony and refuses stylistic consolation.

entries.category: Asia: China, Korea, Vietnam and South Asia
entries.name: Park Wan-suh
entries.description: The Korean War as it happened to a girl and her mother in a Seoul that changed hands four times.
entries.meta: South Korean, 1931–2011. She lost her brother in the war and began publishing at forty, and returned to the same childhood material across four decades.
entries.knownFor: 나목, and the autobiographical novels of a family surviving successive occupations of one city.
entries.signature: The signature is the repeatedly revisited memory — the same months rewritten across a career, with each version admitting something the last could not.

works.title: 그 많던 싱아는 누가 다 먹었을까

entries.category: Asia: China, Korea, Vietnam and South Asia
entries.name: Han Kang
entries.description: The Gwangju massacre narrated from seven positions, one of them a corpse.
entries.meta: South Korean, born 1970. She was born in Gwangju and left months before the 1980 uprising; she received the Nobel in Literature in 2024.
entries.knownFor: 소년이 온다, and its rotating narration across victims, survivors and the dead.
entries.signature: The signature is the second-person address to the dead, which makes the reader occupy a position that cannot answer.

entries.category: Asia: China, Korea, Vietnam and South Asia
entries.name: Bảo Ninh
entries.description: The war told from the winning side as unbearable loss, and officially disfavoured for it.
entries.meta: Vietnamese, born 1952. He served with a North Vietnamese youth brigade; the widely repeated survival statistics attached to his unit originate in publishers' jacket copy and are not independently sourced, so the pack does not reproduce them.
entries.knownFor: Thân phận của tình yêu, published in Vietnam in 1990 and read internationally as the war's essential account.
entries.signature: The signature is the collapsed chronology — a veteran writing a novel he cannot order, with the disorder presented as the only honest sequence available to him.

entries.category: Asia: China, Korea, Vietnam and South Asia
entries.name: Viet Thanh Nguyen
entries.description: The double agent, and a sustained refusal of the American frame around a Vietnamese war.
entries.meta: Vietnamese-American, born 1971. He came to the United States as a child refugee and received the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 2016.
entries.knownFor: The Sympathizer, and the critical work on war memory that accompanies it.
entries.signature: The signature is the confession addressed to a captor — a narrator writing under duress for a reader who is also his interrogator, so every sentence is doing two jobs.

entries.category: Asia: China, Korea, Vietnam and South Asia
entries.name: Saadat Hasan Manto
entries.description: Partition in the shortest possible form, by a writer tried repeatedly for obscenity in both countries.
entries.meta: Indian and Pakistani, 1912–1955. He moved to Lahore after Partition and was prosecuted for obscenity six times, three times in each country, and died at forty-two.
entries.knownFor: The Partition stories, and sketches that deliver a communal killing in a few lines.
entries.signature: The signature is extreme compression — an entire atrocity in a paragraph, with the brevity refusing the reader time to arrange it into meaning.

entries.name: Tim O'Brien
entries.description: The writer who made the unauditability of testimony his subject rather than his problem.
entries.meta: American, born 1946. He was drafted and served as an infantryman in Quang Ngai province; he took the National Book Award in 1979 and the Pritzker Literature Award, a lifetime-achievement prize, in 2013. The Things They Carried was a Pulitzer finalist in 1991 and did not win, a distinction publishers' copy routinely erases.
entries.knownFor: The Things They Carried, and a career spent dismantling the difference between a true war story and a story that is true.
entries.signature: The signature is the self-revising story — an account told, retracted and retold inside the same book, so the reader cannot establish which version happened.

works.title: If I Die in a Combat Zone
In the Lake of the Woods

entries.name: Philip Caputo
entries.description: The memoir that opened the American reckoning with Vietnam, by a Marine officer who was there at the start.
entries.meta: American, 1941–2026. He died in May 2026; a Marine lieutenant in the first ground units committed in 1965, later a correspondent who shared a Pulitzer for reporting in 1972.
entries.knownFor: A Rumor of War, and its account of a war entered with conviction and left without it.
entries.signature: The signature is the officer's ledger — the book keeps count of what was believed on arrival against what remained, and charges the difference to the writer rather than to the war.

entries.name: Michael Herr
entries.description: Reportage written in a register borrowed from music, and the style that infected everything after it.
entries.meta: American, 1940–2016. He covered the war for a magazine, took a decade to finish the book, and later worked on the screenplays of two of the war's major films.
entries.knownFor: Dispatches, and the correspondent's compromised position rendered as the subject rather than concealed.
entries.signature: The signature is the first-person appetite — the writer's own attraction to the war is put on the page, which is what distinguishes the book from every account that claims detachment.

entries.name: Larry Heinemann
entries.description: The war narrated by the dead of a massacred platoon, in a book that won against expectation.
entries.meta: American, 1944–2019. He was drafted and served with an armoured cavalry unit, and took the National Book Award in 1987 for a novel whose win was widely disputed at the time.
entries.knownFor: Paco's Story, and a narrating voice belonging to men who did not survive.
entries.signature: The signature is the collective dead as narrator — a plural voice with no stake in consoling anyone, which relocates the trauma from the survivor into the telling.

entries.name: Gustav Hasford
entries.description: The training-to-Huế arc in a flat brutal idiom, by a Marine combat correspondent.
entries.meta: American, 1947–1993. He served as a Marine combat correspondent and died at forty-five; the novel's two-part structure became the template for the war's best-known film adaptation.
entries.knownFor: The Short-Timers, and a prose that refuses interiority almost entirely.
entries.signature: The signature is the collective register — an emotionally flattened first-person plural that absorbs individuals and registers their loss only as a change in the group's arithmetic.

entries.name: Karl Marlantes
entries.description: Thirty years of revision into the definitive small-unit novel of the war.
entries.meta: American, born 1944. A decorated Marine officer in Vietnam, he worked on the novel for roughly three decades before it found a publisher.
entries.knownFor: Matterhorn, and a hill taken, abandoned and retaken at a cost the book itemises.
entries.signature: The signature is procedural exactness carried to a moral end — the logistics, the radio traffic and the medical evacuation are rendered in full, and the arithmetic is what indicts.

works.title: What It Is Like to Go to War

entries.name: James Webb
entries.description: The platoon novel by a decorated Marine who later served as a senator.
entries.meta: American, born 1946. A Marine platoon and company commander in Vietnam, decorated for valour, later Secretary of the Navy and a United States senator.
entries.knownFor: Fields of Fire, and a novel written from inside the professional infantry's own values rather than against them.
entries.signature: The signature is the insider's defence — the book renders the war's cost without conceding the anti-war reading, which makes it the clearest available test of the pack's claim that both traps are live.

entries.name: Denis Johnson
entries.description: The intelligence war rendered as metaphysics, in a National Book Award-winning novel.
entries.meta: American, 1949–2017. He took the National Book Award in 2007 for a novel about the war's covert side, written by a novelist who had not served in it.
entries.knownFor: Tree of Smoke, and a psychological-operations campaign that consumes everyone attached to it.
entries.signature: The signature is the deliberately unstable frame — a novel that keeps changing what kind of book it is, which is its argument about an unwinnable and unlegible war.

entries.name: Kevin Powers
entries.description: The Iraq novel that found its shape in repetition and aftermath because the deployment supplied none.
entries.meta: American, born 1980. He served as a machine-gunner in Iraq in 2004–05 and published the novel seven years later; it took the Guardian First Book Award in 2012 and the PEN/Hemingway Award in 2013.
entries.knownFor: The Yellow Birds, and a structure organised around a promise the narrator cannot keep.
entries.signature: The signature is the recursive chapter order — the book returns to the same events at different distances, which enacts the intrusive recollection it describes.

works.title: Letter Composed During a Lull in the Fighting

entries.name: Phil Klay
entries.description: Twelve narrators doing twelve different jobs in the same war, and a National Book Award for the collection.
entries.meta: American, born 1983. He served as a Marine public affairs officer in Anbar province in 2007–08 — not as an infantryman, as is routinely stated — and took the National Book Award for Fiction in 2014.
entries.knownFor: Redeployment, and the distribution of one war across mortuary affairs, artillery, chaplaincy, public affairs and civil affairs.
entries.signature: The signature is the occupational voice — each story built from the vocabulary and moral frame of a specific job, so the war is assembled from positions rather than described from one.

entries.name: Elliot Ackerman
entries.description: The war narrated from the other side of it, by a decorated American veteran.
entries.meta: American, born 1980. A Marine officer with multiple tours in Iraq and Afghanistan; his first novel is narrated by an Afghan fighter.
entries.knownFor: Green on Blue, and the deliberate inversion of the vantage his own service would have supplied.
entries.signature: The signature is the refused home vantage — the American position is offstage throughout, which exposes how total its usual centrality is.

entries.name: Ben Fountain
entries.description: The war metabolised by American spectacle, across a single afternoon at a football game.
entries.meta: American, born 1958. A non-veteran novelist who took the National Book Critics Circle Award in 2012 for a novel set entirely at home.
entries.knownFor: Billy Lynn's Long Halftime Walk, and its compression of a war's reception into one halftime show.
entries.signature: The signature is the unbroken present tense inside a public event, so that every civilian encounter is rendered at the speed the soldier has to process it.

entries.name: Siobhan Fallon
entries.description: The war from the married quarters, and the best single answer this canon offers to the home-front problem.
entries.meta: American; her birth year is not established in published sources and the pack does not supply one. She lived at Fort Hood during her husband's two deployments to Iraq and wrote the stories from that position.
entries.knownFor: You Know When the Men Are Gone, a linked collection set almost entirely on the domestic side of a deployment.
entries.signature: The signature is the base as a closed society — a community with its own hierarchy, surveillance and etiquette, rendered with the specificity usually reserved for the unit.

works.title: You Know When the Men Are Gone

entries.name: Bernard Cornwell
entries.description: The Napoleonic military-adventure series as an industrial form, and the tradition's dominant modern practitioner.
entries.meta: British, born 1944. He has written the Napoleonic sequence and several other long series continuously since 1981.
entries.knownFor: The Sharpe novels, and battle rendered from the ranks with unusual technical clarity.
entries.signature: The signature is the ranker's-eye set-piece — the engagement delivered at the level of the firing line, with the serial protagonist's guaranteed survival held in visible tension against it.

entries.name: George MacDonald Fraser
entries.description: The coward-protagonist as a formal solution to the problem of serial survival.
entries.meta: British, 1925–2008. He served in Burma with the Border Regiment and later wrote both the comic series and a plain memoir of that campaign.
entries.knownFor: The Flashman novels, and a protagonist who is a bully, a coward and a liar decorated for accidents.
entries.signature: The signature is the disreputable narrator inside meticulous research — the history is accurate and the witness is contemptible, which lets the books mock the heroic register without abandoning the period.

entries.name: Patrick O'Brian
entries.description: Technical competence rendered as literary pleasure, across twenty novels of one war at sea.
entries.meta: British, 1914–2000. Born Richard Patrick Russ; he changed his name and constructed a personal history that was substantially revised by biographers after his death.
entries.knownFor: The Aubrey-Maturin sequence, and seamanship so precise it functions as characterisation.
entries.signature: The signature is the unglossed technical vocabulary — the reader is trusted to sail on partial understanding, so expertise reads as lived competence rather than instruction.

works.title: The Far Side of the World

entries.name: Alistair MacLean
entries.description: The wartime adventure at its most efficient, and one grim Arctic convoy novel that is not an adventure at all.
entries.meta: British, 1922–1987. He served in the Royal Navy on Arctic and Far East convoys, and drew directly on that service for his first novel.
entries.knownFor: HMS Ulysses, and The Guns of Navarone.
entries.signature: The signature is the attrition novel disguised as an adventure — the first book kills its cast systematically in conditions the author had served in, and the later ones do not.

entries.name: Sven Hassel
entries.description: Enormously popular penal-battalion novels whose author's claimed war service is disputed by researchers. Carded as contested.
entries.meta: Danish, 1917–2012. His account of service in a German penal battalion on the Eastern Front has been challenged by researchers and defended by his family and publishers; the pack states the dispute and adjudicates nothing.
entries.knownFor: The Legion of the Damned sequence, which sold in enormous numbers across Europe.
entries.signature: The signature is relentless episodic brutality with a fixed cast, delivered at a pace that converts atrocity into serial incident — which makes the books the pack's clearest study of consumption as a failure mode.

entries.name: Michael Shaara
entries.description: Gettysburg from four commanders, and a Pulitzer that reshaped the American battle novel.
entries.meta: American, 1928–1988. He served as a sergeant in the 82nd Airborne before the Korean War and saw no combat, contrary to frequent statements; the novel took the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 1975.
entries.knownFor: The Killer Angels, and command-level interiority applied to a documented engagement.
entries.signature: The signature is the dual-command structure — the battle given from both sides at the same depth, with each commander held inside his own information horizon.

entries.name: Tom Clancy
entries.description: The technothriller as a genre and as an argument about defence procurement.
entries.meta: American, 1947–2013. An insurance broker when his first novel was published by a naval institute press, he built the form that dominated the commercial market for two decades.
entries.knownFor: The Hunt for Red October, and a body of work in which the accurate operation of military systems is the pleasure on offer.
entries.signature: The signature is the competence sequence — a system explained while it is used, with the reader placed at the console and never under the ordnance.

entries.name: John Hackett
entries.description: The future-war scenario written by a general, and the canonical dated-prediction case.
entries.meta: British, 1910–1997. A general who commanded at Arnhem and later commanded the British Army of the Rhine, he wrote the scenario with a group of serving and retired officers.
entries.knownFor: The Third World War: August 1985, presented as a plausible extrapolation and now readable as a document of its own assumptions.
entries.signature: The signature is the retrospective future — the book is written as history from beyond its own war, which is what makes its overtaking by events legible as evidence rather than as failure.

entries.name: John Keegan
entries.description: The battle rewritten from the soldier's eye level, and the founding text of this pack's specialist collection.
entries.meta: British, 1934–2012. Prevented by childhood illness from serving, he taught at Sandhurst for twenty-six years and never saw combat, a fact he addressed directly in his own work.
entries.knownFor: The Face of Battle, and its reconstruction of Agincourt, Waterloo and the Somme from the position of the men in them.
entries.signature: The signature is the comparative method — the same questions put to three battles five centuries apart, which converts military history into a study of what combat does to people.

entries.name: S. L. A. Marshall
entries.description: The author of the most-repeated claim in war-writing advice, and of the most substantially disputed one. Carded as contested.
entries.meta: American, 1900–1977. He was commissioned in early 1919, after the Armistice; his ratio-of-fire finding has been challenged on methodological grounds by Roger Spiller and others, and independently tested against Canadian records by Robert Engen. Elements of his own service account have been separately disputed in both directions. The pack states the dispute and adopts no position.
entries.knownFor: Men Against Fire, and the claim that only a small minority of infantrymen fired their weapons.
entries.signature: The signature is the post-combat group interview, which was a real methodological contribution whatever the status of the number it produced.

entries.name: Paul Fussell
entries.description: The criticism that made irony the war's default mode, by a wounded infantry officer.
entries.meta: American, 1924–2012. He was severely wounded as an infantry lieutenant in France in 1945; his study of the First World War's literary memory won the inaugural National Book Critics Circle Award for Criticism, for 1975.
entries.knownFor: The Great War and Modern Memory, and the argument that the war permanently installed irony as the mode of modern memory.
entries.signature: The signature is the literary-critical method applied to soldiers' writing, with the critic's own combat experience admitted into the argument rather than suppressed.

works.title: The Great War and Modern Memory
works.note: nonfiction; NBCC Award for Criticism for 1975

entries.name: Jonathan Shay
entries.description: Moral injury identified through the Iliad, by a clinician working with Vietnam veterans.
entries.meta: American, born 1941. A psychiatrist who worked with Vietnam veterans for decades and read their accounts against Homer.
entries.knownFor: Achilles in Vietnam, and the location of a distinct injury in betrayal of what is right by a legitimate authority.
entries.signature: The signature is the classical text used as clinical instrument — the Iliad read as an accurate account of combat psychology rather than as a literary antecedent.

entries.name: Susan Sontag
entries.description: The ethics of looking at atrocity images, argued twice and differently by the same writer.
entries.meta: American, 1933–2004. Her late book on war photography revises the position she had taken on the same question a quarter of a century earlier.
entries.knownFor: Regarding the Pain of Others, and its account of what looking at images of suffering does and does not accomplish.
entries.signature: The signature is the public self-revision — a critic returning to her own earlier argument and dismantling it, which models the practice the pack asks of its readers.

entries.category: Foundations and the Long Nineteenth Century
entries.name: Iliad
entries.author: Homer
entries.awards: None (predates any prize culture; verified negative by date).
entries.description: The founding war narrative of the Western tradition, and the origin of the interiority problem this pack is organised around: the poem repeatedly…
entries.text: The founding war narrative of the Western tradition, and the origin of the interiority problem this pack is organised around: the poem repeatedly gives the man about to be killed a father, a city and a history, spending its attention on the enemy at exactly the moment the form has least reason to. It also establishes the conventions later war fiction is still arguing with — the catalogue of warriors, the single combat as decisive event, and the lament as the closing register. Carded as long-form verse narrative under the schema's convention for pre-novel material.

entries.category: Foundations and the Long Nineteenth Century
entries.name: History of the Peloponnesian War
entries.author: Thucydides
entries.awards: None (predates any prize culture; verified negative by date).
entries.description: A war history built with the resources of tragedy, by a general who had been relieved for failure and wrote the war he had lost part of. Its…
entries.text: A war history built with the resources of tragedy, by a general who had been relieved for failure and wrote the war he had lost part of. Its composed speeches are a fictional technique inside a work claiming the authority of record, which makes it the earliest sustained instance of the problem the pack's fourth diagnostic question puts to the memoir-novel. The Melian Dialogue remains the reference text for what power says when it has stopped pretending.

entries.category: Foundations and the Long Nineteenth Century
entries.name: Anabasis
entries.author: Xenophon
entries.awards: None (predates any prize culture; verified negative by date).
entries.description: The earliest sustained small-unit account in the tradition: ten thousand mercenaries stranded in hostile country, electing commanders and marching…
entries.text: The earliest sustained small-unit account in the tradition: ten thousand mercenaries stranded in hostile country, electing commanders and marching out. Its subject is logistics and cohesion rather than battle — food, distance, water, and whether the men will follow — which makes it the ancestor of the retreat narrative and of every fiction in which the unit's survival rather than its victory is the plot. Written in the third person under another name.

entries.category: Foundations and the Long Nineteenth Century
entries.name: La Chartreuse de Parme
entries.author: Stendhal
entries.awards: None (predates the French literary prizes; verified negative by date).
entries.description: The Waterloo sequence is the founding scene of the legibility problem: a young man crosses a battlefield and cannot afterwards establish whether he…
entries.text: The Waterloo sequence is the founding scene of the legibility problem: a young man crosses a battlefield and cannot afterwards establish whether he was in the battle. The episode withholds every orientation the reader expects — no map, no overview, no explanation of what the events he witnesses have to do with one another — and it does so a century before industrial war made the technique unavoidable. Everything the genre later discovered about rendering combat from inside is already available here.

entries.category: Foundations and the Long Nineteenth Century
entries.name: Война и мир
entries.author: Leo Tolstoy
entries.awards: None (predates the Russian and international literary prizes; verified negative by date).
entries.description: The nineteenth century's largest argument that battles are not commanded and history is not steered, made structurally rather than stated: the same…
entries.text: The nineteenth century's largest argument that battles are not commanded and history is not steered, made structurally rather than stated: the same events are rendered at staff level and at the level of the man in the line, and the two accounts are left conspicuously unreconciled. Its permanent status as a boundary case is the point — the historical-fiction pack cards it for its claim about the past, and this pack cards it for the best account in the canon of the gap between a battle as experienced and a battle as narrated afterwards.

entries.category: Foundations and the Long Nineteenth Century
entries.name: La Débâcle
entries.author: Émile Zola
entries.awards: None (predates the Prix Goncourt, first awarded 1903; verified negative by date).
entries.description: Sedan rendered as the decomposition of an organism: an army disintegrating through hunger, rumour, exhaustion and administrative failure long before…
entries.text: Sedan rendered as the decomposition of an organism: an army disintegrating through hunger, rumour, exhaustion and administrative failure long before it is defeated in the field. The naturalist method turns out to suit military collapse exactly, because it treats the army as a system with material inputs rather than as a moral agent, and the result is the nineteenth century's most clinical account of how a force stops functioning.

entries.category: Foundations and the Long Nineteenth Century
entries.name: Tales of Soldiers and Civilians
entries.author: Ambrose Bierce
entries.awards: None (predates the American literary prizes; verified negative by date).
entries.description: Short stories built as machines for destroying consolation, by a man who fought at Shiloh and Chickamauga and was severely wounded at Kennesaw…
entries.text: Short stories built as machines for destroying consolation, by a man who fought at Shiloh and Chickamauga and was severely wounded at Kennesaw Mountain. The characteristic construction is a final sentence that retrospectively removes whatever meaning the reader has been assembling, which makes the collection the earliest systematic refusal of the redemptive reading in American war writing. Carded as a story collection under the schema's convention for long-form written fiction.

entries.category: Foundations and the Long Nineteenth Century
entries.name: The Red Badge of Courage
entries.author: Stephen Crane
entries.awards: None (predates the Pulitzer Prize, first awarded 1917; verified negative by date).
entries.description: The American canon's founding combat novel, written by a man born after the war it describes and before he had witnessed any fighting at all — which…
entries.text: The American canon's founding combat novel, written by a man born after the war it describes and before he had witnessed any fighting at all — which makes it the permanent counter-example in the standing dispute. Its achievement is sustained restriction to one frightened consciousness that never learns what happened, with the prose declining every opportunity to explain the day to a reader who wants it explained.

entries.name: Le Feu
entries.author: Henri Barbusse
entries.awards: Prix Goncourt, 1916.
entries.description: The first major combatant novel of the war, written from the line and from hospital and awarded the Goncourt while the fighting had two years to…
entries.text: The first major combatant novel of the war, written from the line and from hospital and awarded the Goncourt while the fighting had two years to run. Its method is the squad as a collective voice speaking its own vernacular, with narration distributed across the group rather than centred on a protagonist — a structural choice that makes the book an argument about class as well as about the war.

entries.name: Im Westen nichts Neues
entries.author: Erich Maria Remarque
entries.awards: None among the major literary prizes (verified negative); banned and publicly burned in Germany from 1933, and the author was later deprived of German citizenship.
entries.description: The definitive statement that the patriotic war novel was no longer writable, and the genre's first global bestseller. Its method is the flat…
entries.text: The definitive statement that the patriotic war novel was no longer writable, and the genre's first global bestseller. Its method is the flat declarative sentence applied to atrocity, with the withholding of commentary doing the moral work rhetoric would have undone. Note that the author's own front-line service was roughly six weeks before he was wounded — a fact the popular account of the book consistently overstates, and one that makes the achievement a matter of construction rather than of transcription.

entries.name: In Stahlgewittern
entries.author: Ernst Jünger
entries.awards: None among the major literary prizes (verified negative).
entries.description: The same war as Remarque's, rendered as an experience with value and without repentance, by a much-decorated storm-troop officer who revised the…
entries.text: The same war as Remarque's, rendered as an experience with value and without repentance, by a much-decorated storm-troop officer who revised the text across six decades. The pack cards it because its existence is a fact about the genre: precise observational description without moral framing produces a book that readers have used to argue both for and against war for a century, and the craft is identical to the craft of the books that reach the opposite conclusion. Carded as autobiographical narrative under the schema's convention.

entries.name: Osudy dobrého vojáka Švejka
entries.author: Jaroslav Hašek
entries.awards: None among the major literary prizes (verified negative).
entries.description: The founding text of the satiric war novel, left unfinished at its author's death four volumes in. Its formal principle is the digression that never…
entries.text: The founding text of the satiric war novel, left unfinished at its author's death four volumes in. Its formal principle is the digression that never returns — an anecdote inside an anecdote inside an order — which enacts the bureaucracy it describes rather than describing it. The protagonist's apparent idiocy is a structural position rather than a character trait: it is the only sane response available to a system that cannot be argued with.

entries.name: Der Streit um den Sergeanten Grischa
entries.author: Arnold Zweig
entries.awards: None among the major literary prizes (verified negative).
entries.description: An army's judicial machinery executes a man everyone involved knows to be innocent, and the novel shows every stage functioning correctly. Military…
entries.text: An army's judicial machinery executes a man everyone involved knows to be innocent, and the novel shows every stage functioning correctly. Military justice turns out to be the war's clearest self-portrait: the horror is procedural rather than malicious, and no individual in the chain does anything a reasonable officer would not have done. It is the earliest major treatment of the theme the pack's specialist collection handles as the exemplary punishment.

entries.name: Krieg
entries.author: Ludwig Renn
entries.awards: None among the major literary prizes (verified negative).
entries.description: The war rendered in a deliberately affectless register that refuses both heroism and protest: events reported in sequence at uniform emphasis, so…
entries.text: The war rendered in a deliberately affectless register that refuses both heroism and protest: events reported in sequence at uniform emphasis, so that every judgement is supplied by the reader rather than the text. Published under a pen name taken from the novel's own narrator, which the author then adopted as his own name — an unusually literal instance of the war memoir's identity problem.

entries.name: Un anno sull'Altipiano
entries.author: Emilio Lussu
entries.awards: None among the major literary prizes (verified negative).
entries.description: The Alpine front, written in exile by an officer of the Sassari Brigade, in which the book's real antagonist is the Italian command. Its method is…
entries.text: The Alpine front, written in exile by an officer of the Sassari Brigade, in which the book's real antagonist is the Italian command. Its method is dry comic understatement applied to lethal incompetence, which makes the arithmetic of impossible attacks legible without editorialising it — the closest thing in the First World War canon to a systematic study of how orders that cannot be obeyed are nevertheless issued and executed.

entries.name: The Middle Parts of Fortune
entries.author: Frederic Manning
entries.awards: None among the major literary prizes (verified negative).
entries.description: The ranker's war in the ranker's language, published anonymously and available for forty years only in an expurgated text that removed the speech…
entries.text: The ranker's war in the ranker's language, published anonymously and available for forty years only in an expurgated text that removed the speech the book exists to record. Its achievement is the unit as a working household — food, shelter, rank and obligation negotiated continuously — and its author wrote as a private in the ranks, not as an officer, which is the fact the whole book depends on.

entries.name: Parade's End
entries.author: Ford Madox Ford
entries.awards: None among the major literary prizes (verified negative).
entries.description: The war placed inside a modernist consciousness rather than reported from a trench, across four novels published between 1924 and 1928. Shell shock…
entries.text: The war placed inside a modernist consciousness rather than reported from a trench, across four novels published between 1924 and 1928. Shell shock is rendered from inside the syntax — the prose fractures where the mind does, using interruption and time-shift so that the technique carries the diagnosis. It is the strongest available demonstration that formal difficulty in war writing can be a clinical instrument rather than an ornament.

entries.name: Goodbye to All That
entries.author: Robert Graves
entries.awards: None among the major literary prizes (verified negative).
entries.description: A memoir constructed as the demolition of an entire culture, with school, regiment, family and war presented as one continuous system of absurdity…
entries.text: A memoir constructed as the demolition of an entire culture, with school, regiment, family and war presented as one continuous system of absurdity and the tone kept dry throughout. The title's finality was literal: the author left England after publication and did not return to live there. Its influence on the war memoir is larger than that of any book that takes the war more solemnly.

entries.name: Voyage au bout de la nuit
entries.author: Louis-Ferdinand Céline
entries.awards: None among the major literary prizes (verified negative); the Prix Goncourt of 1932 went elsewhere, which was itself a public controversy.
entries.description: The war as the founding disgust of a whole prose style, rendered in spoken-language syntax with ellipsis and interruption. Its opening war sequence…
entries.text: The war as the founding disgust of a whole prose style, rendered in spoken-language syntax with ellipsis and interruption. Its opening war sequence is among the most corrosive in the canon and its narrator's contempt extends to himself. The author subsequently wrote antisemitic pamphlets, collaborated, fled France in 1944 and was convicted in absentia before an amnesty; the pack states that record plainly, cards the work's craft, and adjudicates nothing.

entries.name: The Backwash of War
entries.author: Ellen N. La Motte
entries.awards: None among the major literary prizes (verified negative); suppressed in Britain and France during the war, which is the more significant fact about its reception.
entries.description: Nurse's sketches from a French field hospital so unsparing that both Allied governments banned the book until the war was over. The form is the…
entries.text: Nurse's sketches from a French field hospital so unsparing that both Allied governments banned the book until the war was over. The form is the clinical vignette without a frame: short pieces that end exactly where the material stops, with no closing gesture toward meaning. It is the earliest instance in this pack's canon of a war book suppressed not for revealing secrets but for refusing consolation.

entries.name: The Forbidden Zone
entries.author: Mary Borden
entries.awards: None among the major literary prizes (verified negative).
entries.description: Field-hospital prose written by a woman who financed and directed a mobile surgical unit on the French front, and formally the most radical war book…
entries.text: Field-hospital prose written by a woman who financed and directed a mobile surgical unit on the French front, and formally the most radical war book of its decade. It abandons narrative shape entirely for the ward's own rhythm — sketches, prose poems and dialogues assembled without connective tissue — which renders triage as a form rather than as a scene. Written during the war and not published for a decade.

entries.name: Testament of Youth
entries.author: Vera Brittain
entries.awards: None among the major literary prizes (verified negative).
entries.description: The war as bereavement, from the position of the woman who survives everyone: a nursing volunteer who lost her fiancé, her brother and two close…
entries.text: The war as bereavement, from the position of the woman who survives everyone: a nursing volunteer who lost her fiancé, her brother and two close friends. The book's structure is the repeated arrival of notification, and its power is in the repetition rather than in any single death — which makes it the canon's central document of the civilian side of loss, and the clearest demonstration that the home front's material is duration rather than event.

entries.name: The Return of the Soldier
entries.author: Rebecca West
entries.awards: None among the major literary prizes (verified negative).
entries.description: Shell shock seen entirely from the household, published while the war was still being fought. The war never appears; the whole condition is rendered…
entries.text: Shell shock seen entirely from the household, published while the war was still being fought. The war never appears; the whole condition is rendered through three women's competing claims on one damaged man, and the novel's cruellest question is whether curing him is a kindness. It is the earliest major treatment of the return, and it arrives before the war it is the aftermath of has ended.

entries.name: Not So Quiet… Stepdaughters of War
entries.author: Evadne Price
entries.awards: No award record established; recorded as a documentation gap rather than a verified negative.
entries.description: Commissioned as a parody of Remarque and delivered instead as the ambulance driver's war, published under a pseudonym. Its method is sustained…
entries.text: Commissioned as a parody of Remarque and delivered instead as the ambulance driver's war, published under a pseudonym. Its method is sustained second-person address in the present tense, which puts the reader in the ambulance and denies the retrospective distance the memoir tradition assumes. The author's own biography is itself a case in the pack's verification discipline: the widely repeated birth year and the claim of birth at sea originate with her and are reproduced in standard reference works.

entries.name: One of Ours
entries.author: Willa Cather
entries.awards: Pulitzer Prize for the Novel, 1923 (the category was named "Novel" until 1948).
